evidence.explanation: A physical association between presenilin-1 and the cardiac SERCA isoform, demonstrated in explanted human myocardium, which is the mechanistic reason calcium handling rather than amyloid is the proposed route. Graded IN_VITRO because a co-immunoprecipitation is a biochemical assay on tissue lysate, not a clinical observation.

evidence.snippet: We also showed that oligomers alter myocyte Ca(2+) homeostasis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that a calcium-handling defect is achievable in cardiomyocytes in this disease context. INDIRECT because the perturbation is a protein oligomer applied to cultured myocytes, not a PSEN1 variant, so it supports the plausibility of the node rather than the PSEN1 route to it.

steps/1.description:
The proposed effector step: disturbed intracellular calcium regulation in the cardiomyocyte. Two separate observations point at it, and neither was made in a cardiomyocyte carrying the CMD1U allele.
First, cultured skin fibroblasts from PSEN1 and PSEN2 mutation carriers in the founding families showed altered calcium signalling. Fibroblasts are an accessible surrogate, not a contractile cell, and the paper reports the abnormality without asserting a myocardial equivalent.
Second, presenilin-1 co-immunoprecipitates with SERCA2a, the cardiac sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium ATPase, in explanted idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy hearts. That is a physical association in human myocardium and is the most cardiac-specific molecular result in this literature. It is an interaction, not a rate: no measurement of SERCA2a activity in a PSEN1-variant heart exists, so the node carries no direction. The biological process below is tagged DYSREGULATED rather than INCREASED or DECREASED for that reason - the sources say "altered", and choosing a direction would be an invention.

evidence.snippet: PSEN1 knockout in adults led to decreased muscle fibers, widened sarcomere Z lines and reduced lengths of sarcomeres in cardiomyocytes.
evidence.explanation: The ultrastructural phenotype of adult cardiac Psen1 deletion in mouse, which is the whole basis for this node.

evidence.snippet: Cardiovascular loss of function of PSEN1 induced by Sm22a-Cre or Myh6-Cre/ER/tamoxifen also resulted in severe ultrastructural abnormalities, such as relaxed gap junctions between neighboring cardiomyocytes.
evidence.explanation: The intercalated-disc component of the same murine phenotype, obtained with cardiovascular- and cardiomyocyte-restricted deletion.

evidence.snippet: However, the function and mechanism of PSEN1 in cardiomyopathy remains unresolved.
evidence.explanation: The same authors' own statement of what was unresolved when they began, quoted so this node is not read as a mechanism for the human disease. NO_EVIDENCE because the sentence reports the absence of a settled mechanism rather than an experimental result for or against one.

steps/2.description:
A structural cardiomyocyte lesion reported only in mice. Deleting Psen1 from the murine cardiovascular system produces fewer muscle fibres, widened sarcomeric Z-lines, shortened sarcomeres and loosened gap junctions between neighbouring cardiomyocytes, and complete Psen1 nullity causes perinatal death with ventricular dilatation and septal defects.
This node is kept separate from the calcium node and outside the disease's main causal chain on purpose. Every observation behind it comes from deleting the gene, and CMD1U is a heterozygous missense allele of unknown functional consequence. A knockout phenotype tells you what presenilin-1 does in the mouse heart; it does not tell you what Asp333Gly does in a human one, and the authors of that work say the mechanism of PSEN1 in cardiomyopathy remains unresolved. No downstream edge is drawn from it into the human chain for that reason.

evidence.snippet: Our review revealed consensus on several key aspects: the definition of DCM, the use of B-type natriuretic peptides and high-sensitivity troponin in laboratory testing, the essential role of multimodality cardiovascular imaging for initial diagnosis, genetic counselling, and the management of advanced disease.
evidence.explanation: Cited to anchor the node in the recognised disease class rather than to make a mechanistic claim: a systematic review of dilated-cardiomyopathy guidelines reports cross-guideline consensus on the disease definition and on the imaging that establishes it, which is what this node names. INDIRECT because it is about dilated cardiomyopathy generally, not remodeling in a PSEN1 carrier - of which nothing has been reported.

steps/3.description: Adverse structural remodeling of the left ventricle - chamber dilatation with wall thinning - as the shared final common path of the cardiomyopathies. Nothing in the CMD1U literature characterises remodeling in a PSEN1 carrier heart specifically: there is no histology, no fibrosis quantification, and no imaging series. The node is curated because the reported clinical phenotype is dilated cardiomyopathy and this is the step that word names, and it conforms to the shared module rather than claiming disease-specific detail.

evidence.snippet: The PSEN1 mutation was associated with complete penetrance and progressive disease that resulted in the necessity of cardiac transplantation or in death.
evidence.explanation: The observed clinical endpoint in the index family.

steps/4.description: Falling ejection fraction and clinical heart failure, progressing in the reported family to transplantation or death. This is the clinical endpoint of the entity and the only part of the chain observed directly in CMD1U patients.

edges/0.description: The proposed first step. Its support is calcium signalling measured in cultured skin fibroblasts from carriers, not in cardiomyocytes, so the intermediates between the variant and a myocardial calcium defect are unknown.

edges/1.description: Impaired excitation-contraction coupling as a chronic cardiomyocyte insult driving adverse remodeling. This edge is the general cardiomyopathy chain rather than a CMD1U-specific finding; nothing in the PSEN1 literature measures it.

edges/2.description: Chamber dilatation with impaired contraction is by definition the dilated cardiomyopathy phenotype and the substrate for progressive pump failure.

evidence.snippet: PSEN1 | HGNC:9508 | dilated cardiomyopathy 1U | MONDO:0013371 | AD | Disputed | SOP10 | Dilated Cardiomyopathy Gene Curation Expert Panel
evidence.explanation: The current expert-panel classification row, curated against this exact MONDO term. This is the single most important item in the entry for anyone interpreting a PSEN1 variant in a cardiomyopathy patient.

evidence.snippet: Therefore, there is no scorable human genetic evidence.
evidence.explanation: The panel's conclusion about the genetic evidence specifically, and the reason relationship_type is DISPUTED rather than CAUSATIVE.

evidence.snippet: In summary, the evidence presented for this gene-disease relationship does not provide convincing human genetic evidence in support of or refuting the role of PSEN1 and DCM.
evidence.explanation: Quoted so the Disputed classification is not read as stronger than the source supports. The panel explicitly declines to rule the relationship out, which is why this entry curates the locus rather than proposing it be discarded.

evidence.snippet: A total of 315 index patients with DCM were evaluated for sequence variation in PSEN1 and PSEN2.
evidence.explanation: The screen that produced the original gene-disease claim, and the whole of its human genetic evidence base.

evidence.snippet: The mutation was found in an African family in which one family member had AD, while the other six affected relatives were diagnosed with an aggressive heart disorder
evidence.explanation: A later review's description of the index family, showing that the cardiac and the Alzheimer phenotypes were reported in different members of the same pedigree. That co-occurrence is the historical reason PSEN1 was screened in cardiomyopathy at all, and it is also the reason the two literatures are easy to conflate.

genes/0.notes: A separate candidate-gene association study reported a common PSEN1 SNP, rs177415, associated with dilated cardiomyopathy susceptibility in a 282-case, 306-control sample with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.30. It is not curated as a genetic record here. A single small unreplicated candidate-gene association is a different kind of claim from a monogenic locus, the effect size is at the edge of significance, and folding it in would make the CMD1U evidence base look broader than it is. It is recorded in a discussion instead.

evidence.snippet: The recommendations present an evidence-based approach to managing patients with heart failure, with the intent to improve quality of care and align with patients' interests.
evidence.explanation: The guideline this treatment defers to. INDIRECT because it is written for heart failure as a whole and says nothing about PSEN1 - which is the point: no PSEN1-specific regimen exists, so the general pathway is the treatment.

treatments/0.description:
Management of CMD1U is management of dilated cardiomyopathy: there is no PSEN1-directed therapy, no trial in this population, and no reason to expect genotype-specific treatment while the genotype-phenotype relationship itself is disputed. Treatment follows the contemporary heart-failure pathway, which acts on the remodeling and pump-failure end of the chain rather than on any presenilin lesion.
The agents listed below are the standard classes of guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, recorded so the treatment is queryable by drug identity. They are not a CMD1U-specific regimen and no source names them for this locus. Beta-blockers belong in the same list but are not recorded as a therapeutic_agent, because the NCI Thesaurus build configured here has no drug-class term for them that could be verified.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Acts on the clinical endpoint, not on the proposed molecular mechanism. Nothing in the standard regimen targets presenilin-1 or the calcium node above it.

evidence.snippet: The PSEN1 mutation was associated with complete penetrance and progressive disease that resulted in the necessity of cardiac transplantation or in death.
evidence.explanation: Records that transplantation was the outcome in the index family, which is the only treatment observation that exists for this locus.

treatments/1.description: The endpoint intervention for refractory disease, and one that was actually reached in the reported family: the founding paper describes progressive disease resulting in the necessity of cardiac transplantation or in death.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Replaces the failing organ; it does not address the proposed mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Provide a basic view of genetic risk assessment of at-risk asymptomatic relatives of a proband with DCM to inform cardiac surveillance and allow early detection and treatment of DCM to improve long-term outcome.
evidence.explanation: The rationale for surveillance of at-risk relatives, stated by GeneReviews as one of the purposes of its dilated-cardiomyopathy overview: early detection before symptoms so treatment can start sooner.

evidence.snippet: Therefore, there is no scorable human genetic evidence.
evidence.explanation: The basis for declining to recommend genotype-directed surveillance on a PSEN1 result. Surveillance driven by family history is unaffected by this.

treatments/2.description:
Serial cardiac assessment of first-degree relatives of an affected proband. For a late-onset cardiomyopathy this is the intervention with the clearest rationale, because it detects dilatation before symptoms.
Whether surveillance should be triggered by a PSEN1 variant specifically is a different question and this entry answers it no: with the relationship Disputed, a PSEN1 result is not a basis for genotype-directed surveillance. Clinical surveillance of relatives of an affected proband stands on the family history regardless of genotype.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Detects remodeling early rather than modifying it; the benefit comes from starting heart-failure therapy before decompensation.

evidence.snippet: Nonetheless, notable areas of variation included the formation of multidisciplinary management teams, the role of cascade genetic testing, pathways for arrhythmic risk stratification, and the criteria for prophylactic defibrillator implantation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that prophylactic defibrillator criteria are contested across dilated-cardiomyopathy guidelines, which is why this entry records the intervention without asserting a threshold. INDIRECT because the review addresses dilated cardiomyopathy as a class, not this locus.

treatments/3.description:
Device therapy for the arrhythmic risk that accompanies a dilated, poorly contracting ventricle. It is included because it is part of dilated-cardiomyopathy management and because the guidelines disagree about it: a 2025 systematic review found the criteria for prophylactic defibrillator implantation to be one of the areas where dilated-cardiomyopathy guidelines vary, along with arrhythmic risk stratification generally.
Nothing about a PSEN1 result should shift that decision in either direction. There is no reported arrhythmic phenotype for this locus and, with the gene-disease relationship disputed, no basis for treating a PSEN1 variant as the kind of high-risk genotype - LMNA, FLNC, RBM20 - that does modify defibrillator thresholds.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Treats the arrhythmic consequence of the failing, dilated ventricle. It modifies neither the remodeling nor anything upstream of it.

evidence.snippet: DCM may not be related to impaired APP cleavage by gamma secretase, suggesting that PSEN1 (and PSEN2) could impact heart failure through an amyloid-independent mechanism
evidence.explanation: A review's statement of the amyloid-independent framing this hypothesis adopts, and the reason the neuronal amyloid literature is excluded from the entry.

evidence.snippet: PSEN1 D333G was transfected into HEK293 cells but did not result in an alteration in the Ab42/Ab40 ratio.
evidence.explanation: The experimental result behind that framing: the CMD1U allele itself does not shift the amyloid-beta ratio in a heterologous cell line, which is a negative result against an amyloidogenic mechanism rather than positive evidence for a calcium one.

evidence.snippet: Aβ level was tested by immunohistochemistry in our samples and no difference in Aβ expression was present in iDCM compared to controls.
evidence.explanation: The second negative result against an amyloid mechanism, and the one made in the right tissue: amyloid-beta was measured in human dilated-cardiomyopathy myocardium and did not differ from controls. Supports this hypothesis by eliminating its competitor rather than by demonstrating calcium involvement.

evidence.snippet: This gene-disease assertion is supported by expression studies
evidence.explanation: The expert panel's account of what does survive: expression work, which is where the myocardial presenilin-1 and SERCA2a results sit. Quoted to show this hypothesis rests on the only evidence class ClinGen credits, not on the genetic evidence it discounts.

hypotheses/0.description:
The only mechanistic model proposed for CMD1U: a PSEN1 variant perturbs presenilin-1 in the cardiomyocyte, which disturbs sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium handling - plausibly through the presenilin-1/SERCA2a association - and the resulting excitation-contraction defect drives dilatation and pump failure.
It is recorded as ALTERNATIVE, not CANONICAL, because the disease it explains is itself disputed. Two supports exist and both fall short of the claim: carrier calcium signalling was measured in skin fibroblasts, and the PSEN1/SERCA2a co-immunoprecipitation came from idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy hearts carrying promoter variants rather than the CMD1U allele. No cardiomyocyte carrying Asp333Gly has ever been studied.
The model is nevertheless worth keeping, because it is amyloid-independent and is stated as such in the sources. That distinguishes it from the neuronal PSEN1 literature and makes it falsifiable: an isogenic D333G human iPSC-cardiomyocyte line with calcium-transient and SERCA2a-activity readouts would settle it in either direction.

evidence.snippet: Evidence of the association of this gene with DCM was re-evaluated using SOP v10 on May 29th, 2025As a result, the classification did not change.
evidence.explanation: Shows the Disputed verdict survived a fresh review rather than being a stale 2020 call. The sentence is quoted as it appears in the ClinGen record, including the missing sentence break after the date.

evidence.snippet: Unconditional logistic regression adjusting for type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, cigarette smoking, and gender, confirmed the association between that SNP rs177415 of the presenilin-1 gene and the susceptibility of DCM (adjusted OR 1.300, 95% CI 1.013-1.669; P = 0.039).
evidence.explanation: The one other line of human evidence connecting PSEN1 to dilated cardiomyopathy, quoted so the effect size and the p-value are visible. INDIRECT because a common-variant susceptibility signal of this size is a different claim from a monogenic locus and cannot settle the controversy in either direction.

open_questions/0.rationale:
Twenty years after the founding report there is still one family, one paper, and no independent pedigree. ClinGen's expert panel has now looked at the evidence three times - 2020, 2025, 2026 - and each time called it Disputed, on the ground that the reported disease-causing variants are too common in population data to be monogenic causes.
The counter-argument is not nothing. The panel explicitly says its evidence neither supports nor refutes the relationship, and the founding pedigree's segregation was real. Absence of replication in a locus nobody has looked for since is weak evidence of absence.
This is recorded as an open controversy rather than resolved in either direction because the deciding experiment - a modern population-frequency and case-control reassessment of PSEN1 in a large dilated-cardiomyopathy cohort, or a cardiomyocyte model of Asp333Gly - has not been done. It matters practically: it determines whether PSEN1 belongs on a dilated-cardiomyopathy panel.

evidence.snippet: Calcium signaling was altered in cultured skin fibroblasts from PSEN1 and PSEN2 mutation carriers.
evidence.explanation: Names the tissue in which the carrier calcium phenotype was actually observed, which is the mismatch this discussion is about.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in ubiquitously expressed presenilin genes (PSENs) lead to early-onset familial Alzheimer's disease (FAD), but patients carrying the mutation also suffer from heart diseases.
evidence.explanation: Establishes what this study's donors were: patients with an Alzheimer-causing PSEN1 allele. Quoted here rather than a result sentence because the allele is the whole reason the study narrows this mismatch without closing it.

open_questions/1.rationale:
Every piece of evidence for the calcium mechanism comes from the wrong cell, the wrong genotype, or both. Carrier calcium signalling was measured in cultured skin fibroblasts, which are not contractile and do not use SERCA2a. The presenilin-1/SERCA2a co-immunoprecipitation was done in myocardium from sporadic idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy patients carrying promoter variants, not the CMD1U allele. The oligomer calcium experiment perturbed cardiomyocytes with protein oligomers rather than with a PSEN1 variant. And the mouse work deletes the gene rather than introducing the missense allele, and yields a diastolic, small-ventricle phenotype rather than a dilated one.
One study comes close and is worth being precise about. PSEN1 delta-exon-9 patient iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, compared against isogenic controls, show a sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium leak - the right cell type, a clean genetic comparison, and a dissected mechanism. But delta-exon-9 is a familial Alzheimer disease allele, not Asp333Gly, and the donors were dementia patients. It therefore narrows the mismatch rather than resolving it: a PSEN1 variant can disturb calcium in a human cardiomyocyte, which was not previously shown, but nothing says this variant does.
This is a HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH rather than a plain knowledge gap because the evidence is not absent - five distinct experimental results exist and each is internally sound. What is missing is any demonstration that they compose into the human disease mechanism in the relevant cell and genotype.

evidence.snippet: This report suggests an expansion of the phenotypic spectrum associated with PSEN1 variants and highlights the need for further investigation of potential cardiac manifestations in PSEN1 variant carriers.
evidence.explanation: The report's own claim, quoted to show what it does and does not establish. INDIRECT because the phenotype is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in a carrier of a different variant, so it speaks to the breadth of PSEN1 cardiac claims rather than to CMD1U.

open_questions/2.rationale:
A 2026 case report describes a heterozygous PSEN1 variant in a man with nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and later ventricular fibrillation, framed by its authors as expanding the cardiac phenotype of PSEN1. That is a different variant and a different cardiomyopathy - hypertrophic, not dilated - so it is no evidence for CMD1U and is not curated as such.
It is recorded because it bears on how the whole PSEN1 cardiac literature should be read. When single case reports attach a gene to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, dilated cardiomyopathy, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy exome cohorts in turn, each on tiny numbers, the pattern is more consistent with a much-sequenced gene accruing incidental variants than with a coherent cardiac disease entity. That reading is the same one ClinGen's population-frequency argument arrives at from a different direction.

evidence.snippet: This positively charged residue, when mutated in other small heat-shock proteins, results in various human disorders.
evidence.explanation: Supports treating the K141 position, rather than HSPB8 dosage generally, as the lesion this entry starts from.

evidence.snippet: Mice expressing mutant Hspb8 (Lys141Asn) mimic the human disease, whereas mice lacking Hspb8 show no overt phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates that a null allele does not recapitulate the disease, supporting the gain-of-function interpretation over haploinsufficiency. The K141N knock-in model reproduces the human phenotype while the knockout does not.

steps/1.description: Heterozygous missense substitution of the K141 lysine in the alpha-crystallin domain of HSPB8. The two reported founding alleles, K141N and K141E, change the same positively charged residue, which is required for the structural and functional integrity of small heat shock proteins of this family.

evidence.snippet: Coimmunoprecipitation experiments showed greater binding of both HSPB8 mutants to the interacting partner HSPB1.
evidence.explanation: The measurement that defines this node.

steps/2.description: Both K141 mutants coimmunoprecipitate more of the partner small heat shock protein HSPB1 than wild-type HSPB8 does, indicating an abnormally avid rather than an absent chaperone interaction.

evidence.snippet: Stv and its mammalian ortholog BAG-3 coordinate the activity of Hsc70 and the small heat shock protein HspB8 during disposal that is initiated by the chaperone-associated ubiquitin ligase CHIP and the autophagic ubiquitin adaptor p62.
evidence.explanation: Establishes HSPB8's normal role in the CASA pathway, which is what a hot-spot variant in that protein puts at risk.

evidence.snippet: BAG3-HSPB8 is a sub-complex at the basis of a larger protein complex, known as the chaperone-assisted-selective-autophagy (CASA) complex.
evidence.explanation: Names HSPB8 and BAG3 as the core of the CASA complex, supporting the identity of the pathway curated at this node.

steps/3.description: HSPB8 works with the co-chaperone BAG3 as the sub-complex at the base of chaperone-assisted selective autophagy (CASA), which disposes of damaged and misfolded clients through Hsc70, the ubiquitin ligase CHIP and the autophagy adaptor p62. Disturbance of this complex is the proteostatic failure curated as the cellular lesion of dHMN2A. Note that the CASA machinery is characterised in muscle and in BAG3-mutant cell models rather than in K141-HSPB8 motor neurons.

evidence.snippet: Expression of mutant HSPB8 in cultured cells promoted formation of intracellular aggregates.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates aggregate formation as a consequence of the causal variants.

evidence.snippet: These include disruption of axonal transport, RNA processing defects, protein aggregation and inclusion body formation, disrupted calcium channel activity, and loss of neuroprotective signalling.
evidence.explanation: Places protein aggregation among the established pathogenic mechanisms of dHMN, supporting the node's relevance to this disease group rather than only to a transfected cell line.

steps/4.description: Expression of mutant HSPB8 promotes formation of intracellular aggregates in cultured cells. Protein aggregation and inclusion body formation is one of the recurring pathogenic mechanisms of the distal hereditary motor neuropathies as a group.

evidence.snippet: The distal hereditary motor neuropathies (dHMN) comprise a heterogeneous group of diseases that share the common feature of a length-dependent predominantly motor neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: Supports the length-dependent, predominantly motor character of the lesion curated at this node.

steps/5.description: Degeneration of the distal portions of the longest lower motor neuron axons, which is the lesion shared across the distal hereditary motor neuropathies and the reason weakness begins in the feet and progresses proximally.

evidence.snippet: slowly progressive length-dependent distal muscle weakness and atrophy, without sensory involvement
evidence.explanation: States the weakness, its distribution and its slowly progressive course.

steps/6.description: Slowly progressive, length-dependent weakness of distal limb muscles, the defining clinical feature of the distal hereditary motor neuropathies.

evidence.snippet: Distal hereditary motor neuropathies are pure motor disorders of the peripheral nervous system resulting in severe atrophy and wasting of distal limb muscles.
evidence.explanation: Describes the distal wasting that this phenotype records, in the paper that reports the HSPB8 families.

steps/7.description: Severe atrophy and wasting of distal limb muscles secondary to chronic denervation.

evidence.snippet: Coimmunoprecipitation experiments showed greater binding of both HSPB8 mutants to the interacting partner HSPB1.
evidence.explanation: Directly measures the altered interaction as a consequence of the two hot-spot substitutions, which is the edge asserted here.

edges/1.description: The substituted residue changes how mutant HSPB8 engages its partner small heat shock protein.

edges/2.description: Curated as the mechanistic link between the altered small heat shock protein interaction and the CASA pathway that HSPB8 serves. The sources here establish HSPB8's role in that pathway and the mutants' altered binding; they do not measure CASA flux in K141 HSPB8 motor neurons, so the edge is marked indirect.

evidence.snippet: mutant BAG3 trapped ubiquitinylated client proteins at the aggresome, preventing their efficient clearance
evidence.explanation: Shows the same CASA sub-complex failing to clear its ubiquitinated clients and those clients accumulating, which is the step this edge asserts. The lesion measured is in BAG3 rather than HSPB8, so this is support for the pathway step, not for the HSPB8 allele.

edges/3.description: Failure to clear misfolded clients leaves them to accumulate as aggregates.

evidence.snippet: In motor neurons, expression of both HSPB8 K141N and K141E mutations clearly resulted in neurite degeneration, as manifested by a reduction in number of neurites per cell, as well as in a reduction in average length of the neurites.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the K141 mutant allele causes neurite loss in cultured motor neurons, which is the degeneration this edge asserts. Aggregation is the curated but unmeasured intermediate — the paper does not measure aggregates as the intervening step, which is why this edge carries INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES and this item is graded INDIRECT.

evidence.snippet: While overt in motor neurons, these phenotypes were only very mildly present in sensory neurons and completely absent in cortical neurons.
evidence.explanation: Establishes cell-type selectivity: the degeneration is motor-neuron-specific, with sensory neurons only mildly affected and cortical neurons spared. The paper's own conclusion is selectivity rather than length-dependence.

evidence.snippet: We did not detect any signs of apoptosis in motor neurons, showing that mutant HSPB8 resulted in neurite degeneration without inducing neuronal death.
evidence.explanation: Constrains what this node asserts: the lesion is neurite degeneration, not death of the motor neuron. Cuts against reading the paper as demonstrating loss of the cell body.

edges/4.description: Mutant HSPB8 expression causes neurite degeneration in motor neurons. Cell-type selectivity studies establish that this phenotype is motor-neuron-specific. The length-dependent distal distribution is curator inference from the clinical pattern of the disease, not a finding of the cited cell-culture work.

evidence.snippet: Hereditary motor neuropathies (HMN) were first defined as a group of neuromuscular disorders characterized by lower motor neuron dysfunction, slowly progressive length-dependent distal muscle weakness and atrophy, without sensory involvement.
evidence.explanation: States lower motor neuron dysfunction and length-dependent distal weakness as one clinical entity, which is the edge drawn here.

evidence.snippet: Distal hereditary motor neuropathies are pure motor disorders of the peripheral nervous system resulting in severe atrophy and wasting of distal limb muscles.
evidence.explanation: Attributes the distal muscle atrophy to the motor neuropathy itself.

evidence.snippet: We found a second mutation (K141E) in two smaller families. Both mutations target the same amino acid, which is essential to the structural and functional integrity of the small heat-shock protein alphaA-crystallin.
evidence.explanation: Names the second allele at the same codon and states why that residue matters structurally, supporting a hot-spot rather than a scattered loss-of-function variant spectrum.

evidence.snippet: The causative genes have implicated proteins with diverse functions such as protein misfolding (HSPB1, HSPB8, BSCL2), RNA metabolism (IGHMBP2, SETX, GARS), axonal transport (HSPB1, DYNC1H1, DCTN1) and cation-channel dysfunction (ATP7A and TRPV4) in motor-nerve disease.
evidence.explanation: Places HSPB8 in the protein-misfolding class of dHMN genes, which is the mechanistic class this entry curates.

evidence.snippet: WES and tNGS identified a heterozygous change in HSPB8 in both families: c.421A > G p.K141E in family 1 and c.151insC p.P173SfsX43 in family 2.
evidence.explanation: Documents an HSPB8 allele outside the K141 hot-spot and reports it beside K141E, supporting the allelic axis recorded in the variant list rather than a single-hot-spot variant spectrum.

treatments/0.description: There is no disease-modifying therapy for dHMN2A. Management is supportive: physiotherapy, orthotic management of foot drop, and maintenance of mobility and function. This entry records the treatment category rather than a specific validated regimen because no trial evidence exists for this subtype in the sources curated here.

treatments/1.description: Exercise and stretching to preserve range of movement and delay contracture in the distal limbs.

treatments/2.description: Counseling for an autosomal dominant disorder with a 50% recurrence risk for the offspring of an affected individual, and predictive testing where the familial HSPB8 variant is known.

evidence.snippet: Biosensor interaction analyses revealed loss of binding to BMPR1A and BMPR1B ectodomains for the L441P mutant
evidence.explanation: Identifies the initiating molecular lesion of the du Pan GDF5 allele as failure to engage the type I receptor ectodomains.

evidence.snippet: The binding to NOGGIN was normal for both mutants.
evidence.explanation: Antagonist binding is preserved, so the lesion is specifically at the receptor interface rather than a general loss of ligand folding or of partner interactions.

evidence.snippet: The majority of patients with these disorders have biallelic loss-of-function mutations of GDF5.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic GDF5 loss of function as the commonest route into the disorder.

evidence.snippet: ACD cannot only be caused by GDF5 mutations, but in rare cases also by loss-of-function BMPR1B mutations.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the receptor as the alternative locus for the same disorder.

steps/2.description: The initiating lesion is a partial, not complete, loss of function in either half of the GDF5-BMPR1B ligand-receptor pair. Reported du Pan alleles are missense changes that leave a folded protein with reduced activity rather than truncating alleles that remove it.

evidence.snippet: GDF5 belongs to the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) family and binds to the BMP receptors BMPR1A and BMPR1B, with a preference for BMPR1B
evidence.explanation: Establishes the ligand-receptor relationship this node represents.

evidence.snippet: The phenotypic severity gradient of the clinically and radiologically related acromesomelic chondrodysplasia spectrum of skeletal disorders may be due to the extent of functional impairment of the ligand-receptor pair GDF5-BMPR1B.
evidence.explanation: States the dose-response model in which du Pan syndrome occupies the high-residual-signalling end.

evidence.snippet: SMAD1/5/8 phosphorylation in nascent human mesenchymal stem cells (HMSCs) was stimulated weakly by rhGDF5 but strongly by rhBMP7.
evidence.explanation: Establishes SMAD1/5/8 phosphorylation as the transducer engaged by GDF5 in a human chondrogenic system, which is the basis for annotating SMAD signalling on this node. Support is partial, and deliberately so: GDF5's own SMAD stimulation is reported as weak, so SMAD phosphorylation may not be the whole of how GDF5 acts here.

steps/3.description: GDF5 signals through BMPR1B, its preferred type I receptor. In du Pan syndrome this signalling is reduced but retained, which is the proposed explanation for why the same pathway lesion yields a mild rather than a devastating limb phenotype. This is a quantitative, dose-dependent claim about a normally regulated pathway, not a qualitative escape from regulation.

evidence.snippet: The patient showed skeletal malformation of both hands and feet that included complex brachydactyly with the thumbs most severely affected, postaxial polydactyly of both hands, shortened toes as well as a bilateral hypoplasia of the fibula.
evidence.explanation: Documents the bilateral hand-and-foot malformation bundle with fibular hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: All affected individuals showed either reductions or absence of bones in the limbs, and appendicular bone dysmorphogenesis with unaffected axial bones.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that the lesion is appendicular and spares the axial skeleton.

steps/4.description: The output is a hand-and-foot malformation bundle - complex brachydactyly with hypoplastic or absent phalanges and metacarpals, and short deviated toes - accompanied by fibular hypoplasia, on a background of normal or near-normal stature. The bilateral hand-plus-foot pattern is the serially homologous signature of a limb patterning lesion.

evidence.snippet: p.(Arg31Cys) mutation causing du Pan dysplasia leads to a significant loss of BMPR1B function, but to a lesser extent than the previously reported p.Cys53Arg mutation
evidence.explanation: Reporter assays show a graded, partial reduction of receptor function.

edges/2.description: A hypomorphic allele in ligand or receptor directly lowers, without abolishing, signalling through the pair.

evidence.snippet: Our patient shows du Pan dysplasia with a mild phenotype. He has a normal height as well as no short femur, tibia, humerus, ulna or radius.
evidence.explanation: Documents preserved long-bone growth alongside the distal malformation.

edges/3.description: Retained signalling permits the skeletal elements to form and grow, so the deficit is confined to the most signal-dependent structures of the distal limb and the fibula.

evidence.snippet: Affected individuals were homozygous for a missense mutation, T1322C, in the coding region of the CDMP1 gene.
evidence.explanation: Establishes GDF5 as a cause of du Pan syndrome.

evidence.snippet: The T1322C change predicts a leu441pro substitution in the mature domain of the CDMP1 protein.
evidence.explanation: Localises the allele to the mature domain of the ligand.

evidence.snippet: Biosensor interaction analyses revealed loss of binding to BMPR1A and BMPR1B ectodomains for the L441P mutant
evidence.explanation: Direct binding measurement identifies the molecular defect of the du Pan GDF5 allele as loss of type I receptor engagement rather than a non-specific conformational change.

evidence.snippet: They cause brachydactyly type A2 (L441P) and symphalangism (R438L)
evidence.explanation: The same p.Leu441Pro allele produces brachydactyly type A2 in the heterozygous state, establishing the dosage relationship with homozygous du Pan syndrome.

evidence.snippet: We show that the homozygous c.91C>T, p.(Arg31Cys) mutation causing du Pan dysplasia leads to a significant loss of BMPR1B function, but to a lesser extent than the previously reported p.Cys53Arg mutation that results in the more severe Grebe dysplasia.
evidence.explanation: Functional assays quantify the du Pan allele as hypomorphic relative to the Grebe-causing allele in the same gene.

evidence.snippet: The analysis identified the biallelic variant NM_001203.3:c.821A > G;p.(Gln274Arg) in BMPR1B, a gene encoding bone morphogenetic protein receptor 1B.
evidence.explanation: Adds a second reported BMPR1B allele causing du Pan dysplasia.

evidence.snippet: GDF5 (NM_000557.5) sequencing identified a homozygous pathogenic variant c.1322T>C, p.(Leu441Pro) in the fetus and confirmed the carrier status in the mother.
evidence.explanation: Documents molecular confirmation of carrier status in a family, the step on which recurrence-risk counselling depends.

evidence.snippet: Three new heterozygous mutations clustered on one allele of the CDMP1 gene were identified in the affected individuals resulting in the first familial case with dominant Du Pan syndrome.
evidence.explanation: The dominantly transmitted kindred is the reason recurrence-risk counselling here has to follow the molecular result rather than an assumed recessive model.

treatments/0.description: Counselling for an autosomal recessive disorder, with the added complication that the causative GDF5 allele is not silent in carriers: p.Leu441Pro heterozygous causes brachydactyly type A2, so a "carrier" parent may have a visible hand phenotype of their own. One kindred also transmits the disorder dominantly through three cis variants on a single allele, which changes the recurrence risk entirely and is why counselling should follow the family's molecular result rather than the diagnosis label.

evidence.snippet: leads to a significant loss of BMPR1B function, but to a lesser extent than the previously reported p.Cys53Arg mutation that results in the more severe Grebe dysplasia
evidence.explanation: Two alleles of one gene ranked by residual function match the severity order of the two diagnoses.

evidence.snippet: They cause brachydactyly type A2 (L441P) and symphalangism (R438L)
evidence.explanation: Supplies the allele-dose half of the model: the du Pan GDF5 allele in one copy gives an isolated brachydactyly.

hypotheses/0.description: The acromesomelic GDF5-BMPR1B disorders are one mechanism read at different doses. How much signalling an allele leaves, rather than which of the two genes it hits, determines whether the result is du Pan syndrome, Grebe dysplasia, or in the heterozygous state a brachydactyly. The strongest test is within BMPR1B, where the du Pan allele p.Arg31Cys and the Grebe allele p.Cys53Arg were assayed side by side and ranked in the order the phenotypes predict. The same logic holds for GDF5 p.Leu441Pro, which gives brachydactyly type A2 heterozygous and du Pan syndrome homozygous.

evidence.snippet: whereas the R438L mutant showed normal binding to BMPR1B but increased binding to BMPR1A, the receptor normally activated by BMP2
evidence.explanation: Documents an allele that changes receptor preference rather than overall binding strength.

evidence.snippet: the symphalangism phenotype (R438L) is caused by a loss of receptor-binding specificity, resulting in a gain of function by the acquisition of BMP2-like properties
evidence.explanation: States the specificity mechanism explicitly, as an alternative to a purely quantitative account of GDF5 allele effects.

hypotheses/1.description: A competing reading of the same interface data is that what matters is not only how much receptor binding an allele leaves, but which receptor it binds. GDF5 p.Arg438Leu, one residue away from the du Pan allele, keeps normal BMPR1B binding but gains BMPR1A binding and causes symphalangism, a joint-fusion phenotype rather than a hypoplasia. On this view the du Pan and Grebe alleles sit at the loss end of a two-dimensional space whose other axis is receptor choice, and a purely quantitative dose model cannot predict the phenotype of an allele that redistributes binding rather than reducing it. This has not been tested against any acromesomelic allele.

open_questions/0.rationale: The treatments section is deliberately limited to genetic counselling, which is the one intervention the published literature for this disorder actually documents. Reconstructive and orthopaedic surgery, prosthetics, and physiotherapy are all plausible for a limb malformation of this severity and are presumably used in practice, but a search of the indexed literature returned no disease-specific management report for du Pan syndrome to cite. Curating them from general skeletal-dysplasia practice would be inference, not evidence, so the gap is recorded rather than filled. A case series reporting functional outcomes after surgical or prosthetic management would close it.

evidence.snippet: Our case expands the phenotypical overlap between the different ACD types, du Pan and Grebe.
evidence.explanation: The authors frame their finding as widening, not narrowing, the phenotypic overlap.

open_questions/1.rationale: Polydactyly was the last candidate discriminator and it fell in 2024, when a BMPR1B case was reported with bilateral postaxial polydactyly. With so few published cases in either group, no feature is currently established as gene-specific, which is why this entry curates both aetiologies under one disease concept rather than splitting them.

open_questions/2.rationale: A single Polish family transmits du Pan syndrome dominantly through one allele carrying three variants in the mature domain. The synergy is inferred from the pedigree, not measured, and no second dominant family has been reported in the twenty years since. Until it is functionally tested, this entry records the dominant inheritance block as an explicit exception rather than as an alternative mode of inheritance.

evidence.snippet: Similar to the molecular pathology of SDS, mutant EFL1 proteins do not promote the release of cytoplasmic Tif6 from the 60S subunit, likely preventing the formation of mature ribosomes.
evidence.explanation: Functional studies in the discovery paper support impaired EIF6/Tif6 release as the proximal defect in EFL1-related SDS.

evidence.snippet: Cellular defects in these individuals include impaired ribosomal subunit joining and attenuated global protein translation as a consequence of defective eIF6 eviction.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived cellular studies directly show that defective EIF6 eviction disrupts ribosomal subunit joining in EFL1-related disease.

steps/1.description: EFL1 encodes the elongation factor-like GTPase that cooperates with SBDS in the final cytoplasmic maturation step of the 60S ribosomal subunit. Disease variants impair EIF6 eviction from pre-60S particles, blocking normal late ribosomal large-subunit maturation.

evidence.snippet: Here we present 3 unrelated Korean SDS patients who carry biallelic pathogenic variants in EFL1 with biased allele frequencies, resulting from a bone marrow-specific somatic uniparental disomy in chromosome 15.
evidence.explanation: This establishes the phenomenon as bone marrow-specific somatic UPD in patients with biallelic germline EFL1 disease.

evidence.snippet: The loss of EFL1 resulted in a pronounced inhibition of terminal oligopyrimidine element-containing ribosomal protein transcript 80S assembly.
evidence.explanation: The clonal shift is partial rescue, not correction of the underlying ribosome-assembly defect.

steps/2.description: Bone marrow-restricted somatic uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 can skew EFL1 allele balance toward a relatively milder pathogenic allele. This is a somatic hematopoietic adaptation rather than a germline causal gene item, and the rescued clone can still retain impaired 80S ribosome assembly.

evidence.snippet: Functional analysis of patient-derived B-lymphoblastoid and SV40-transformed fibroblast cell lines suggests that the compound heterozygous EFL1 variants impaired mature ribosome formation leading to compromised protein synthesis, ultimately resulting in a severe form of Shwachman-Diamond syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived cell lines from a severe infantile case directly link EFL1 dysfunction to impaired mature ribosome formation and reduced protein synthesis.

steps/3.description: Defective EFL1 function compromises mature ribosome formation and reduces overall protein synthesis, providing a mechanistic basis for the tissue-specific pancreatic, hematopoietic, growth, and skeletal phenotype.

evidence.snippet: This study aims to identify the molecular basis of an SDS-like disease, manifested by pancytopenia, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and skeletal abnormalities in six patients from three unrelated families.
evidence.explanation: The discovery cohort directly documents pancytopenia as a defining hematologic manifestation of EFL1-related SDS.

steps/4.description: Infantile pancytopenia is a recurrent hematologic presentation in the initial EFL1-related cohort.

evidence.snippet: This study aims to identify the molecular basis of an SDS-like disease, manifested by pancytopenia, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and skeletal abnormalities in six patients from three unrelated families.
evidence.explanation: The same discovery cohort establishes exocrine pancreatic insufficiency as part of the core clinical phenotype.

steps/5.description: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is a core gastrointestinal feature of EFL1-related Shwachman-Diamond syndrome.

evidence.snippet: In almost all affected children, persistent or intermittent neutropenia is an early finding.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews identifies neutropenia as a common early finding in the Shwachman-Diamond syndrome spectrum that includes EFL1-related disease.

steps/6.description: Persistent or intermittent neutropenia is a common early hematologic feature across Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, including the EFL1-associated recessive subtype.

evidence.snippet: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS) is a recessive disorder typified by bone marrow failure and predisposition to hematological malignancies.
evidence.explanation: The EFL1-specific causative series places SDS2 within the SDS spectrum of leukemia-predisposition ribosomopathies and supports oncologic surveillance for myeloid malignancy.

steps/7.description: EFL1-related Shwachman-Diamond syndrome carries a risk of myeloid malignant transformation, including myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia, within the broader SDS ribosomopathy spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Short stature and recurrent infections are common.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews explicitly identifies short stature as a common clinical feature in Shwachman-Diamond syndrome caused by EFL1, DNAJC21, or SBDS.

steps/8.description: Short stature is a common growth manifestation within the Shwachman-Diamond syndrome spectrum and is included in the MONDO textual definition of SDS2.

evidence.snippet: We report a pediatric patient who presented with a metaphyseal dysplasia and was found to have biallelic variants in EFL1 on reanalysis of trio whole-exome sequencing data.
evidence.explanation: This EFL1-specific case report directly supports metaphyseal dysplasia as part of the clinical spectrum.

steps/9.description: Metaphyseal dysplasia expands the recognized skeletal phenotype of EFL1-related disease and supports separation from classic SBDS-related SDS at the level of case-based phenotype curation.

evidence.snippet: Cellular defects in these individuals include impaired ribosomal subunit joining and attenuated global protein translation as a consequence of defective eIF6 eviction.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived cellular data connect defective EIF6 eviction to impaired ribosomal subunit joining and reduced global translation.

edges/2.description: Impaired late 60S maturation reduces productive ribosome assembly and translation.

evidence.snippet: In mice, Efl1 deficiency recapitulates key aspects of the SDS phenotype.
evidence.explanation: EFL1 deficiency recapitulating SDS in vivo supports a causal bridge from the ribosome defect to hematopoietic disease manifestations.

edges/3.description: Hematopoietic output is vulnerable to the translation defect.

evidence.snippet: In mice, Efl1 deficiency recapitulates key aspects of the SDS phenotype.
evidence.explanation: The EFL1-specific model links deficient ribosome licensing to the multisystem SDS phenotype that includes pancreatic disease.

edges/4.description: Exocrine pancreatic function is impaired downstream of the ribosomopathy.

evidence.snippet: In almost all affected children, persistent or intermittent neutropenia is an early finding.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports neutropenia as an early hematologic manifestation within the SDS spectrum that includes EFL1-related disease.

edges/5.description: Myeloid output is commonly reduced within the hematopoietic phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Short stature and recurrent infections are common.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports short stature as a common SDS-spectrum feature requiring growth surveillance in EFL1-related disease.

edges/6.description: Reduced protein synthesis contributes to impaired somatic growth.

evidence.snippet: We report a pediatric patient who presented with a metaphyseal dysplasia and was found to have biallelic variants in EFL1 on reanalysis of trio whole-exome sequencing data.
evidence.explanation: An EFL1-specific case links biallelic EFL1 disease to metaphyseal dysplasia in the SDS-like skeletal phenotype.

edges/7.description: Skeletal development is perturbed as part of the SDS2 phenotype.

evidence.snippet: By identifying biallelic EFL1 mutations in SDS, we define this leukemia predisposition disorder as a ribosomopathy that is caused by corruption of a fundamental, conserved mechanism, which licenses entry of the large ribosomal subunit into translation.
evidence.explanation: The EFL1 discovery paper explicitly frames the disorder as a leukemia predisposition ribosomopathy.

edges/8.description: The EFL1 ribosomopathy belongs to the SDS leukemia-predisposition spectrum with risk for MDS or AML.

evidence.snippet: Therefore, we propose a more accurate pathogenesis mechanism of EFL1 dysfunction that eventually leads to aberrant translational control and ribosomopathy.
evidence.explanation: The somatic-UPD report connects EFL1 dysfunction to persistent abnormal translational control and ribosomopathy.

edges/9.description: The selected milder EFL1 genotype still impairs 80S ribosome assembly and leaves residual ribosomopathy.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report biallelic mutations in EFL1 in 3 unrelated individuals with clinical features of SDS.
evidence.explanation: This establishes EFL1 as the causal disease gene in molecularly confirmed SDS2.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic pathogenic EFL1 variants define SDS2 and impair the late ribosome-maturation step shared with SBDS.

evidence.snippet: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is treated with oral pancreatic enzymes and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents pancreatic enzyme replacement as standard management for the pancreatic component of SDS, including EFL1-related disease.

treatments/0.description: Oral pancreatic enzyme replacement with fat-soluble vitamin supplementation is used to manage exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in the SDS spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Assessment of nutritional status and measurement of serum concentration of fat-soluble vitamins every six months.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports scheduled nutrition and fat-soluble vitamin monitoring for SDS management.

treatments/1.description: Nutritional status and fat-soluble vitamin concentrations should be followed longitudinally because exocrine pancreatic dysfunction can cause malabsorption and malnutrition.

evidence.snippet: Complete blood count with white blood cell differential and platelet count at least every three to six months; bone marrow examination every one to three years or more frequently if bone marrow changes are observed.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews gives explicit blood-count and marrow-examination surveillance intervals for SDS.

treatments/2.description: Serial complete blood counts with differential and platelet count, together with periodic bone marrow examination, monitor cytopenias, marrow failure, MDS, and AML risk in the SDS spectrum.

evidence.snippet: If recurrent infections are severe and absolute neutrophil counts are persistently ≤500/mm3, treatment with granulocyte-colony stimulation factor (G-CSF) can be considered and may be especially helpful when interventions such as complex dental procedures or orthopedic surgery are being considered.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports G-CSF pharmacotherapy for severe persistent neutropenia in SDS, including the EFL1-related recessive subtype.

evidence.snippet: Prolonged use of cytokine and hematopoietic growth factors (e.g., G-CSF) should be considered with caution.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews adds a caution against prolonged growth-factor use in SDS.

treatments/3.description: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor pharmacotherapy can be used for severe recurrent infection with persistent severe neutropenia in the SDS spectrum, while prolonged cytokine or hematopoietic growth-factor exposure should be approached cautiously.

evidence.snippet: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) should be considered for treatment of severe bone marrow failure, MDS, or AML.
evidence.explanation: This review supports HSCT as the escalation therapy for severe marrow complications in SDS.

treatments/4.description: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is considered for severe bone marrow failure or myeloid malignant transformation in the SDS spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Monitor for orthopedic complications with radiographs of the hips and knees during the most rapid growth stages.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports radiographic orthopedic monitoring during rapid growth.

evidence.snippet: Assess growth and for clinical signs and symptoms of additional endocrine manifestations every six months.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports six-monthly growth and endocrine assessment.

treatments/5.description: Orthopedic imaging during rapid growth stages and regular growth/endocrine assessment are used to monitor skeletal dysplasia, asymmetric growth, and endocrine manifestations.

evidence.snippet: Multidisciplinary team management of liver disease;
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews includes liver disease management in SDS multidisciplinary care.

evidence.snippet: Hepatic phenotypes of EFL1-related Shwachman-Diamond syndrome in a biopsy-validated study.
evidence.explanation: This EFL1-specific biopsy-validated report supports including hepatic involvement in follow-up considerations.

treatments/6.description: Liver involvement should be considered in EFL1-related SDS follow-up, with multidisciplinary management when liver disease is present.

evidence.snippet: If both parents are known to be heterozygous for an autosomal recessive SDS-related pathogenic variant, each sib of an affected individual has at conception a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being a clinically asymptomatic carrier, and a 25% chance of being unaffected and not a carrier.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports autosomal recessive recurrence-risk counseling for EFL1-related SDS.

evidence.snippet: It is appropriate to evaluate the older and younger sibs of a proband in order to identify those who will benefit from treatment and preventive measures as soon as possible. It is essential to evaluate any potential related donor for SDS to avoid using an asymptomatic relative with SDS as an HSCT donor.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports at-risk sibling evaluation and donor screening before related-donor HSCT.

treatments/7.description: Counsel families about autosomal recessive recurrence risk, carrier testing, prenatal or preimplantation testing when familial variants are known, and the need to evaluate related HSCT donor candidates for SDS.

evidence.snippet: Encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis (ECCL) is a rare neurocutaneous disorder caused by somatic FGFR1 and KRAS variants.
evidence.explanation: Confirms somatic FGFR1 variants as a cause of ECCL.

steps/1.description: Postzygotic activating mutations in FGFR1 occur during early embryonic development, leading to mosaic overactivation of FGFR1 signaling in affected tissues. This drives aberrant proliferation of mesenchymal and neural crest-derived cells, producing lipomas, cutaneous hamartomas, and CNS anomalies in a mosaic distribution. ECCL shares significant phenotypic overlap with mosaic RASopathies due to convergent activation of the RAS-MAPK pathway.

evidence.snippet: Key clinical features include hairless fatty tissue nevus of the scalp, choristoma of the eye and intraspinal and intracerebral lipomas.
evidence.explanation: Intracerebral and intraspinal lipomas are listed as key clinical features.

evidence.snippet: central nervous system lipomas
evidence.explanation: Orphanet's definition lists central nervous system lipomas as a typical ECCL feature.

steps/2.description: Intracerebral and intraspinal lipomas are characteristic CNS manifestations. They may cause ventriculomegaly and cerebral atrophy.

evidence.snippet: It is characterized by unilateral ocular, cutaneous and central nervous system anomalies.
evidence.explanation: Unilateral cutaneous anomalies are a defining feature of ECCL.

evidence.snippet: well-demarcated hairless fatty nevus on the scalp
evidence.explanation: Orphanet's definition supports the characteristic cutaneous fatty nevus.

steps/3.description: Hairless fatty tissue nevus of the scalp (nevus psiloliparus) and facial hamartomas are characteristic cutaneous features, typically unilateral.

evidence.snippet: Key clinical features include hairless fatty tissue nevus of the scalp, choristoma of the eye and intraspinal and intracerebral lipomas.
evidence.explanation: Choristoma of the eye is listed as a key clinical feature of ECCL.

evidence.snippet: benign ocular tumors
evidence.explanation: Orphanet's definition supports benign ocular tumors/choristomas as typical ECCL features.

steps/4.description: Choristoma (dermoid or lipodermoid) of the eye, typically epibulbar, is a key diagnostic feature of ECCL. Limbal dermoids are the most common ocular manifestation.

evidence.snippet: HP:0001250 | Seizure | Very frequent (99-80%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet classifies seizure as very frequent in ECCL.

steps/5.description: Seizures can occur as a neurologic consequence of ECCL-associated CNS malformations.

evidence.snippet: HP:0001249 | Intellectual disability | Very frequent (99-80%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet classifies intellectual disability as very frequent in ECCL.

steps/6.description: Intellectual disability can occur in ECCL with central nervous system lipomas and malformations.

evidence.snippet: Typical clinical features include a well-demarcated hairless fatty nevus on the scalp, benign ocular tumors, and central nervous system lipomas
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists central nervous system lipomas among typical ECCL clinical features.

edges/1.description: Mosaic FGFR1/RAS-MAPK activation in developing tissues produces CNS lipomatous malformations.

evidence.snippet: Typical clinical features include a well-demarcated hairless fatty nevus on the scalp, benign ocular tumors, and central nervous system lipomas
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists a hairless fatty scalp nevus among typical ECCL clinical features.

edges/2.description: Mosaic FGFR1/RAS-MAPK activation in developing cutaneous tissues produces fatty nevi and related skin hamartomas.

evidence.snippet: Typical clinical features include a well-demarcated hairless fatty nevus on the scalp, benign ocular tumors, and central nervous system lipomas
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists benign ocular tumors among typical ECCL clinical features.

edges/3.description: Mosaic FGFR1/RAS-MAPK activation in ocular tissues contributes to benign ocular tumors/choristomas.

evidence.snippet: central nervous system lipomas, leading sometimes to seizures, spasticity, and intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: Orphanet explicitly links CNS lipomas in ECCL to seizures.

edges/4.description: CNS lipomas and malformations can produce seizures.

evidence.snippet: central nervous system lipomas, leading sometimes to seizures, spasticity, and intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: Orphanet explicitly links CNS lipomas in ECCL to intellectual disability.

edges/5.description: CNS lipomas and malformations can impair neurodevelopment.

evidence.snippet: next-generation sequencing of affected tissue identified a pathologic FGFR1 p.K656E variant, thereby establishing a molecular diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: Identifies p.K656E as a pathogenic FGFR1 variant in ECCL.

genes/0.notes: Postzygotic somatic activating mutations in FGFR1 (e.g., p.K656E) cause ECCL. Somatic KRAS variants can also cause ECCL. Genetic testing of affected tissue (not blood) is typically required for molecular diagnosis. Patients with FGFR1-associated ECCL carry a risk of developing malignant brain tumors.

treatments/0.description: Surgical management of intracranial lipomas and associated complications such as hydrocephalus or mass effect.

evidence.snippet: Patients with FGFR1-associated ECCL carry a risk of developing malignant brain tumors; thus, genetic testing of patients with suspected ECCL has important management implications.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the need for brain tumor surveillance in FGFR1-associated ECCL.

treatments/1.description: Patients with FGFR1-associated ECCL carry a risk of developing malignant brain tumors, necessitating regular neuroimaging surveillance.

evidence.snippet: The mutation, p.Gln1124X, leads to the loss of hemidesmosomal inner plaques and a complete absence of skin immunostaining for BPAG1-e, as well as reduced labeling for plectin, the beta4 integrin subunit, and for type XVII collagen.
evidence.explanation: Direct observation in patient skin of the inner-plaque loss and wider hemidesmosomal destabilization this node asserts.

evidence.snippet: The 38-year-old affected individual has lifelong generalized trauma-induced spontaneous blisters and erosions, particularly around the ankles.
evidence.explanation: Supports the downstream edge to keratinocyte cytolysis: the same individual has lifelong trauma-induced blistering.

steps/8.description: Biallelic DST nonsense variants abolish the epithelial isoform of bullous pemphigoid antigen 1 (BPAG1-e, BP230), the hemidesmosomal inner-plaque protein that anchors keratin intermediate filaments at the basal pole of the keratinocyte. Inner plaques are lost and labelling for plectin, the beta-4 integrin subunit and type XVII collagen is reduced, so the defect destabilizes the wider hemidesmosome rather than one component alone. This is the node the EBS BP230 subtype row acts at.

evidence.snippet: We have further identified keratin 14 (KRT14) as a KLHL24 substrate and found that KLHL24-ΔN28 induces excessive ubiquitination and degradation of KRT14.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the substrate relationship and the direction of the effect this node asserts.

evidence.snippet: Using a knock-in mouse model, we have confirmed that the Klhl24 mutations lead to stabilized Klhl24-ΔN28 and cause Krt14 degradation.
evidence.explanation: In vivo confirmation in a knock-in mouse that the stabilized receptor is what degrades keratin 14.

steps/9.description: Heterozygous start-codon variants in KLHL24 produce a receptor lacking its first 28 residues, which can no longer autoubiquitinate and therefore accumulates. Keratin 14 is a substrate of this receptor, so the stabilized form drives excessive ubiquitination and degradation of keratin 14. The basal keratin network is depleted without any mutation in a keratin gene, which is why this node is drawn separately from the dominant-negative route. This is the node the EBS KLHL24 subtype row acts at.

evidence.snippet: Most cases of EBS are due to dominantly acting mutations in keratin 14 (K14) or K5, the type I and II intermediate filament (IF) proteins that copolymerize to form a pancytoplasmic network of 10 nm filaments in basal keratinocytes of epidermis and related epithelia
evidence.explanation: Confirms K5/K14 as the obligate IF pair in basal keratinocytes and dominant mutations as the cause of EBS.

evidence.snippet: the most important and most commonly occurring molecular defects in these patients are the defects of keratins 5 and14 (KRT5 and KRT14)
evidence.explanation: Confirms KRT5 and KRT14 defects as the primary molecular basis of EBS.

steps/10.description: Mutations in KRT5 or KRT14 genes disrupt the keratin intermediate filament network in basal keratinocytes of the epidermis. Keratins 5 and 14 are the obligate type II and type I intermediate filament partners that copolymerize to form the 10 nm filament network providing mechanical resilience to basal keratinocytes.

evidence.snippet: Defects in K5-K14 filament network architecture cause basal keratinocytes to become fragile, and account for their rupture upon exposure to mechanical trauma
evidence.explanation: Confirms that disrupted keratin filament architecture causes basal keratinocyte fragility and rupture.

evidence.snippet: Keratin aggregates display impaired dynamics of assembly and diminished solubility and appear to be the trigger for endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress upon being phosphorylated by MAPKs
evidence.explanation: Confirms that mutant keratins form aggregates with impaired dynamics, triggering downstream ER stress signaling.

steps/11.description: Mutant keratins exert a dominant-negative effect by incorporating into keratin filaments and poisoning the entire filament network. This disrupts filament architecture and leads to keratin aggregate formation, particularly under conditions of mechanical or thermal stress.

evidence.snippet: Plectin is a giant cytoskeletal crosslinker and intermediate filament stabilizing protein. Mutations in the human plectin gene (PLEC) cause several rare diseases that are grouped under the term plectinopathies
evidence.explanation: Confirms plectin as a cytoskeletal crosslinker whose mutations cause plectinopathies including EBS-MD.

evidence.snippet: Plectin deficiency causes autosomal recessive epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS) with involvement of the skin and other organs, such as muscle and gastrointestinal tract, depending on the expression pattern of the defective protein
evidence.explanation: Confirms plectin deficiency causes EBS with multi-organ involvement including skin and muscle.

steps/12.description: Mutations in PLEC disrupt plectin, a giant cytoskeletal crosslinker that connects the keratin intermediate filament network to hemidesmosomes at the dermal-epidermal junction and to the desmin cytoskeleton in muscle. Loss of plectin causes a dual phenotype affecting both skin (blistering) and skeletal muscle (progressive dystrophy).

evidence.snippet: Analysis of an affected person's skin showed loss of Slac2-b immunostaining (C-terminal antibody), disruption of keratinocyte adhesion within the lower epidermis, and an increased number of perinuclear vesicles.
evidence.explanation: Direct observation in patient skin of the vesicle accumulation and adhesion loss this node asserts.

evidence.snippet: A role for Slac2-b in keratinocyte biology was supported by findings of cytoskeletal disruption (mainly keratin intermediate filaments) and decreased keratinocyte adhesion in both keratinocytes from an affected subject and after shRNA knockdown of Slac2-b in normal keratinocytes.
evidence.explanation: Cultured-keratinocyte and knockdown evidence that the adhesion and keratin-filament defect follows from loss of Slac2-b specifically.

steps/13.description: Biallelic EXPH5 truncating variants remove the C-terminus of exophilin-5 (Slac2-b), a Rab27B effector in intracellular vesicle trafficking. The product is not a structural component of the keratin-hemidesmosome apparatus, as the keratin, plectin and BPAG1-e routes' products are; the route to fragility runs instead through disordered vesicle handling, with perinuclear and plasma-membrane-proximal vesicle accumulation, keratin filament disruption and reduced keratinocyte adhesion in the lower epidermis. This is the node the EBS EXPH5 subtype row acts at.

evidence.snippet: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS) is a mechano-bullous disorder characterized by intraepidermal blistering within the basal keratinocytes as a result of trauma to the skin
evidence.explanation: Confirms intraepidermal blistering within basal keratinocytes as the hallmark of EBS.

evidence.snippet: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS) is a group of inherited keratinopathies that, in most cases, arise due to mutations in keratins and lead to intraepidermal ruptures
evidence.explanation: Confirms that keratin mutations lead to intraepidermal rupture.

steps/14.description: Basal keratinocytes with disrupted keratin networks rupture (cytolyse) when subjected to mechanical trauma. The blistering in EBS is intraepidermal, occurring within the basal cell layer rather than at tissue interfaces, distinguishing it from junctional and dystrophic EB.

evidence.snippet: Histology showed suprabasal clefting and acantholysis throughout the spinous layer, mimicking pemphigus. Electron microscopy revealed disconnection of keratin intermediate filaments from desmosomes.
evidence.explanation: Direct observation of the suprabasal cleavage plane and the keratin-desmosome disconnection this node asserts, in the desmoplakin route.

evidence.snippet: One specific component of desmosomes is plakophilin 1 (PKP1), which is mainly expressed in the spinous layer of the epidermis. Loss-of-function autosomal recessive mutations in PKP1 result in ectodermal dysplasia-skin fragility (EDSF) syndrome
evidence.explanation: Sources the plakophilin route and the spinous-layer expression that puts this node's cleavage plane above the basal keratinocytes.

evidence.snippet: Skin fragility and nail involvement were present in all affected individuals (18/18), with most cases showing palmoplantar keratoderma (16/18), alopecia/hypotrichosis (16/18) and perioral fissuring/cheilitis (12/15; not commented on in 3 cases).
evidence.explanation: The frequencies behind this node's edges to palmoplantar keratoderma and nail dystrophy, from the authors' review of all published biallelic PKP1 cases.

steps/15.description: The two suprabasal routes in this entry. Loss of plakophilin 1, a desmosomal plaque protein expressed mainly in the spinous layer, or truncation of the desmoplakin tail that carries desmoplakin's intermediate filament-binding subdomains, detaches keratin filaments from desmosomes above the basal layer. The cleavage plane is therefore suprabasal rather than intrabasal, and the histology is acantholysis resembling pemphigus rather than basal-cell cytolysis. This node is drawn separately from the basal routes for that reason, and is where the EBS-PD and LAEB subtype rows act.

evidence.snippet: after thermal stress a reduced stability of the keratin filaments was demonstrable in the epidermolysis bullosa simplex cell lines, with filaments breaking into aggregates
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that thermal stress causes keratin filament breakdown into aggregates in EBS cell lines, explaining heat-exacerbated blistering.

steps/16.description: Mutant keratin filament networks are thermally unstable. Elevated temperature causes filament breakdown into aggregates, explaining the clinical observation that blistering worsens in warm weather and with increased perspiration. This is particularly prominent in localized EBS.

evidence.snippet: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS) is characterized by fragility of the skin (and mucosal epithelia in some instances) that results in non-scarring blisters and erosions caused by minor mechanical trauma
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms non-scarring blisters from minor mechanical trauma as the hallmark of EBS.

evidence.snippet: Epidermolysis bullosa (EB) is an inherited, heterogeneous group of rare genetic dermatoses characterized by mucocutaneous fragility and blister formation, inducible by often minimal trauma
evidence.explanation: Nature Reviews Disease Primers confirms blister formation from minimal trauma as the defining feature of EB.

steps/17.description: Intraepidermal blistering caused by basal keratinocyte fragility. Blisters arise at sites of mechanical trauma and generally heal without significant scarring, distinguishing EBS from dystrophic EB.

evidence.snippet: after thermal stress a reduced stability of the keratin filaments was demonstrable in the epidermolysis bullosa simplex cell lines, with filaments breaking into aggregates
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates thermal instability of mutant keratin filaments, providing the molecular basis for heat-exacerbated blistering.

steps/18.description: Worsening of blistering during warm weather or with increased physical activity and perspiration. Caused by thermal instability of mutant keratin filament networks. Particularly prominent in localized EBS affecting hands and feet.

evidence.snippet: Additional features can include hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles (keratoderma), nail dystrophy, milia, and hyper- and/or hypopigmentation
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms palmoplantar keratoderma as an additional feature of EBS.

steps/19.description: Thickening of the skin on palms and soles, particularly prominent in EBS severe (Dowling-Meara) subtype. May develop progressively with age.

evidence.snippet: PLEC mutations lead to EBS with nail dystrophy
evidence.explanation: Confirms nail dystrophy as a recognized feature of PLEC-associated EBS.

steps/20.description: Abnormal nail growth and morphology including thickened, dystrophic, or absent nails. Present in severe EBS subtypes and EBS with muscular dystrophy.

evidence.snippet: The most common disorder is autosomal recessive disease epidermolysis bullosa simplex with muscular dystrophy (EBS-MD), which is characterized by skin blistering and progressive muscle weakness
evidence.explanation: Confirms progressive muscle weakness as a defining feature of EBS-MD.

evidence.snippet: Skeletal muscle biopsies from EBS-MD patients and plectin-deficient mice revealed severe dystrophic features with variation in fiber size, degenerative myofibrillar changes, mitochondrial alterations, and pathological desmin-positive protein aggregates
evidence.explanation: Confirms dystrophic muscle pathology in both human EBS-MD patients and plectin-deficient mouse models.

steps/21.description: Progressive muscular dystrophy in EBS with muscular dystrophy (EBS-MD) caused by PLEC mutations. Plectin is essential for muscle cytoskeletal integrity. Skeletal muscle biopsies show dystrophic features with variation in fiber size, degenerative myofibrillar changes, and pathological desmin-positive protein aggregates.

edges/8.description: Mutant keratins poison the filament network by incorporating into filaments and destabilizing them.

edges/9.description: Disrupted keratin network renders basal keratinocytes fragile and prone to rupture under mechanical stress.

edges/10.description: Cytolysis of the basal keratinocyte is what produces the clinical blister, and is why the cleavage plane is intraepidermal rather than at the dermal-epidermal junction. Every mechanistic route in this entry except the suprabasal desmosomal one reaches the clinical phenotype through this node.

edges/11.description: Disrupted hemidesmosome-cytoskeleton linkage leads to skin fragility.

edges/12.description: The same plectin loss disrupts the desmin cytoskeleton of skeletal muscle, which is the extracutaneous half of the EBS-MD phenotype and is why that subtype row is the only one in this entry carrying a myopathy.

edges/13.description: Thermal breakdown of the mutant filament network is the mechanism behind the seasonal and exertional worsening recorded as a phenotype.

edges/14.description: Loss of the hemidesmosomal inner plaque leaves basal keratinocytes unable to resist shear, producing the same trauma-induced intraepidermal separation as the keratin and plectin routes.

edges/15.description: Reduced keratinocyte adhesion and keratin filament disruption in the lower epidermis converge on the same trauma-induced intraepidermal separation as the structural routes.

edges/16.description: Depletion of keratin 14 protein leaves the basal keratin network unable to bear mechanical load, reaching the same cytolysis node as the dominant-negative keratin variants.

edges/17.description: Suprabasal acantholysis produces superficial erosions and blistering, the shared clinical endpoint with the basal routes even though the cleavage plane differs.

edges/18.description: Palmoplantar keratoderma is a cardinal feature of the plakophilin route rather than an incidental one, reported in 16 of 18 published biallelic PKP1 cases, so the desmosomal defect reaches this phenotype directly and not only through blistering.
