edges/19.description: Nail involvement is present in every published biallelic PKP1 case, making it one of the two constant features of the plakophilin route alongside skin fragility.

evidence.snippet: 18 were found to harbor heterozygous mutations in the keratin 5 or keratin 14 genes, KRT5 and KRT14, respectively
evidence.explanation: Confirms heterozygous KRT5 mutations as a cause of EBS.

evidence.snippet: the most important and most commonly occurring molecular defects in these patients are the defects of keratins 5 and14 (KRT5 and KRT14)
evidence.explanation: Confirms KRT5 as one of the two principal genes mutated in EBS.

genes/0.notes: Keratin 5 gene on chromosome 12q13.13. Encodes the type II keratin that pairs with keratin 14 in basal keratinocytes. Dominant-negative missense mutations, particularly in the helix boundary motifs, cause EBS. Hotspot mutations in the 1A and 2B rod domain helix boundaries correlate with more severe phenotypes. No `subtype` foreign key is set on this record: KRT5 is the causal gene of six of this entry's subtype rows (localized, generalized intermediate, generalized severe, the recessive KRT5 row, mottled pigmentation, and migratory circinate erythema) and the slot holds one value. The gene-to-row mapping is carried on the rows themselves, each of which binds KRT5 in its `genes` list.

evidence.snippet: Most cases of EBS are due to dominantly acting mutations in keratin 14 (K14) or K5
evidence.explanation: Confirms dominant KRT14 mutations as a major cause of EBS.

evidence.snippet: many cases result from de novo mutations in KRT5 and KRT14 genes
evidence.explanation: Confirms that many EBS cases arise from de novo KRT14 mutations.

genes/1.notes: Keratin 14 gene on chromosome 17q21.2. Encodes the type I keratin partner of keratin 5 in basal keratinocytes. Dominant-negative missense mutations cause EBS localized through severe. Biallelic loss-of-function (null) mutations cause autosomal recessive EBS with severe generalized blistering. No `subtype` foreign key is set on this record, for the same reason as KRT5 above: KRT14 is the causal gene of four subtype rows (localized, generalized intermediate, generalized severe, and the recessive KRT14-null row) and the slot holds one value.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in the human plectin gene (PLEC) cause several rare diseases that are grouped under the term plectinopathies
evidence.explanation: Confirms PLEC mutations as causative for plectinopathies including EBS-MD.

evidence.snippet: in 14 cases, the disease was associated with mutations in both alleles of the plectin gene
evidence.explanation: Confirms biallelic plectin mutations in EBS patients, establishing recessive inheritance.

genes/2.notes: Plectin gene on chromosome 8q24.3. Encodes a giant (>500 kDa) cytoskeletal crosslinker protein. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations cause EBS with muscular dystrophy. Plectin links the keratin intermediate filament network to hemidesmosomes in skin and to the desmin cytoskeleton in muscle. No `subtype` foreign key is set on this record: PLEC causes both the recessive EBS with muscular dystrophy row and the dominant EBS Ogna row, and the slot holds one value.

evidence.snippet: biallelic pathogenic variants in CD151, DST, or EXPH5
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists DST as a gene with biallelic pathogenic variants causing autosomal recessive EBS.

genes/3.notes: Dystonin gene (also known as BPAG1) on chromosome 6p12.1. Encodes a cytoskeletal linker protein related to plectin. Rare biallelic mutations cause EBS with additional features.

evidence.snippet: biallelic pathogenic variants in CD151, DST, or EXPH5
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists EXPH5 as a gene with biallelic pathogenic variants causing autosomal recessive EBS.

genes/4.notes: Exophilin 5 gene on chromosome 11q22.3. Encodes a Rab27b effector involved in melanosome and lamellar body transport. Biallelic mutations cause a rare autosomal recessive form of EBS.

evidence.snippet: We have identified start-codon mutations in the KLHL24 gene in five patients with EB.
evidence.explanation: Identifies KLHL24 start-codon mutations as a novel cause of EBS through stabilized truncated protein that excessively degrades KRT14.

evidence.snippet: monoallelic mutations, c.1A>G and c.2T>C, in the translation initiation codon of the gene encoding kelch-like protein 24 (KLHL24) in 14 individuals with a distinct skin-fragility phenotype and skin cleavage within basal keratinocytes
evidence.explanation: Independently confirms KLHL24 initiation codon mutations in 14 individuals with skin fragility and basal keratinocyte cleavage.

genes/5.notes: Kelch-like family member 24 gene on chromosome 3q27.1. Encodes a CUL3-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase substrate receptor. Gain-of-function mutations in the translation initiation codon (c.1A>G, c.2T>C) produce a truncated protein (KLHL24-deltaN28) that escapes autoubiquitination and causes excessive ubiquitin-mediated degradation of keratin 14 (KRT14). Patients present with extensive skin denudation at birth and dilated cardiomyopathy. The c.1A>G mutation has occurred de novo and is recurrent across unrelated families from different countries.

evidence.snippet: In patient 1 we identified a homozygous nonsense mutation, p.R672X, in the PKP1 gene (encoding plakophilin 1).
evidence.explanation: A biallelic PKP1 truncating variant in a patient with ectodermal dysplasia-skin fragility syndrome.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, PKP1 is not expressed in the heart, which accounts for the lack of cardiomyopathy in patient 1.
evidence.explanation: Sources the cardiac contrast recorded in these notes, which is the main clinical discriminator between the PKP1 and DSP suprabasal routes.

genes/6.notes: Plakophilin 1, an armadillo-family desmosomal plaque protein expressed mainly in the spinous layer. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause the suprabasal EBS subtype recorded here as EBS-PD, also named ectodermal dysplasia-skin fragility syndrome. The gene is not expressed in the heart, which is what separates this entity clinically from the DSP route below despite their overlapping skin and hair phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: Aberrant mRNA transcripts that predict premature termination of translation with loss of the three intermediate filament-binding subdomains in the DP tail were detected by RT-PCR.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the specific functional consequence, loss of the intermediate filament-binding subdomains of the desmoplakin tail.

evidence.snippet: Loss-of-function mutations in the DSP gene can result in a phenotype similar to ectodermal dysplasia-skin fragility syndrome resulting from PKP1 mutations but only DSP pathology is associated with cardiac disease.
evidence.explanation: Sources the phenotypic overlap with the PKP1 route and the cardiac expression difference recorded in these notes.

genes/7.notes: Desmoplakin, the desmosomal plaque protein that links the intermediate filament network to the desmosomal cadherins. Only the lethal acantholytic epidermolysis bullosa end of the DSP skin spectrum is curated on this entry, as the LAEB subtype row; the milder biallelic DSP skin phenotypes have their own entries (Skin_Fragility_Woolly_Hair_Syndrome, Carvajal_Syndrome), as do the DSP cardiomyopathies. Unlike PKP1, DSP is expressed in the heart, so the DSP route can carry cardiac disease.

evidence.snippet: Supportive care to protect the skin from blistering; use of dressings that will protect the skin and promote healing of wounds
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms supportive wound care as the primary management strategy for EBS.

treatments/0.description: Supportive wound care is the mainstay of EBS management. Includes use of non-adherent dressings to protect fragile skin and promote healing of blistered areas. Blister lancing with sterile technique to prevent blister extension.

evidence.snippet: Excessive heat exposure may exacerbate blistering and infection. Avoid poorly fitting or coarse-textured clothing/footwear and activities that traumatize the skin
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists heat exposure and skin trauma as agents to avoid in EBS management.

treatments/1.description: Minimizing exposure to heat, excessive physical activity, and friction to prevent blistering episodes. Includes wearing loose-fitting clothing, soft footwear, and avoiding high ambient temperatures.

evidence.snippet: Aluminum chloride (20%) applied to palms and soles can reduce sweating and therefore minimize blister formation in some individuals with EBS
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms aluminum chloride antiperspirant as a treatment to reduce sweating-induced blistering.

treatments/2.description: Topical antiperspirant application to palms and soles to reduce perspiration-induced blistering, especially in localized EBS.

evidence.snippet: Identification and management of specific causes of pain and itching; management with a pain specialist as needed
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms pain and itch management as part of EBS care.

treatments/3.description: Analgesic therapy for pain associated with blistering and erosions. May include topical and systemic pain medications depending on severity.

evidence.snippet: appropriate footwear and physical therapy to preserve ambulation
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms physical therapy to preserve ambulation as part of EBS management.

treatments/4.description: Rehabilitation and physical therapy for patients with EBS-MD to maintain mobility and muscle function as muscular dystrophy progresses.

evidence.snippet: These findings have implications for genetic counseling and prenatal diagnosis for EBS
evidence.explanation: Confirms the importance of genetic counseling for EBS families, particularly given de novo mutations and mixed inheritance patterns.

treatments/5.description: Genetic counseling for affected families regarding inheritance patterns, recurrence risk, and prenatal diagnosis options. Important given both dominant and recessive forms and significant de novo mutation rate.

evidence.snippet: Of the patients receiving diacerein, 86% in episode 1 and 37.5% in episode 2 met the primary end point (vs 14% and 17% with placebo, respectively). This effect was still significant after the follow-up
evidence.explanation: Phase 2/3 crossover trial demonstrating diacerein efficacy in reducing EBS blisters compared to placebo.

evidence.snippet: Although there was no significant difference in outcomes between the groups, further study may elucidate the effects of diacerein on EBS lesions, especially in patients with severe EBS
evidence.explanation: Larger RCT (n=54) did not meet primary endpoint overall, though post hoc analysis suggested benefit in severe EBS subgroup.

treatments/6.description: Topical diacerein 1% ointment, an anti-inflammatory agent that inhibits IL-1beta signaling. A phase 2/3 crossover trial (n=17) showed 86% of diacerein-treated patients achieved >40% blister reduction versus 14% with placebo. However, a larger randomized controlled trial (n=54) found no significant difference in the primary endpoint (>=60% BSA reduction at 8 weeks), though post hoc analysis in severe EBS showed a potential signal (46.2% vs 15.4% achieving optimal skin scores). Multiple ongoing trials continue to evaluate diacerein in EBS.

evidence.snippet: treatment with a pharmacological activator of Nrf2, two transcription factors eliciting distinct transcriptional programs, alleviates the blistering caused by a K14 deficiency in an EBS mouse model, correlating with K17 induction in basal epidermal keratinocytes. Nrf2 induction is brought about by treatment with sulforaphane, a natural product
evidence.explanation: Mouse model demonstrates sulforaphane activates Nrf2 to induce compensatory K17 expression in basal keratinocytes, alleviating blistering in K14-deficient EBS.

treatments/7.description: Sulforaphane, a natural product from cruciferous vegetables, activates the Nrf2 transcription factor to induce compensatory keratins K16/K17 in basal keratinocytes. In an EBS mouse model with K14 deficiency, sulforaphane treatment alleviated blistering by upregulating K17 expression. This represents an attractive preclinical approach exploiting functional redundancy within the keratin gene family.

evidence.snippet: Serous adenofibroma of the fallopian tube is a rare, benign tumour of the female genital tract.
evidence.explanation: Supports benign localized neoplastic proliferation in tubal tissue.

evidence.snippet: A paratubal leiomyoma is an exceptionally rare benign smooth muscle tumor arising from paratubal tissue, with only sporadic cases reported in the literature.
evidence.explanation: Extends the benign localized growth model to the paratubal smooth muscle subtype.

steps/0.description: Benign epithelial-stromal or smooth muscle proliferation arises in the fallopian tube or adjacent paratubal tissue and remains spatially confined rather than adopting invasive malignant behavior.

evidence.snippet: Small cysts of 0.5–3 cm in diameter are mostly incidentally found at the fimbriae end, with coarse papillary excrescences lined by epithelial cells and connective tissue stroma without nuclear pleomorphism or mitosis.
evidence.explanation: Supports the benign epithelial-stromal architecture of tubal adenofibroma lesions.

evidence.snippet: A diagnostic laparoscopy revealed a well-circumscribed solid mass arising from the mesosalpinx, separate from the ovary and fallopian tube and consistent with a paratubal mass, which was successfully excised laparoscopically.
evidence.explanation: Supports circumscribed solid benign lesion formation in the paratubal smooth muscle subtype.

steps/1.description: Benign tubal lesions develop papillary, cystic, fibrous, or solid architecture while remaining well circumscribed and non-destructive.

evidence.snippet: This report presents an atypical case of a 17-year-old girl with a tubal serous adenofibroma that presented with a palpable mass occupying the entire abdomen accompanied by urinary symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Supports progression from a confined lesion to large-volume mass effect.

evidence.snippet: A transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a complex left adnexal mass with calcifications, and computed tomography (CT) confirmed a 7.8 × 5.5 × 4.7 cm lesion suggestive of an ovarian malignancy.
evidence.explanation: Supports anatomically significant enlargement of benign adnexal lesions.

steps/2.description: Ongoing enlargement of a confined tubal or paratubal lesion can expand the adnexa, occupy abdominal space, and distort local anatomy without invasion.

evidence.snippet: A thorough history and abdominal examination should be performed and may help delineate adnexal etiologies of pain or discomfort.
evidence.explanation: Supports adnexal tissue distortion as a clinically relevant pain-generating context.

steps/3.description: Distortion and stretching of local adnexal tissues create a mechanical basis for pain or discomfort in symptomatic cases.

evidence.snippet: The clinical picture derived from heterotopic extraovarian sex cord-stromal proliferation indicated a disordered hypothalamus-pituitary-ovary axis.
evidence.explanation: Supports an endocrine dysregulation branch in selected benign tubal adenofibromas.

steps/4.description: In uncommon adenofibroma presentations with heterotopic sex cord-stromal elements, altered endocrine signaling can disrupt reproductive cycling.

evidence.snippet: From histopathological findings, the lesion was identified as a serous fallopian tube adenofibroma.
evidence.explanation: Confirms definitive detection through postoperative histopathology.

evidence.snippet: This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of differentiating paratubal leiomyomas from ovarian tumors based on imaging alone. Histopathological examination is essential for confirmation.
evidence.explanation: Supports final diagnostic confirmation by pathology after imaging/surgical workup.

steps/5.description: Most lesions are identified through pelvic imaging, operative evaluation, or histopathologic examination after resection.

evidence.snippet: This report presents an atypical case of a 17-year-old girl with a tubal serous adenofibroma that presented with a palpable mass occupying the entire abdomen accompanied by urinary symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports abdominal mass presentation in benign tubal neoplasm.

steps/6.description: Benign fallopian tube tumors may be detected as an incidental abdominal or adnexal mass.

evidence.snippet: A thorough history and abdominal examination should be performed and may help delineate adnexal etiologies of pain or discomfort.
evidence.explanation: Supports pain/discomfort as a core presenting clinical axis in tubal pathology.

steps/7.description: Local adnexal distortion can cause intermittent pelvic pain.

evidence.snippet: A 23-year-old woman with normal secondary sexual characters and 46, XX karyotype, presented to the gynecology clinic complaining of irregular menstrual cycles.
evidence.explanation: Supports menstrual-cycle disturbance in a benign tubal adenofibroma case.

steps/8.description: Menstrual irregularity can occur in selected adenofibroma presentations.

edges/0.description: Localized proliferation yields a non-invasive circumscribed tubal or paratubal lesion.

edges/1.description: Selected lesions containing hormonally active stromal elements may perturb reproductive endocrine signaling.

edges/2.description: Continued localized growth can expand the lesion and distort adjacent adnexal anatomy.

evidence.snippet: This report presents an atypical case of a 17-year-old girl with a tubal serous adenofibroma that presented with a palpable mass occupying the entire abdomen accompanied by urinary symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Supports abdominal mass as a direct consequence of lesion enlargement.

edges/3.description: Large confined lesions become clinically appreciable as abdominal or adnexal masses.

edges/4.description: Expanding lesions impose pressure and stretch on adnexal tissues.

edges/5.description: Anatomically visible lesions enter imaging and operative diagnostic workflows.

evidence.snippet: A thorough history and abdominal examination should be performed and may help delineate adnexal etiologies of pain or discomfort.
evidence.explanation: Supports pelvic pain as a downstream phenotype of symptomatic adnexal pathology.

edges/6.description: Mechanical irritation from the enlarged adnexal lesion can manifest as pelvic pain.

evidence.snippet: A 23-year-old woman with normal secondary sexual characters and 46, XX karyotype, presented to the gynecology clinic complaining of irregular menstrual cycles.
evidence.explanation: Supports menstrual irregularity as a direct downstream phenotype of this endocrine branch.

edges/7.description: Reproductive endocrine dysregulation can present as menstrual irregularity.

evidence.snippet: She underwent a laparoscopic surgery with drainage of 1800 mL of yellow, citrine liquid from the cyst and left salpingectomy with no complications.
evidence.explanation: Supports definitive surgical management with favorable short-term outcome.

evidence.snippet: When surgical intervention is indicated, laparoscopy can often provide a safe and effective means of definitive diagnosis and treatment.
evidence.explanation: Supports laparoscopy as an effective therapeutic and diagnostic approach.

treatments/0.description: Definitive management is usually surgical removal when diagnosis is uncertain or symptoms are present.

evidence.snippet: For those patients with fertility requirements, some fertility-preserving techniques can be used to allow complete resection of the leiomyoma and avoid tubal damage.
evidence.explanation: Supports fertility-preserving surgical strategy in benign tubal leiomyoma management.

treatments/1.description: In selected patients with fertility goals, tubal leiomyoma excision may be performed with techniques aimed at preserving tubal patency.

evidence.snippet: Tumors of Fallopian tubes are rare in general, and they are the rarest tumors of female genital tract.
evidence.explanation: Motivates the need for denominator-based epidemiologic studies.

open_questions/0.rationale: Current evidence is dominated by case reports and small retrospective series, limiting quantitative prevalence estimates and subtype-specific risk stratification.

evidence.snippet: This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of differentiating paratubal leiomyomas from ovarian tumors based on imaging alone. Histopathological examination is essential for confirmation.
evidence.explanation: Supports unresolved preoperative discrimination challenges.

open_questions/1.rationale: Benign lesions can appear radiologically malignant, and robust prospective triage criteria are not yet standardized for rare tubal neoplasms.

open_questions/2.rationale: Existing literature lacks systematic multi-omic profiling and long-term recurrence-linked molecular annotations across benign tubal tumor classes.

evidence.snippet: MSH3, the MSH2-binding partner in the MutSβ complex, is required for 98% of germ line expansions and all somatic expansions in this model.
evidence.explanation: A Fragile X mouse model shows the MutSβ (MSH2-MSH3) complex is required for all somatic CGG expansion, the CGG-class instance of the module's aberrant-MMR mechanism.

evidence.snippet: MLH1/MLH3 (MutLγ), a protein complex that can act downstream of MutSβ in MMR, is also required for all germ line and somatic expansions.
evidence.explanation: The same Fragile X model shows the MutLγ (MLH1-MLH3) effector complex acting downstream of MutSβ is required for CGG expansion, with EXO1 protective — the machinery of the module's amplifier node.

steps/1.description: The FMR1 CGG repeat is processed by an aberrant DNA mismatch-repair route: the MutSβ (MSH2-MSH3) recognition complex, with the MutLγ (MLH1-MLH3) effector complex acting downstream, is required for germline and somatic CGG expansion in knock-in mouse models of the fragile X-associated disorders. This is the CGG-class instance of the module's aberrant-MMR machinery and lies upstream of the full-mutation methylation silencing that abolishes FMRP. Unlike the CAG/CTG disorders, ongoing post-mitotic somatic expansion is not established as the rate-limiting driver of fragile X syndrome onset — in humans the premutation to full-mutation transition is predominantly a maternal-germline / early-embryonic event and the silencing is already set developmentally — so this node conforms only at the molecular MMR-processing level, not at the module's somatic post-mitotic expansion node.

evidence.snippet: more than 99% of individuals have a CGG expansion (>200 triplets) in the 5' UTR of the gene, and FMR1 mutations and duplication/deletion are responsible for the remaining (<1%) molecular diagnoses of FXS.
evidence.explanation: This review establishes the full-mutation CGG expansion as the dominant molecular diagnosis for fragile X syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Such expanded alleles, known as full mutation (FM) alleles, are epigenetically silenced in differentiated cells thus resulting in the loss of FMRP, a protein important for learning and memory.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived stem-cell and neuronal differentiation work supports epigenetic silencing of full-mutation alleles and consequent FMRP loss.

evidence.snippet: Targeted demethylation of the CGG expansion by dCas9-Tet1/single guide RNA (sgRNA) switched the heterochromatin status of the upstream FMR1 promoter to an active chromatin state, restoring a persistent expression of FMR1 in FXS iPSCs.
evidence.explanation: Removing the methylation reactivates FMR1 and rescues the electrophysiological abnormality of the derived neurons, so methylation-dependent silencing is the operative lesion at this node rather than a correlate of it.

steps/2.description: The canonical initiating event is expansion of the FMR1 5' UTR CGG repeat above 200 repeats. Full-mutation alleles become epigenetically silenced in differentiated cells, which reduces or abolishes fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP).

evidence.snippet: Numerous studies have demonstrated that FMRP interacts with both coding and non-coding RNAs and represses protein synthesis at dendritic and synaptic locations.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports FMRP as a translational repressor at neuronal dendritic and synaptic sites.

evidence.snippet: FMRP is an mRNA-binding protein that functions at many synapses to inhibit local translation stimulated by metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) 1 and 5.
evidence.explanation: This supports the mechanism linking FMRP loss to dysregulated local synaptic translation.

evidence.snippet: We developed a brain polyribosome-programmed translation system, revealing that FMRP reversibly stalls ribosomes specifically on its target mRNAs.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the molecular action that is lost at this node. FMRP holds ribosomes in a reversible stall on its own target transcripts, so removing it releases those transcripts specifically rather than raising translation indiscriminately.

evidence.snippet: IQ scores were positively correlated with FXP levels in males and females with full mutation FXS demonstrating the clinical utility of this method.
evidence.explanation: Residual FMRP tracks cognitive outcome in both sexes with the full mutation, so the deficit at this node is graded rather than all or none. The measurement is peripheral (dried blood spots), not brain tissue.

steps/3.description: FMRP normally binds coding and non-coding RNAs and restrains translation at dendritic and synaptic locations. Loss of FMRP removes this brake, increasing basal protein translation and uncoupling translation from neuronal activity.

evidence.snippet: Loss of FMRP in mice results in widespread changes in chromatin regulation and aberrant gene expression.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the chromatin consequence of FMRP loss as a distinct outcome from the synaptic one, arising from a different set of FMRP target transcripts.

evidence.snippet: Inhibition of Brd4 function alleviated many of the phenotypes associated with FXS.
evidence.explanation: Pharmacological reversal through a chromatin reader, rather than through the mGluR pathway, is what supports treating this as a causal arm rather than an incidental transcriptional signature.

steps/4.description: Most characterized FMRP targets encode synaptic proteins, but FMRP also represses transcripts encoding transcriptional and chromatin-associated regulators, among them the BET protein BRD4. Losing that repression produces widespread chromatin misregulation and aberrant gene expression, and BET inhibition reverses several fragile X phenotypes in mice. This arm runs in parallel to the synaptic translation branch and is the best pharmacologically supported of the non-synaptic effector arms, but the evidence is currently mouse based and the intermediates between chromatin misregulation and circuit dysfunction are unresolved.

evidence.snippet: In the absence of FMRP, the basal protein translation is enhanced and not responsive to neuronal stimulation.
evidence.explanation: This supports enhanced basal protein translation after FMRP loss.

evidence.snippet: Recent studies on the biology of FMRP and the signaling pathways downstream of mGluR1/5 have yielded deeper insight into how synaptic protein synthesis and plasticity are regulated by experience.
evidence.explanation: This places mGluR1/5-linked signaling and synaptic protein synthesis within the fragile X pathophysiology framework.

steps/5.description: With FMRP absent, basal translation is enhanced and mGluR1/5-linked local translation is no longer appropriately regulated. This distorts the experience-dependent protein synthesis needed for synaptic plasticity.

evidence.snippet: Loss of FMRP, as in fragile X syndrome (FXS), is a leading monogenic cause of autism and results in altered structural and functional synaptic plasticity, widely described in the hippocampus and cortex.
evidence.explanation: This supports altered structural and functional synaptic plasticity as a downstream effect of FMRP loss.

evidence.snippet: Utilizing a cortical-striatal co-culture model, we find that striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs) lacking FMRP fail to make normal increases in PSD95 expression over a short time period and have significant deficits in dendritic spine density and colocalized synaptic puncta at the later measured time point compared to wildtype (WT) MSNs.
evidence.explanation: This in vitro model links FMRP loss to abnormal postsynaptic marker expression, dendritic spine density, and synaptic puncta.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, spine density was increased in both apical and basal dendrites during early development but normalized to wild-type levels in adulthood.
evidence.explanation: Golgi-Cox analysis across four developmental stages from P14 to P150 shows the raised spine density is a developmental feature that resolves, so this node should not be read as asserting a persistent adult spine excess.

evidence.snippet: We identified a progressive reduction in dendritic complexity, reflected by decreased Sholl intersections and reduced dendritic branch number and length.
evidence.explanation: The same study reports the complementary half of the dissociation: while spine density normalizes, dendritic arbor complexity declines with age, which is the structural change that persists into mature circuits. Single unreplicated mouse study in hippocampal CA1 principal neurons.

steps/6.description: FMRP loss disrupts synapse structure and dendritic spine maturation. Patient and model-system literature consistently links fragile X syndrome to altered structural and functional synaptic plasticity, with cell-type and brain-region-specific changes in synapse density and spine morphology. The spine component of this node is age dependent in the mouse rather than static: density is raised during early development and returns to wild-type levels by adulthood, while dendritic branching complexity falls progressively with age. Curate adult structural claims accordingly.

evidence.snippet: Our astrocyte-specific Fmr1 KO (cKO) mouse model reveals reduced inhibitory connectivity and impaired cortical responses to sound.
evidence.explanation: Restricting the Fmr1 deletion to astrocytes still produces the inhibitory and cortical-processing deficit, establishing that this arm does not require neuronal FMRP loss.

evidence.snippet: Blocking astrocyte GABA transport enables higher PV expression, improves EEG responses to frequency-modulated sound, and corrects aberrant exploratory behavior.
evidence.explanation: The rescue arm identifies astrocytic GABA transport specifically, rather than astrocyte dysfunction generally, as the step that carries the circuit-level and behavioral consequences.

evidence.snippet: Human FXS astrocytes derived from patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cells and mouse Fmr1 knockout (KO) astrocytes display a significant increase in levels of GABA and GABA-synthesizing enzyme GAD65/67.
evidence.explanation: The cell-culture arm shows the same GABA and GAD65/67 elevation in patient-derived human astrocytes as in mouse, which is the only human evidence currently attached to this node.

steps/7.description: FMRP is lost in astrocytes as well as neurons. Human FXS iPSC-derived and mouse Fmr1 knockout astrocytes accumulate GABA and the GABA-synthesizing enzymes GAD65/67, and deleting Fmr1 in astrocytes alone reduces inhibitory connectivity and degrades the fidelity of cortical temporal processing. This is a non-neuronal effector arm of FMRP loss that the synaptic translation branch does not cover. Blocking astrocytic GABA transport in the conditional knockout restores parvalbumin expression, EEG responses and exploratory behavior, which is what makes this a mechanism rather than a correlation. Evidence is currently one conditional-knockout study with a human cellular arm, so the node is model derived and awaits replication.

evidence.snippet: Fragile X is the most common known inherited cause of intellectual disability and autism, and it typically results from transcriptional silencing of FMR1 and loss of the encoded protein, FMRP (fragile X mental retardation protein).
evidence.explanation: This ties the neurodevelopmental phenotypes to FMR1 silencing and FMRP loss.

steps/8.description: Synaptic translation and spine abnormalities converge on disrupted neural circuit development and function. This branch accounts for the core cognitive and behavioral manifestations of fragile X syndrome, including intellectual disability, autistic behavior, and hyperactivity.

evidence.snippet: Deficiency of FMRP (fragile X mental retardation protein) appears to lead to increased neuronal excitability and susceptibility to epilepsy, but particularly seems to facilitate mechanisms leading to the BFEC pattern.
evidence.explanation: This clinical review explicitly connects FMRP deficiency to neuronal excitability and epilepsy susceptibility in fragile X syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Our data demonstrate that restoration of greater than 5% of overall FMRP expression levels or greater than 20% FMRP-expressing neurons in a mosaic pattern is sufficient to normalize a FMRP-dependent, hyperactive phenotype in FXS iPSC-derived neurons.
evidence.explanation: Titrating FMRP back into patient-derived excitatory neurons shows the hyperactive phenotype at this node is FMRP dependent and reversible, and sets a low restoration threshold (above 5% of normal FMRP, or above 20% of neurons expressing it) for correcting it in that model system.

steps/9.description: A subset of individuals with fragile X syndrome develop seizures. FMRP deficiency is proposed to increase neuronal excitability and susceptibility to epilepsy, often with childhood-onset focal seizure patterns.

evidence.snippet: Fragile X is the most common known inherited cause of intellectual disability and autism, and it typically results from transcriptional silencing of FMR1 and loss of the encoded protein, FMRP (fragile X mental retardation protein).
evidence.explanation: This supports intellectual disability as a core fragile X manifestation linked to FMR1 silencing and FMRP loss.

steps/10.description: Intellectual disability is a cardinal neurodevelopmental manifestation of fragile X syndrome and is generally more severe in males with full-mutation FMR1 silencing.

evidence.snippet: HP:0002342 | Intellectual disability, moderate | Very frequent (99-80%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet's curated HPO table classifies moderate intellectual disability as very frequent in Fragile X syndrome.

steps/11.description: Moderate intellectual disability is one documented severity within the variable cognitive phenotype of fragile X syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is the leading genetic cause of autism, accounting for approximately 5% of autism cases with as many as 50% of individuals with FXS meeting DSM-IV-TR criteria for autistic disorder.
evidence.explanation: This review supports autism as a frequent comorbid neurodevelopmental phenotype in fragile X syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Fragile X is the most common known inherited cause of intellectual disability and autism, and it typically results from transcriptional silencing of FMR1 and loss of the encoded protein, FMRP (fragile X mental retardation protein).
evidence.explanation: This supports the FMR1/FMRP mechanistic link to autism-related features.

steps/12.description: Autism spectrum disorder is diagnosed in a substantial subset of individuals with fragile X syndrome. Estimates depend on sex, age, ascertainment, and diagnostic criteria; autistic traits can also occur without meeting full diagnostic criteria.

edges/5.description: Loss of FMRP increases basal translation and disrupts mGluR-triggered translational control at synapses.

edges/8.description: Dysregulated local translation alters synaptic plasticity programs that shape dendritic spine and synapse maturation.

edges/9.description: Abnormal synaptic protein synthesis and plasticity impair the neural circuit functions required for cognition, social behavior, and attention.

evidence.snippet: Numerous studies have demonstrated that FMRP interacts with both coding and non-coding RNAs and represses protein synthesis at dendritic and synaptic locations.
evidence.explanation: Canonical mechanism reference used as the seed for the hypothesis-search deep-research run.

hypotheses/0.description: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is caused by CGG-trinucleotide repeat expansion (>200 repeats) in the 5' UTR of FMR1 on Xq27.3, leading to hypermethylation and transcriptional silencing of FMR1 and loss of its protein product FMRP. FMRP is an RNA-binding protein that represses translation of hundreds of synaptic mRNAs at dendrites and is required for the metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR)-dependent regulation of synaptic protein synthesis. Loss of FMRP produces excessive and decoupled local protein synthesis, leading to exaggerated mGluR-LTD, abnormal dendritic spine morphology, altered excitatory/inhibitory balance, and the cognitive and behavioral phenotypes of FXS. mGluR5 antagonists, GABAergic modulators, and IGF-1 / BDNF / MAPK-pathway perturbation studies in Fmr1-knockout mice and human iPSC-derived neurons all corroborate the canonical FMRP-loss / dysregulated synaptic-translation model.

evidence.snippet:
Although a specific ab-
normality of the connective tissue has not yet been
shown, the prevalence of connective tissue signs has sug-
gested that there is an underlying connective tissue
anomaly, perhaps similar to that observed in CTDs (in
particular, Marfan Syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos Syn-
drome); the precise association between FXS and signs
of connective tissue abnormality still awaits biochemical
and molecular explanation [38].
evidence.explanation: The review explicitly identifies the unresolved molecular basis of connective-tissue signs.

open_questions/0.rationale: The prior physical-phenotype node restated a clinical feature list and assigned fibroblast and developmental processes without mechanistic evidence. The clinical literature supports these findings, but the cited review explicitly leaves the biochemical and molecular explanation unresolved; no shared causal mechanism is asserted here.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that macroorchidism in Fmr1 knockout male mice is caused by an increased rate of Sertoli cell proliferation.
evidence.explanation: Direct model-organism evidence; the corresponding human mechanism remains unverified.

open_questions/1.rationale: A mouse experiment establishes increased Sertoli-cell proliferation, but the human clinical sources document enlargement and age dependence without establishing that cellular intermediate. The mouse mechanism is retained as a research lead rather than a proven human causal edge.

open_questions/2.rationale: FMRP loss and synaptic dysfunction establish the broad neurodevelopmental disease mechanism, but the reviewed clinical evidence does not isolate a causal chain for each of these findings. Sleep and behavioral features have plausible neural contributors; growth, ocular, gastrointestinal and otological findings require separate tissue explanations. These phenotype associations are retained without adding arrows solely from coexistence.

evidence.snippet: Mavoglurant, a selective metabotropic glutamate receptor subtype-5 antagonist, has shown positive neuronal and behavioral effects in preclinical studies, but failed to demonstrate any behavioral benefits in two 12-week, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, phase IIb studies in adults and adolescents with FXS.
evidence.explanation: Documents the failure of the mGluR theory's central therapeutic prediction in the age group tested, and the mismatch with the preclinical result that motivated the trials.

evidence.snippet: The study shows that negative modulation of mGluR5 activity improves eye gaze behavior and alters sympathetically-driven reactivity to faces in patients with FXS, providing preliminary evidence of this drug's impact on behavior in humans with the disorder.
evidence.explanation: An eye-tracking biobehavioral probe embedded in the same trials did detect a drug effect, which is why the endpoint explanation for the failure cannot be dismissed.

open_questions/3.rationale: The mGluR theory's one testable clinical prediction has now failed twice over: two phase 2b mavoglurant trials in adolescents and adults missed their behavioral primary endpoints, and the later FXLEARN phase 3 trial in 3 to 6 year olds missed its primary language outcome. Yet mavoglurant did move biobehavioral measures in the same patients, so the drug was reaching its target. Nothing published so far separates the two explanations, and the distinction matters for what this entry asserts: whether the synaptic translation node is the therapeutically relevant driver of the cognitive and behavioral phenotype, or one arm among several. Expert reviews attribute the gap to trial design rather than to the model, but that is opinion rather than a result and should not be curated as a finding.

evidence.snippet: We report that the genomes of FXS cells are inherently unstable and accumulate twice as many DSBs as those from an unaffected control.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the genome-instability observation in patient-derived cells. The study does not link it to any neural or clinical phenotype, which is the gap.

evidence.snippet: Metabolic tracing in FXS neurons demonstrates a dearth of glutamine deamidation to glutamate, which reduces anaplerosis into the TCA cycle, potentially hindering the bioenergetic and biosynthetic functions of mitochondria.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the metabolic observation in patient iPSC-derived neurons. The authors themselves hedge the disease link, and no causal test of it has been reported.

open_questions/4.rationale: FMRP loss has documented consequences that this entry's pathograph does not connect to any phenotype. Patient fibroblasts accumulate twice the double-strand breaks of controls, with breaks colocalizing with R-loop forming sequences under replication stress; patient iPSC-derived neurons show reduced glutaminolysis and impaired anaplerotic supply to the TCA cycle. Both are measured in patient-derived cells, so neither is a model artifact, but neither has been traced to a neural or clinical outcome, and no experiment has separated nuclear from cytoplasmic FMRP function. Until that is done, the entry curates these as observations rather than as arms of the causal chain, and the astrocytic and chromatin arms are curated as nodes only because each has an intervention that reverses a downstream phenotype.

evidence.snippet: As expected, in the presence of APV, we found more LTD in the mouse KO than in WT. This, however, was only observed in the p30-60 age group.
evidence.explanation: States both limits on the phenotype in one sentence pair: it requires NMDA-receptor blockade and it is confined to a single postnatal window.

open_questions/5.rationale: Exaggerated mGluR-LTD is the signature electrophysiological phenotype of the canonical model, but in the Fmr1 knockout mouse it appears only between P30 and P60, and only when NMDA receptors are pharmacologically blocked; the same study concludes that hyperactive GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors, not the mGluR arm alone, underlie the difference. The phenotype has never been demonstrated in human brain tissue or human neuronal preparations. So the entry's mGluR node rests on a mouse measurement whose scope is narrower than the claim usually made from it, and the translational status of the phenotype is the open question rather than its existence.

evidence.snippet: Either GRIN2B or GRIN2A, encoding the NMDA receptor subunits NR2B and NR2A, was found to be disrupted by chromosome translocation breakpoints in individuals with mental retardation and/or epilepsy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes GRIN2B (GluN2B/NR2B) disruption as a cause of intellectual disability and epilepsy.

steps/1.description: De novo heterozygous missense or protein-truncating variants in GRIN2B alter the GluN2B subunit of the NMDA receptor. Because GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors predominate in the developing forebrain, variants perturb the receptor at a developmentally critical window.

evidence.snippet: Functional consequences of variants were diverse, revealing various potential gain-of-function and loss-of-function mechanisms and a retained sensitivity to the use-dependent blocker memantine.
evidence.explanation: Functional characterization identified gain-of-function variant mechanisms.

steps/2.description: A subset of GRIN2B missense variants increases NMDA receptor activity by enhancing agonist (glutamate/glycine) potency, increasing channel open probability or calcium permeability, or reducing voltage-dependent magnesium block, producing excessive NMDA-receptor-mediated current and calcium influx.

evidence.snippet: Functional consequences of variants were diverse, revealing various potential gain-of-function and loss-of-function mechanisms and a retained sensitivity to the use-dependent blocker memantine.
evidence.explanation: Functional characterization identified loss-of-function variant mechanisms.

steps/3.description: Other GRIN2B variants (protein-truncating variants and missense variants that reduce surface trafficking, agonist potency, or current, sometimes dominant-negatively) decrease NMDA receptor function, reducing NMDA-receptor-mediated signaling.

evidence.snippet: N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors mediate excitatory neurotransmission in the mammalian brain.
evidence.explanation: NMDA receptors mediate excitatory neurotransmission, so GRIN2B variants dysregulate this signaling.

steps/4.description: Whether from excessive or deficient receptor activity, the net consequence is disruption of the tightly regulated NMDA-receptor-mediated glutamatergic signaling and calcium-dependent downstream cascades that developing neurons depend on.

steps/5.description: NMDA receptors, and GluN2B in particular, drive dendritic and synaptic maturation and activity-dependent plasticity (long-term potentiation and depression). Their dysregulation impairs synapse organization and plasticity, the substrate of the disorder's developmental delay and intellectual disability.

evidence.snippet: Muscle tone abnormalities (spasticity and/or hypotonia, occasionally associated with feeding difficulties), as well as epilepsy and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) / behavioral issues, are common.
evidence.explanation: Epilepsy is a common manifestation, reflecting the cortical excitation-inhibition imbalance produced by disrupted NMDAR signaling.

steps/6.description: Dysregulated NMDA-receptor signaling shifts the balance between excitation and inhibition in developing cortical networks, producing neuronal hyperexcitability and hypersynchrony that generate seizures.

edges/2.description: Truncating and other missense variants reduce receptor function.
