hypotheses/0.description:
The prevailing reading of MYBPC3 genotype-phenotype relations: hypertrophic, noncompaction, restrictive and dilated presentations are positions on a single continuum, and residual functional cMyBP-C is the variable that sets which one a carrier occupies: a single truncating allele gives adult hypertrophic disease, a biallelic genotype gives severe neonatal disease with noncompaction and septal defects. On this account nothing qualitatively different happens at the low-dose end, and the LVNC phenotype is what severe sarcomeric insufficiency looks like when it strikes during cardiac development.
Only one point on that curve is actually measured anywhere in this entry: approximately 20% residual cMyBP-C in affected cardiac tissue from a compound heterozygote carrying a loss-of-function allele in trans with an unstable missense allele. That is one genotype, not the truncating/ truncating configuration the biallelic subtype is defined by, and no residual-protein figure is available for the heterozygous state or for truncating homozygotes. The half-dose expectation that the model rests on is a haploinsufficiency inference, and the isogenic premature-termination-codon iPSC-CMs curated under `experimental_models` cut against it directly: MYBPC3 transcript fell while protein did not. The model's other weakness is that it explains a severity gradient without explaining a change in kind, and one family carrying a single allele can display three different phenotypes among its members.

evidence.snippet: However, the mechanism leading to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in heterozygous MYBPC3(+/-) individuals is myocyte hypertrophy (increased cell size), whereas the mechanism leading to cardiac dilation in homozygous Mybpc3(-/-) mice is primarily myocyte hyperplasia.
evidence.explanation: The mono- versus bi-allelic divergence in cellular mechanism that this hypothesis generalizes from.

evidence.snippet: Immunofluorescence staining revealed significant hyperplasia in the mutant's total cardiac and ventricular cardiomyocytes.
evidence.explanation: Cross-species replication in a zebrafish cMyBP-C knockout. Hyperplasia arising independently in fish and mouse argues the proliferative response is a conserved consequence of losing cMyBP-C rather than a murine artifact, which is what this hypothesis needs to be worth testing in human tissue. It does not carry the hypothesis's second half: in this model the extra cardiomyocytes accompany a thicker, more compact wall, so hyperplasia here is not producing a compaction failure. Hence INDIRECT.

hypotheses/1.description: A mechanistically distinct account of why the low-dose end diverges in kind rather than only in degree. In homozygous cMyBP-C-deficient mice, myocytes complete an extra round of division after birth and accumulate as supernumerary mononuclear cells; the heart enlarges by hyperplasia, whereas the heterozygous state enlarges it by hypertrophy. The authors conclude that cMyBP-C normally inhibits postnatal myocyte cytokinesis. If that inhibition is dose-sensitive, near-complete loss would extend the proliferative window across precisely the period in which the ventricle finishes converting trabecular to compact myocardium, offering a route from a quantitative protein deficit to a qualitatively different developmental outcome. This is a hypothesis about the human disease, not a finding in it: the mice develop dilation, not noncompaction, and no compaction measurement is reported. A zebrafish cMyBP-C knockout shows the same cardiomyocyte hyperplasia, so the proliferative response is at least conserved rather than murine. That strengthens the first half of the hypothesis and cuts against the second: in the fish the extra cardiomyocytes accompany a thicker, more compact ventricular wall, which is the opposite of a compaction failure. Whatever routes hyperplasia to noncompaction in humans, if anything does, is not supplied by either model.

evidence.snippet: MYBPC has unexpected inhibitory functions during postnatal myocyte cytokinesis and cell cycle progression.
evidence.explanation: The finding that turns this gap from wholly open into one with a named candidate mechanism to test. Cited on the discussion because it bears on the question posed, not because it answers it.

open_questions/0.rationale:
The clinical genetics literature robustly documents the correlation between MYBPC3 allelic dose and phenotype (biallelic loss to severe neonatal noncompaction; monoallelic loss to adult hypertrophic disease), but the mechanistic step converting a quantitative cMyBP-C deficit into a qualitatively different developmental outcome (failure of fetal myocardial compaction, rather than postnatal hypertrophic remodeling) is not established in the cited literature. This differs from the CMH4 myosin super-relaxed-state mechanism, which explains hypercontractility from partial haploinsufficiency but has not been shown to explain the developmental compaction defect at near-complete loss.
A candidate has since been added to this entry rather than left implicit: the homozygous cMyBP-C-deficient mouse shows that the same protein deficit reaches a different cellular endpoint at different allelic dose - hyperplasia through extended postnatal myocyte division at the null dose, hypertrophy at the heterozygous dose - and the authors attribute this to a normal inhibitory role of cMyBP-C in postnatal cytokinesis. That would supply the missing qualitative step, since the extended proliferative window overlaps the period of trabecular-to-compact remodeling. It does not close the gap: the mice develop dilation rather than noncompaction, no compaction measurement is reported, and the extrapolation from myocyte cell-cycle behaviour to ventricular wall architecture is the curator's, not the paper's. The hypothesis is carried as `mechanistic_hypotheses#cytokinesis_brake_release` with status EMERGING.

evidence.snippet: Homozygous cardiac myosin binding protein C-deficient (Mybpc(t/t)) mice develop dramatic cardiac dilation shortly after birth; heart size increases almost twofold.
evidence.explanation: The mismatch stated in the sharpest available form: the biallelic-null mouse phenotype is dilation, and the human biallelic phenotype this entity is named for is noncompaction.

evidence.snippet: The MYBPC3-edited piglet exhibited a compound heterozygous mutation leading to a markedly low level of mutant MYBPC3 protein and cardiac hypertrophy, reflecting the situation in infants.
evidence.explanation: The large-animal attempt reaches hypertrophy, not noncompaction, so the mismatch is not confined to rodents.

open_questions/1.rationale:
Of the models attached here, four reach a biallelic or null MYBPC3 state and none reaches the phenotype the entity is named for. The homozygous cMyBP-C-deficient mouse dilates; the compound heterozygous cloned pig hypertrophies and dies perinatally; the zebrafish knockout makes its ventricle *more* compact, with a thicker wall, which is the opposite failure; the biallelic hiPSC line is a resource report with no phenotype assayed, and its two-dimensional cardiomyocytes have no ventricular wall in which compaction could be scored. (The remaining human line, the premature-termination-codon iPSC-CMs, is heterozygous and does not reach the allelic state at all.) So the defining lesion of this entity - persistence of a noncompacted, hypertrabeculated ventricular wall - currently rests entirely on human imaging and autopsy, with no experimental system in which it can be perturbed or rescued.
This is a mismatch worth stating rather than a gap in curation. The mouse and pig phenotypes are not merely weaker versions of the human one, they are different phenotypes, and in the zebrafish the difference is one of sign rather than degree. Species differences in the timing of ventricular compaction relative to birth are a plausible reason. Until a model reproduces the compaction defect, therapeutic inferences from the rescue experiments in this entry - the neonatal exon-skipping rescue and the Tet-Off reversibility result - bear on contractile and hypertrophic phenotypes, not on whether a compaction defect is preventable or reversible.
Two 2024 human systems surfaced by the same deep-research pass were left out and the reason belongs here rather than nowhere: MYBPC3 p.D389V cardiac organoids showing mavacamten-reversible hypercontractility (doi:10.3390/cells13221913), and MYBPC3 c.1377delC iPSC-CM metabolic remodeling (doi:10.1038/s41598-024-62530-0). Both are heterozygous missense- or single-frameshift-allele HCM systems, further from the biallelic genotype than the lines curated above, and neither scores compaction. The organoid one is worth revisiting, since a cardiac organoid is exactly the system the experiment proposed below would need. The report also surfaced NCT06024759, a generic-LVNC risk registry with no MYBPC3-specific arm, which is why `clinical_trials` remains empty.

evidence.snippet: This is a complex system involving several host receptors and a major parasite-derived variant antigen (PfEMP1) expressed on the surface of the infected erythrocyte membrane. Previous studies have suggested a role for ICAM-1 in the pathology of cerebral malaria, although these have been inconclusive. In this study we have examined the cytoadherence patterns of 101 patient isolates from varying clinical syndromes to CD36 and ICAM-1, and have used variant ICAM-1 proteins to further characterise this adhesive phenotype. Our results show that increased binding to CD36 is associated with uncomplicated malaria while ICAM-1 adhesion is raised in parasites from cerebral malaria cases.

steps/1.description: In severe falciparum malaria, parasitized erythrocytes sequester in the microvasculature, promoting endothelial injury, impaired perfusion, and downstream organ dysfunction. Sequestration is mediated by Plasmodium falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 (PfEMP1), a variant surface antigen family encoded by the var multigene family and displayed on the infected-erythrocyte surface, which binds host endothelial receptors including CD36 and ICAM-1; receptor usage differs by clinical syndrome, with increased CD36 binding associated with uncomplicated malaria and increased ICAM-1 binding associated with cerebral malaria.

open_questions/0.rationale: Severe malarial anemia has two well-established arms: increased destruction and clearance of uninfected erythrocytes, and suppressed or ineffective erythrocyte production. This entry models the first arm. Its quantitative source is a 1999 retrospective model of non-immune adults undergoing induced malaria therapy, which reports dyserythropoiesis as insignificant in that dataset - a model output, not a marrow measurement, and from a population unlike the pediatric endemic syndrome the term "severe malarial anemia" names elsewhere in this file. A 2022 review of the marrow arm draws on children with malarial anemia and describes ineffective erythropoiesis and dyserythropoiesis as general features of malaria across Plasmodium species. The two are not straightforwardly reconcilable, and the relative contribution is recorded here as unsettled rather than being resolved in the node description. Modelling the erythropoietic arm as its own pathophysiology node is the natural follow-up.

evidence.snippet: A total of 18 different variants were identified, including 10 missense variants,1 nonsense variant, 2 splice site variants, 4 frameshift variants, and 2 small in-frame duplications. Approximately half of these patients carried the missense variant c.371 T > C(p. I124T).
evidence.explanation: The allelic spectrum tallied across every case reported to that point, which is the claim this trigger node makes.

evidence.snippet: The mechanism of disease is loss of function.
evidence.explanation: The mechanism the expert panel assigns, which is what the functional_impact_category on this node records.

steps/2.description: Two damaged copies of NDUFAF6 (formerly C8orf38), which encodes a mitochondrial complex I assembly factor. The reported spectrum spans several mutation classes. Across the 24 patients tallied in the 2026 review, eighteen distinct variants have been reported - ten missense, one nonsense, two splice-site, four frameshift and two small in-frame duplications - and roughly half of those patients carry a single recurrent missense allele, c.371T>C p.Ile124Thr. The largest single cohort adds nineteen further distinct variants from eighteen families. Only the canonical transcript NM_152416.4 encodes the mitochondrially targeted protein, which is why a deep intronic variant altering isoform choice can be pathogenic without changing any coding sequence.

evidence.snippet: Human NDUFAF6 is a mitochondria-targeted 333-amino acid protein belonging to the family of squalene and phytoene synthases.
evidence.explanation: The protein family, size and subcellular targeting, from the sequence and structural analysis that characterised NDUFAF6.

steps/3.description: NDUFAF6 acts at the initial stages of complex I assembly. It is a mitochondria-targeted 333-amino-acid peripheral membrane protein of the squalene and phytoene synthase family, an assignment that is itself informative: sequence and structure suggest it retains some enzymatic activity, but one that has diverged considerably from the canonical members of that family, so what it actually catalyses here is not established. Not every metazoan has an ortholog, which means complex I biogenesis does not require it in all organisms. Losing it removes a component from the step at which the nuclear-encoded matrix arm and the mtDNA-encoded membrane arm are first brought together.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, upon inactivation of NDUFAF6, we found a dramatic reduction of NDUFS3 belonging to the Q module, an intermediate reduction of NDUFS1 belonging to the N module and an even milder decrease of NDUFB11 belonging to the P module.
evidence.explanation: The module-graded subunit loss in patient material, which is the gel-level signature of a Q-module assembly block.

steps/4.description: NDUFS8 is a core subunit of the Q module. Without NDUFAF6 it is not incorporated, and the module does not mature. The consequence is visible on patient gels as a module-graded loss of subunits: Q-module NDUFS3 falls dramatically, N-module NDUFS1 intermediately, and P-module NDUFB11 least. That gradient is itself informative, because it is the known turnover order of complex I modules when assembly fails rather than a random loss.

evidence.snippet: In the absence of ND1 in patient cells, early- and mid-stage intermediate complexes were still formed; however, assembly of late-stage intermediates was impaired, indicating a convergence point in the assembly process.
evidence.explanation: Which stage of assembly stalls, which is what distinguishes this node from a general statement that assembly is reduced.

steps/5.description: In fibroblasts from a patient with a C8orf38 mutation, steady-state complex I was almost undetectable and biogenesis of the mtDNA-encoded ND1 subunit was defective. Early- and mid-stage intermediates still formed; it was late-stage assembly that failed, identifying a convergence point in the pathway. Complementation with wild-type C8orf38 restored both ND1 and complex I.

evidence.snippet: Residual respiratory-chain complex (RCC) activity was reduced both in cultured fibroblasts (n = 9; range 40–86%) and in muscle (n = 6; range 28–80%).
evidence.explanation: The quantified residual activity in both tissues sampled, which is the numeric basis for calling this deficiency partial.

evidence.snippet: We validate a subset of these predictions using RNAi, including C8orf38, which we further show harbors an inherited mutation in a lethal, infantile CI deficiency.
evidence.explanation: The founding observation linking this gene to inherited complex I deficiency, from the integrative-genomics screen that identified it.

steps/6.description: Too little functioning NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase, with the other respiratory chain complexes spared. The deficiency is partial rather than complete and the residual activity has been quantified: across the reviewed cases, residual respiratory chain complex activity was 40 to 86 percent of control in cultured fibroblasts and 28 to 80 percent in muscle. That residual enzyme is the most likely explanation for the comparatively preserved motor function this disease shows against other Leigh syndrome genotypes, and it is also why a near-normal fibroblast assay does not exclude the diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: CI deficiency also led to significant respirasome (CI/III2/IV) depletion and accumulation of homodimeric complex III, consistent with previously characterized CI assembly defects.
evidence.explanation: The measurement of supercomplex loss in patient material.

steps/7.description: Loss of the assembled CI/III2/IV supercomplex, with homodimeric complex III accumulating in its place. This is a recognised downstream signature of complex I assembly defects rather than a separate lesion, and it is recorded here because it is measured directly in this disease's patient material.

evidence.snippet: Meanwhile, cellular ATP production was decreased, and mitochondrial ROS was increased.
evidence.explanation: The two readouts this node names, measured in patient-derived cells.

evidence.snippet: establishing that LOF variants consistently fail to restore ATP levels and complex I assembly
evidence.explanation: The 2026 review's restatement of the deep mutational scan's ATP result. It is not this paper's own experiment and not independent of PMID:38720117, which is its source; it is cited because the scan's own cached full text carries no equivalent ATP-rescue sentence to quote directly. IN_VITRO grades the work described, REVIEW_SYNTHESIS records that the citing paper is restating it.

steps/8.description: The cellular bioenergetic failure: less ATP generated by oxidative phosphorylation and more mitochondrial reactive oxygen species. Demonstrated in patient-derived immortalized B lymphocytes, and independently in the deep mutational scan, where loss-of-function NDUFAF6 variants consistently fail to restore ATP levels.

evidence.snippet: Brain magnetic resonance showed symmetric and bilateral cytotoxic lesions in the putamen and proliferation of the lenticular-striate arteries, latter spreading to the caudate and progressing to cavitation and volume loss.
evidence.explanation: The anatomy and the progression of the lesion, which is what this tissue-level node asserts.

evidence.snippet: typically associated with characteristic basal ganglia lesions on MRI, predominantly involving the putamen (14 of 14) and, to a lesser extent, the caudate nucleus (6 of 14)
evidence.explanation: The putamen-first distribution with counts, across the published literature rather than a single family.

steps/9.description:
Symmetrical destruction of the striatum, putamen first. In the deeply phenotyped kindred the lesions were cytotoxic, involved proliferation of the lenticulo-striate arteries, and spread from putamen to caudate before cavitating with volume loss. Across the published literature the putamen was involved in every case in which the basal ganglia were described, and the caudate in fewer than half. This tissue selectivity - rather than the enzyme deficiency, which is present in fibroblasts and muscle too - is what makes the disease a neurological one.
The cell type bound below is inferred rather than sourced. No NDUFAF6 study names a cell type: the imaging and the one published description of the lesion are at tissue level, and no neuropathology has been reported for any patient. Medium spiny neurons are the principal projection neuron of the striatum and so are the cell the lesion is presumed to destroy, but which striatal populations are lost, and in what order, is unknown in this disease.

evidence.snippet: All individuals exhibited pronounced neurodevelopmental regression during infancy or early childhood (7 months to 6 years), characterized by the loss of previously acquired motor milestones, dystonia, and significant delay or loss of language.
evidence.explanation: The feature, its age window, and what is lost, across every case reported to that point.

evidence.snippet: The clinical presentation showed wide phenotypic variability, from mild to severe psychomotor regression (74%) most commonly before the age of 5 years, hypotonia (22%), movement disorders (30%), and hypertonia (15%).
evidence.explanation: The rate in the largest single cohort, which is the lower of the two published readings.

steps/10.description: Loss of previously acquired motor milestones and of language, the presenting feature in nearly every reported patient and the one that defines the onset of the disease. Onset is in infancy or early childhood, most commonly before the age of five.

evidence.snippet: Generalized dystonia was reported in 71% of published cases, with onset typically occurring between 4 and 11 years of age (median: 5.4 years). In our cohort, generalized dystonia was present in 41% of cases, with a similarly early onset consistent with the literature (range: 14 months to 10 years; median: 3 years).
evidence.explanation: Both rates and both onset distributions, from the source that reports them side by side.

evidence.snippet: Three siblings developed gait dystonia in infancy followed by rapid progression to generalised dystonia and psychomotor regression.
evidence.explanation: The progression from focal gait dystonia to the generalised form, in one kindred.

steps/11.description: The characteristic movement disorder. It typically begins as gait dystonia and progresses to generalised dystonia, often with dysarthria and eventual loss of ambulation. Onset is early - median around three years in the largest cohort, around five in the published literature.

evidence.snippet: All patients (21/21) exhibited basal ganglia neuronal degeneration on MRI, and the imaging findings met the criteria for “bilateral striatal necrosis” (BSN) (30).
evidence.explanation: The count and the explicit statement that formal BSN criteria were met.

evidence.snippet: Bilateral striatal necrosis lesions were the most characteristic features on cranial MRI (67%) although white matter abnormalities were also noted (15%), occasionally accompanied by cystic formations, suggestive of early neurodevelopmental anomalies.
evidence.explanation: The rate in the largest cohort, set against the alternative imaging pattern.

steps/12.description: The neuroimaging hallmark: symmetrical basal ganglia lesions meeting published criteria for bilateral striatal necrosis. It is the finding that identifies the disease radiologically and it is present in every published case in which basal ganglia imaging was reported.

evidence.snippet: often accompanied by severe dysarthria and eventual loss of ambulation, frequently leading to wheelchair dependence
evidence.explanation: The feature and its severity, as reported in the largest cohort.

steps/13.description: Severe dysarthria, described alongside the movement disorder in the families in which speech was reported. It is the speech counterpart of the extrapyramidal syndrome rather than a separate deficit, and it sits alongside the delay or loss of language that is part of the developmental regression.

evidence.snippet: often accompanied by severe dysarthria and eventual loss of ambulation, frequently leading to wheelchair dependence
evidence.explanation: The outcome and the dependence it leads to, as reported in the largest cohort.

steps/14.description: Progressive loss of independent walking, ending in wheelchair dependence. It is the motor endpoint of the disease in those who survive the early years, and it is the outcome against which this disease's comparatively preserved motor function is measured.

evidence.snippet: Additional features often include dystonia, dysphagia, and intermittent metabolic crises triggered by concurrent infections.
evidence.explanation: The feature and its trigger, named in the review of every reported case.

evidence.snippet: P1 developed an early metabolic decompensation which evolved into multisystem involvement with a stable, normal neurological examination
evidence.explanation: A decompensation event in an individual patient, and the recovery that shows these episodes are not uniformly terminal.

steps/15.description: Intermittent episodes of metabolic decompensation precipitated by concurrent infection. These are the acute events that punctuate an otherwise gradual course, and in the largest cohort they are where the stepwise losses happen: one sibling recovered completely from an early decompensation while another died of one. Avoiding metabolic stressors is consequently a management aim rather than only a prognostic observation.

evidence.snippet: Patient mutations were associated with the absence of the NDUFAF6 protein and reduced activity and assembly of mature complex I in fibroblasts.
evidence.explanation: The step from allele to missing assembly factor, measured as protein absence in the patients' own cells rather than inferred from the enzyme deficiency.

edges/1.description: The alleles reduce or abolish the assembly factor itself. In the three-sibling kindred the protein was undetectable; across the largest cohort the functional studies show a deleterious effect on NDUFAF6 protein expression.

evidence.snippet: Guided by these data, biochemical analyses and cross-linking mass spectrometry, we discovered that the CIAF NDUFAF6 facilitates incorporation of NDUFS8 into CI and reveal that NDUFS8 overexpression rectifies NDUFAF6 deficiency.
evidence.explanation: The step from absent factor to the specific subunit that fails to be incorporated, with the rescue experiment that makes it causal rather than correlative.

edges/2.description: The specific biochemical job the factor does, established by deep mutational scanning of thousands of NDUFAF6 variants together with cross-linking mass spectrometry.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that C8orf38 is a crucial factor required for the translation and/or integration of ND1 into an early-stage assembly intermediate and that mutation of C8orf38 disrupts the initial stages of complex I biogenesis.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own conclusion on what losing the factor does to ND1 and to the initial stages of assembly.

edges/3.description: The older and independently derived account of the same block, from patient fibroblasts and complementation: without the factor, the mtDNA-encoded ND1 subunit is not made or not stabilised, and assembly halts at a defined convergence point.

evidence.snippet: Blue native gel electrophoresis demonstrated isolated reductions in CI steady-state levels and enzymatic activity across all patients, without complete loss, indicating residual functional CI.
evidence.explanation: The step from failed assembly to reduced holoenzyme, measured across the whole cohort, and the residual-activity qualification that the rest of this entry turns on.

edges/4.description: Too little mature holoenzyme is produced. The cohort data make the key quantitative point that the loss is partial in every patient studied.

evidence.snippet: Complementation with wild-type C8orf38 restored the levels of both ND1 and complex I, confirming the C8orf38 mutation as the cause of the complex I defect in the patient.
evidence.explanation: The rescue that localises the enzyme deficiency to this gene and to this assembly step.

edges/5.description: The assembly block is what produces the enzyme deficiency, shown by the complementation that restores both together.

evidence.snippet: CI deficiency also led to significant respirasome (CI/III2/IV) depletion and accumulation of homodimeric complex III, consistent with previously characterized CI assembly defects.
evidence.explanation: The step from holoenzyme deficiency to supercomplex loss, with the complex III accumulation that shows it is a redistribution rather than a second primary defect.

edges/6.description: Less monomeric complex I means less of it available to enter respiratory supercomplexes, with a matching accumulation of the complex III homodimer that would otherwise be bound into them.

evidence.snippet: The deficiency of mature super complex of complex I was confirmed in patient-derived immortalized B lymphocytes. Meanwhile, cellular ATP production was decreased, and mitochondrial ROS was increased.
evidence.explanation: The step from assembly deficiency to the two downstream bioenergetic readouts, measured in the same patient cells.

edges/7.description: The bioenergetic consequence, measured in patient-derived immortalized B lymphocytes.

evidence.snippet: These variants disrupt the assembly of complex I and reduce its activity, leading to MC1DN17.
evidence.explanation: The source states the causal path from assembly failure through reduced activity to the disease, but does not measure the energy deficit in striatal tissue, which is why this evidence is graded INDIRECT.

edges/8.description: The step from a cell-wide energy deficit to the selective destruction of the striatum is the least established link in this chain, and the intermediates are unknown. No NDUFAF6 study has measured energy failure in striatal tissue; the inference rests on the consistency of the imaging finding across patients and on the general relationship between complex I deficiency and basal ganglia vulnerability in Leigh syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Brain magnetic resonance showed symmetric and bilateral cytotoxic lesions in the putamen and proliferation of the lenticular-striate arteries, latter spreading to the caudate and progressing to cavitation and volume loss.
evidence.explanation: The imaging description of the tissue lesion, which is what makes the MRI finding a reading of this node rather than an independent observation.

edges/9.description: The imaging finding is the radiological appearance of this tissue lesion, not a separate event: the MRI shows the cytotoxic damage, its spread from putamen to caudate, and its progression to cavitation and volume loss.

evidence.snippet: NDUFAF6-related Leigh syndrome is a relevant cause of childhood onset dystonia and isolated bilateral striatal necrosis.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own pairing of the striatal lesion with the dystonia, which is the claim this edge makes.

edges/10.description: Striatal destruction is the lesion behind the extrapyramidal movement disorder, which is the clinical feature the disease is named for in the 2019 series.

evidence.snippet: A literature review of 14 NDUFAF6 patients showed a consistent phenotype of an early childhood insidious onset neurological regression with prominent dystonia associated with basal ganglia degeneration and long survival.
evidence.explanation: The regression and the basal ganglia degeneration reported as one associated phenotype across the reviewed patients.

edges/11.description: Basal ganglia degeneration and the neurological regression are reported as one clinical picture in this disease, the regression being what the striatal damage costs the child.

evidence.snippet: movement disorders such as dystonia, bradykinesia, and spastic–dystonic tetraparesis were present, often accompanied by severe dysarthria and eventual loss of ambulation, frequently leading to wheelchair dependence
evidence.explanation: The source pairs the dysarthria with the movement disorder in the same clause, which is what this edge asserts.

edges/12.description: Severe dysarthria accompanies the movement disorder in the families in which it was described. The causal direction here is the curator's inference, not the source's claim: the source says "often accompanied by", which is co-occurrence. Dystonic dysarthria from orofacial and laryngeal involvement is the clinically expected reading in a generalised dystonia, but these patients also have the language loss of the developmental regression, and no source separates the two contributions.

evidence.snippet: movement disorders such as dystonia, bradykinesia, and spastic–dystonic tetraparesis were present, often accompanied by severe dysarthria and eventual loss of ambulation, frequently leading to wheelchair dependence
evidence.explanation: The source states loss of ambulation as the eventual outcome of the movement disorder, which is the causal direction this edge records.

edges/13.description: The motor endpoint of the progressive movement disorder, reaching wheelchair dependence.

evidence.snippet: Additional features often include dystonia, dysphagia, and intermittent metabolic crises triggered by concurrent infections.
evidence.explanation: The clinical association between infection and crisis. It is INDIRECT because the source reports the trigger, not the bioenergetic measurement this edge's target names.

edges/14.description: Infection precipitates decompensation in a patient whose baseline ATP production is already reduced. The intermediates are unknown: no NDUFAF6 study measures bioenergetic state during an infective episode, so the link rests on the reported clinical association between infection and crisis plus the management advice that follows from it.

evidence.snippet: intermittent metabolic crises triggered by concurrent infections
evidence.explanation: The precipitating relationship, stated by the source in the same words this edge asserts.

edges/15.description: The source states the precipitating relationship directly: the crises are triggered by concurrent infections. Unlike the bioenergetic edge above, no inference step is involved - this is the association the literature reports, at the level at which it reports it.

evidence.snippet: NDUFAF6 | HGNC:28625 | Leigh syndrome | MONDO:0009723 | AR | Definitive | SOP7 | Mitochondrial Diseases Gene Curation Expert Panel | 2020-11-23T19:42:12.660Z
evidence.explanation: The expert-panel validity classification against Leigh syndrome, which is the strongest available statement that this gene causes this disease.

evidence.snippet: This curation included eight unique variants identified in seven cases from seven publications (PMIDs: 18614015, 30642748, 29531337, 27623250, 28639102, 31967322, 32020600). Segregation data includes 3 affected individuals from one kindred (PMID: 30642748).
evidence.explanation: The case and segregation evidence the panel scored, which is what makes the Definitive call auditable.

evidence.snippet: Complementation assay underlined a recovery of complex I activity after transduction of the wild-type gene.
evidence.explanation: The rescue in the patient's own cells, which is what makes this a mechanism rather than a statistical association.

genes/0.notes:
NDUFAF6 (HGNC:28625, "NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase complex assembly factor 6") is at 8q22.1. Its previous symbol is C8orf38, the name under which the gene was described in 2008 and the name used in the older assembly literature; the HGNC record also lists the aliases lncREST and MGC40214.
The ClinGen Mitochondrial Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel has curated this gene twice, and the pair is worth reading together. In April 2020 (SOP7) it classified NDUFAF6 against Leigh syndrome (MONDO:0009723) as Definitive. In June 2024 (SOP10), jointly with the Tubulopathy Expert Panel, it re-curated the gene against primary mitochondrial disease (MONDO:0044970), explicitly lumping the NDUFAF6 phenotype - including the Acadian renal presentation - into one entity under the ClinGen Lumping and Splitting Framework. dismech splits the same biology per gene and per phenotype, so neither ClinGen target is this entry's disease term. Both assertions are cited as gene-disease validity evidence, which they are at any granularity; nothing here depends on adopting either MONDO identifier.

evidence.snippet: There are currently no disease-modifying treatments available; only supportive care can be provided.
evidence.explanation: The explicit statement that no disease-modifying option exists, from the most recent systematic review of the disease.

evidence.snippet: Management remains primarily supportive and symptomatic, encompassing seizure control, management of dystonia, nutritional support, avoidance of metabolic stressors (e.g., infections), and individualized rehabilitation
evidence.explanation: The components the review names, which is what "supportive care" consists of in this disease rather than a generic label.

evidence.snippet: The proband underwent physical therapy and nutrient cocktail therapy, but his physical impairment gradually worsened.
evidence.explanation: The only reported treatment course and its outcome in a single patient, including that the impairment progressed under it.

treatments/0.description: There is no disease-modifying treatment. Management is supportive: the 2026 review states this explicitly after surveying every reported case. The one published account of active management in a single patient describes physical therapy and a nutrient cocktail, under which the physical impairment nonetheless gradually worsened - which is recorded here because it is the only reported outcome of treatment in this disease, not because it recommends the approach.

evidence.snippet: Management remains primarily supportive and symptomatic, encompassing seizure control, management of dystonia, nutritional support, avoidance of metabolic stressors (e.g., infections), and individualized rehabilitation
evidence.explanation: The recommendation and the example of a stressor it names, from the systematic review of every reported case.

treatments/1.description: Avoiding the precipitants of metabolic decompensation, infection foremost among them, with prompt treatment of intercurrent illness. This is the one management measure in this disease that acts on the mechanism rather than on a symptom, since it targets the acute demand that a complex I-deficient cell cannot meet. No trial supports it in NDUFAF6 disease; it is recommended practice, and is recorded as such.

evidence.snippet: Management remains primarily supportive and symptomatic, encompassing seizure control, management of dystonia, nutritional support, avoidance of metabolic stressors (e.g., infections), and individualized rehabilitation
evidence.explanation: The management components named for this disease.

evidence.snippet: The proband underwent physical therapy and nutrient cocktail therapy, but his physical impairment gradually worsened.
evidence.explanation: The only reported course of active management and its outcome, which is why this is recorded as symptomatic rather than disease-modifying.

treatments/2.description: Symptomatic management of the movement disorder together with individualized rehabilitation, nutritional support and seizure control. The single published account of active management in this disease describes physical therapy and a nutrient cocktail under which the impairment nonetheless progressed, so the aim is function and comfort rather than alteration of the course.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, the genotype does not adequately predict long-term outcome. The age of onset and disease progression in patients carrying these variants often demonstrate unpredictability.
evidence.explanation: The limit on what counselling can currently say about prognosis, stated by the review that looked for a correlation and did not find one.

treatments/3.description: Autosomal recessive counselling, with a one-in-four sibling recurrence risk. Prognostic counselling is the harder part and is currently limited by the absence of any genotype-phenotype correlation: the sequencing result identifies the disease but does not predict the course.

evidence.snippet: All but one patient were alive at the time of publication; the exception died at 34 months (18).
evidence.explanation: The low-mortality figure, from the review of published cases.

evidence.snippet: Twelve patients died and for 10 of them this occurred before 12 years.
evidence.explanation: The high-mortality figure, from the previously unreported cohort.

evidence.snippet: Patients with mutations in NDUFAF6, SURF1, and ECHS1 had better outcomes than those with mutations in other nDNA encoded genes.
evidence.explanation: Graded REFUTE against the ascertainment explanation specifically, not against the discrepancy. This series was ascertained through a national patient registry rather than through the published literature, so it is not subject to the publication bias the rationale invokes, and it still finds NDUFAF6 outcomes better than other nuclear genotypes.

evidence.snippet: There was a significant difference in onset age between NDUFAF6 deficient patients who maintained head control (N = 5) and patients either deceased or who had lost head control (N = 3; P = .004).
evidence.explanation: The size of the NDUFAF6 subgroup, and the age-at-onset effect within it that makes onset age a candidate confounder behind the two cohorts' differing mortality.

evidence.snippet: We also made inquiry via the Japan Mitochondrial Disease Research Organization Data Bank (J‐MO Bank), a Japanese patient registry for mitochondrial disorders
evidence.explanation: The ascertainment route, which is what makes this series a test of the publication-bias explanation rather than another instance of it.

open_questions/0.rationale:
Two systematic accounts of this disease were published within weeks of each other and they do not agree about the thing families most want to know. The review of 24 published cases reports that all but one patient were alive at the time of publication, a mortality of 1 in 24, and concludes that NDUFAF6 patients have a better prognosis than other nuclear-gene Leigh syndrome. The 27-patient cohort reports 12 deaths, 37 percent, with 10 of them before 12 years.
Ascertainment is the obvious explanation and the direction is predictable once stated. Published single-case reports and small series are written about living patients under follow-up, so a review of the published literature under-counts deaths systematically. A previously unreported multi-centre cohort assembled from diagnostic services captures completed courses. Neither is a population sample.
But ascertainment is not the whole answer, and the evidence that complicates it is the reason this is recorded as open rather than explained. A Japanese national study surveyed 166 Leigh syndrome patients through a patient registry rather than through the literature - which is exactly the design the ascertainment argument calls for - and found that NDUFAF6 patients had better outcomes than those with variants in other nuclear genes. Its NDUFAF6 subgroup is small, eight individuals, of whom five retained head control and three had died or lost it. So the favourable-prognosis claim survives in a registry-ascertained series, and cannot simply be dismissed as a publication artefact of the case-report literature.
That leaves a sharper question than the one the discrepancy first suggests. The same study reports that within NDUFAF6 specifically, later onset went with better outcome - so the prognostic variable may be age at onset rather than genotype, and a cohort's mortality would then track how much infantile-onset disease it happened to capture. That would explain both 2026 figures without either being wrong. Testing it needs age-at-onset stratified survival across the pooled cohorts, which no published analysis has done.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, P1 developed renal Fanconi syndrome and carried the same deep intronic NDUFAF6 variant described in a homozygous state in the Acadian population and associated with the same clinical condition.
evidence.explanation: The single patient in whom the two phenotypes and the two allele classes meet, which is what makes the boundary uncertain.

evidence.snippet: Of note, while not yet reported in the medical literature, members of this Expert Panel knew of additional cases who were compound heterozygous for this variant in addition to a different variant who did not have the Acadian variant of Fanconi syndrome phenotype but rather a multiorgan system disorder.
evidence.explanation: The panel's unpublished observation pointing the same way from the other phenotype, which is why the allele-combination hypothesis is worth testing.

open_questions/1.rationale:
NDUFAF6 causes two clinically separate diseases. MC1DN17 is Leigh syndrome with striatal necrosis. The Acadian variant of Fanconi syndrome is a renal and pulmonary disease - proximal tubular dysfunction from birth, progressive chronic kidney disease, pulmonary interstitial fibrosis - in a Nova Scotia founder population homozygous for a deep intronic allele, and dismech curates it separately as FRTS5 within Fanconi Renotubular Syndrome.
The boundary is not clean, which is what makes this a gap rather than a settled split. One patient in the largest MC1DN17 cohort developed renal Fanconi syndrome and carried that same Acadian deep intronic allele, on a Leigh syndrome background. His affected brother died before it could be known whether he would have done the same. The cohort authors raise, and explicitly decline to settle, the possibility that a more deleterious allele in trans modulates renal penetrance. The ClinGen panel notes from the other direction that its members know of unpublished compound heterozygotes for the Acadian allele who had a multi-organ disorder rather than the Acadian renal phenotype.
So the two entities may be separated by allele combination, by founder-population modifiers, or by neither. Until that is settled the split between this entry and FRTS5 is a curation decision that follows the clinical literature, not a demonstrated biological boundary.

evidence.snippet: They were found to be homozygous for a novel c.1601T>G (p.Leu534Arg) mutation in the OPA1 gene, which resulted in a marked loss of steady-state levels of the native OPA1 protein.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the causal homozygous OPA1 variant and its consequence, a marked loss of steady-state OPA1 protein.

evidence.snippet: Our modelling work suggests that this amino acid substitution, in the close vicinity of the protein's critical GTPase domain, could destabilise the protein, accounting for the significantly reduced OPA1 protein level observed on western blot analysis
evidence.explanation: In silico modelling result linking the p.Leu534Arg substitution near the catalytic GTPase domain to protein destabilization and the reduced steady-state OPA1 measured on western blot. This is the source's vicinity framing; the domain-membership framing is the next item.

evidence.snippet: This previously unreported OPA1 variant affects the GTPase catalytic domain
evidence.explanation: Domain-annotation lookup (mitodyn OPA1 database) placing the variant in the GTPase catalytic domain. Recorded alongside the modelling sentence above because the two say different things about position, and the entry deliberately carries both rather than resolving the boundary call.

evidence.snippet: OPA1 encodes for a large multimeric dynamin-like GTPase protein, which localises to the inner mitochondrial membrane where it plays a crucial role in mediating mitochondrial fusion.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the molecular identity and inner-membrane localisation of the affected protein.

steps/1.description: OPA1 is a large, multimeric, dynamin-like GTPase that localises to the inner mitochondrial membrane. In MTDPS14B the homozygous c.1601T>G (p.Leu534Arg) substitution replaces a highly conserved hydrophobic leucine with arginine immediately adjacent to the catalytic GTPase domain. In silico modelling predicts that this destabilises the protein fold, and western blotting of patient skeletal muscle confirms a marked reduction in steady-state native OPA1. Because OPA1 acts as an oligomer, the complete absence of a wild-type allele in the homozygous state is expected to further compromise stability through impaired oligomerisation.

evidence.snippet: there was evidence of significant mtDNA depletion with a 78% decrease for patient I-1 and a 78% decrease for patient I-2 compared with control values
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the mtDNA depletion in patient skeletal muscle that defines this disorder as a mtDNA depletion syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Long-range PCR performed on homogenate DNA extracted from the muscle biopsy specimens of the two affected sisters did not reveal any multiple mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) deletions
evidence.explanation: Distinguishes the depletion phenotype from the multiple-mtDNA-deletion phenotype otherwise associated with OPA1 mutation carriers.

evidence.snippet: silencing of the OPA1 variants including exon 4b leads to mtDNA depletion, secondary to inhibition of mtDNA replication, and to marked alteration of mtDNA distribution in nucleoid and nucleoid distribution throughout the mitochondrial network
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates in human cells that loss of exon-4b-containing OPA1 isoforms causes mtDNA depletion through inhibited replication, the mechanism proposed for the muscle mtDNA depletion in this disorder.

evidence.snippet: might contribute to nucleoid attachment to the inner mitochondrial membrane and promotes mtDNA replication and distribution
evidence.explanation: Identifies the exon-4b-derived peptide as the physical link between OPA1 and mtDNA nucleoids.

steps/2.description: Beyond membrane fusion, OPA1 is required for maintenance of the mitochondrial genome. A small hydrophobic peptide derived from the OPA1 isoform containing alternatively spliced exon 4b is embedded in the inner membrane and co-immunoprecipitates with nucleoid components, tethering nucleoids to the inner membrane and promoting mtDNA replication and distribution. Silencing exon-4b-containing OPA1 isoforms in human cells causes mtDNA depletion secondary to inhibited mtDNA replication. In MTDPS14B, quantitative PCR of patient skeletal muscle showed a roughly 78% reduction in mtDNA copy number in both affected sisters, while long-range PCR found no multiple mtDNA deletions — the depletion phenotype, not the deletion phenotype seen in older OPA1 mutation carriers, is what places this disorder in the mtDNA depletion syndrome series.

evidence.snippet: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) assay of muscle biopsy from patient I-2 disclosed large mitochondria with incomplete fusion of the inner mitochondrial membrane
evidence.explanation: Direct ultrastructural demonstration of defective inner mitochondrial membrane fusion in patient muscle.

evidence.snippet: Mitochondrial morphology was consistent with abnormal mitochondrial membrane fusion.
evidence.explanation: Summarises the morphological finding as abnormal mitochondrial membrane fusion in the affected siblings.

steps/3.description: OPA1 mediates fusion of the inner mitochondrial membrane. Transmission electron microscopy of patient skeletal muscle in MTDPS14B disclosed large mitochondria with incomplete fusion of the inner mitochondrial membrane — the directly observed structural correlate of the fusion defect in these patients. This node carries only what was measured in patient tissue; the cristae arm is modelled separately because it was NOT observed in these biopsies and because OPA1 fusion and cristae-shaping are genetically and molecularly distinct functions.

evidence.snippet: it controls the shape of mitochondrial cristae, keeping their junctions tight during apoptosis
evidence.explanation: Establishes that OPA1 shapes cristae and keeps cristae junctions tight. The claim reaches MTDPS14B by inference: this is general OPA1 cell biology rather than a finding in patient tissue.

evidence.snippet: we investigate the relationship between respiratory function and mitochondrial ultrastructure and provide evidence that cristae shape determines the assembly and stability of RCS and hence mitochondrial respiratory efficiency
evidence.explanation: Provides the general mechanistic link between cristae shape and respiratory chain supercomplex assembly. The step to MTDPS14B is an inference: this is general cell and mouse biology rather than patient data. The paper spans in vitro and in vivo (Opa1 mouse) arms, and this item is tagged for its cell-based arm.

steps/4.description: INFERRED NODE — not observed in MTDPS14B patient tissue. OPA1 oligomers spanning the intermembrane space and inner membrane keep cristae junctions tight, and cristae shape determines the assembly and stability of respiratory chain supercomplexes. Loss of OPA1 is therefore expected to disorganize cristae and destabilise supercomplexes, giving a second route from the OPA1 lesion to the measured respiratory chain deficiency alongside the mtDNA depletion arm. The evidence for this node is general OPA1 cell biology; no cristae abnormality was reported in the patient biopsies, whose only reported ultrastructural finding was incomplete inner-membrane fusion.

evidence.snippet: Mitochondrial respiratory chain complex activities were globally decreased in skeletal muscle biopsies.
evidence.explanation: Documents the combined respiratory chain deficiency in patient muscle.

evidence.snippet: This analysis revealed global decrease in all the respiratory chain complexes when normalised to CS activity in both patients, with complexes I and IV being the most affected
evidence.explanation: Specifies the complex I and IV predominance expected of an mtDNA maintenance defect.

steps/5.description: The convergent consequence of cristae disorganization and mtDNA depletion is a combined oxidative phosphorylation defect. Curators should not transfer phenotype or management claims between these allelic disorders: this entry is the recessive, cardioencephalomyopathic entity only. open_questions/0.rationale: The mouse models that exist bracket the human disease rather than model it. Homozygous Opa1 nulls die in utero, so they overshoot; heterozygous mice develop a cardiomyopathy only at 5 months, so they undershoot both the severity and the timing. The human allele is a destabilising missense change that must retain enough residual function to permit organogenesis and a year of postnatal life, and no model carrying it has been reported. Any claim that a mouse phenotype recapitulates the human infantile cardiomyopathy therefore rests on an unmodelled dose-response relationship.

open_questions/1.rationale: OMIM split the original MTDPS14 designation into 14A and 14B, both OPA1 disorders. MONDO:0014820 records no causal-gene relationship of its own, while MONDO:0980967 does — an asymmetry that makes automated gene-identity checks return SKIP for this entry. The published biallelic OPA1 spectrum is continuous rather than bimodal, and the single defining family for 14B is too small to establish whether cardiomyopathy is definitional or incidental. Until that is resolved, curators must anchor on OMIM:616896 rather than on the clinical label, and must not merge 14A material into this entry.

The mechanism differs from achondroplasia-type mutations that predominantly affect growth plate chondrocytes.

steps/3.description: The P250R FGFR3 receptor, with its altered ligand specificity, drives sustained MAPK/ERK signaling in osteoblast-lineage cells of the cranial suture. treatments/0.description: Surgical correction of craniosynostosis when indicated. Timing and approach depend on severity and uni- vs bilateral involvement. One operation is frequently not the end of it: in an operated craniosynostosis cohort, 58% of children with a single-gene cause required repeat craniofacial surgery, against 17% of those with a chromosomal cause. The authors read this as a mechanistic difference rather than a severity one — a mutation that continuously disrupts physiological signalling in the suture keeps driving fusion after the suture is released, whereas a chromosomal cause produces a more indolent, secondary craniosynostosis. For an FGFR gain-of-function disorder this makes reoperation an expected part of the course, and is a direct argument for the pharmacological suture-directed approaches now under investigation.
