genes/1.notes: NTRK2 encodes TRKB receptor. Less commonly involved in oncogenic fusions than NTRK1 or NTRK3. Found in various tumor types including gliomas.

evidence.snippet: NTRK gene fusions are sporadic genetic alterations that can occur across tumor entities.
evidence.explanation: Abstract notes NTRK gene fusions occur across tumor entities, supporting NTRK3 fusion involvement.

genes/2.notes: NTRK3 encodes TRKC receptor. ETV6-NTRK3 fusion is characteristic of secretory breast carcinoma (>90%) and infantile fibrosarcoma (>90%). Also found in other pediatric and adult tumors.

evidence.snippet: If NTRK gene fusions are detected, TRK inhibitors such as entrectinib and larotrectinib can be used regardless of the tumor entity.
evidence.explanation: Abstract states larotrectinib can be used when NTRK fusions are detected.

treatments/0.description: Highly selective TRK inhibitor approved for adult and pediatric solid tumors with NTRK gene fusions. Demonstrates remarkable efficacy across tumor types with overall response rate of approximately 75% and durable responses. First tumor-agnostic TRK inhibitor approval.

evidence.snippet: If NTRK gene fusions are detected, TRK inhibitors such as entrectinib and larotrectinib can be used regardless of the tumor entity.
evidence.explanation: Abstract states entrectinib can be used when NTRK fusions are detected.

treatments/1.description: TRK inhibitor with additional activity against ROS1 and ALK. Approved for NTRK fusion-positive solid tumors in adults and children. Penetrates CNS, providing activity against brain metastases.

treatments/2.description: Next-generation TRK inhibitor designed to overcome resistance mutations including solvent front mutations (G595R, G623R). Option for patients who progress on first-generation TRK inhibitors.

evidence.snippet: LMX1B haploinsufficiency causes Nail-patella syndrome (NPS; MIM 161200), characterized by nail dysplasia, absent/hypoplastic patellae, chronic kidney disease, and glaucoma.
evidence.explanation: States the human haploinsufficiency mechanism and the multiorgan phenotype it produces.

steps/1.description: Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in LMX1B (a LIM-homeodomain transcription factor on 9q33.3) reduce functional LMX1B dosage below a developmental threshold in every LMX1B-expressing lineage. Haploinsufficiency is the predominant mechanism (supported by whole-gene deletion phenocopies), though a subset of homeodomain missense alleles that abolish DNA binding can act by a dominant-negative mechanism. The reduced transcription-factor activity is the shared initiating lesion for the organ-specific branches below.

evidence.snippet: Although LMX1B is a developmental LIM-homeodomain transcription factor, it is expressed in post-natal life in the glomerular podocyte, suggesting a regulatory role in that cell.
evidence.explanation: Establishes LMX1B expression and regulatory role in the podocyte, the cell targeted in NPS nephropathy.

evidence.snippet: Our report establishes the importance of LMX1B in fully differentiated podocytes and argues that LMX1B is essential for the maintenance of an appropriately structured actin cytoskeleton in podocytes.
evidence.explanation: Shows LMX1B is required for maintenance of adult podocytes, relevant to progressive nephropathy.

steps/2.description: LMX1B is expressed in glomerular podocytes into postnatal life and is required to induce and maintain the podocyte differentiation program, including type IV collagen genes (COL4A3/COL4A4) and slit-diaphragm genes (NPHS2/podocin, CD2AP). Reduced LMX1B activity impairs this program and also the maintenance of the mature podocyte actin cytoskeleton.

evidence.snippet: LMX1B is emerging as a key transcription factor for normal mitochondrial function and its expression is much higher in TM3 cells than other limbal cells.
evidence.explanation: Grounds the trabecular meshwork branch in LMX1B-dependent TM cell biology.

steps/3.description: LMX1B is one of the most active transcription factors in the anterior-segment trabecular meshwork and is most highly expressed in the contractile, metabolically active TM3 cell subtype. In an Lmx1b homeodomain-variant (V265D) mouse model, TM3 cells show mitochondrial swelling with reduced cristae, implicating mitochondrial dysfunction in outflow failure.

evidence.snippet: Analyses of lmx1b mutant mice have revealed the role of Lmx1b in the development of mesencephalic dopaminergic neurons and the serotonergic system
evidence.explanation: Supports the monoaminergic developmental role underlying the neurologic/neuropsychiatric branch.

steps/4.description: LMX1B is required for the specification and maintenance of midbrain dopaminergic and hindbrain serotonergic neurons and for dorsal spinal cord sensory-relay interneurons. Reduced dosage is proposed to underlie the reduced pain/temperature sensation and the elevated ADHD/depressive symptomatology reported in NPS. This branch is the most inferential, resting largely on mouse neurodevelopmental biology with human correlation from a survey study.

evidence.snippet: Lmx1b is induced by Wnt7a from the dorsal ectoderm, and its expression is restricted to the dorsal mesoderm
evidence.explanation: Places LMX1B in the dorsalizing limb-patterning pathway whose failure underlies the skeletal tetrad.

steps/5.description: In the dorsal limb mesenchyme LMX1B is the master dorsalizing transcription factor (induced by Wnt7a from the dorsal ectoderm). Reduced dosage produces a partial "double-ventral" limb, manifesting as dysplasia of dorsal-derived structures: nails, patellae, elbows, and the iliac horns. In mice, complete loss yields symmetrical ventral-ventral autopods lacking nails and patellae.

evidence.snippet: patients with NPS show characteristic irregular thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, including deposits of bundles of striated type III collagen fibers in the lamina densa
evidence.explanation: Describes the pathognomonic GBM ultrastructural lesion produced by this mechanism.

steps/6.description: Reduced type IV collagen (alpha3/alpha4) deposition and podocyte dysfunction produce the characteristic ultrastructural GBM lesion of NPS: irregular ("moth-eaten") thickening with electron-lucent zones and deposits of fibrillar collagen. The filtration barrier defect causes proteinuria, hematuria, and, in a subset, FSGS-type glomerulosclerosis progressing to kidney failure.

evidence.snippet: Heterozygous Icst causes glaucomatous eye defects and is semi-lethal, probably due to kidney failure.
evidence.explanation: The dominant-negative Lmx1b allele produces glaucomatous eye disease, modeling the ocular outflow phenotype.

steps/7.description: Impaired aqueous-humor outflow through the dysfunctional trabecular meshwork raises intraocular pressure, the proximate driver of the open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension seen at increased frequency and younger age in NPS.

evidence.snippet: Nail-patella syndrome (NPS) encompasses the classic clinical tetrad of nail abnormalities, abnormal and unstable patella with knee abnormalities, limited elbow mobility, and iliac horns on radiographs.
evidence.explanation: Nail abnormalities are the first, defining element of the NPS tetrad.

steps/8.description: Nails may be absent, hypoplastic, or dystrophic; ridged, pitted, discolored, or split, following a radial-to-ulnar severity gradient (thumb most severe). A defining tetrad feature.

evidence.snippet: The patellae may be small, irregularly shaped, or absent.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes the patellar dysplasia (hypoplasia to aplasia) that defines the second tetrad feature.

steps/9.description: The patellae may be small, irregularly shaped, or absent, causing recurrent subluxation/dislocation, instability, and early osteoarthritis.

evidence.snippet: elbow dysplasia, often involving posterior subluxation of the radial head
evidence.explanation: Documents the radial-head component of NPS elbow dysplasia.

steps/10.description: Elbow dysplasia with limitation of extension, pronation and supination, cubitus valgus, antecubital pterygia, and posterior subluxation of the radial head.

evidence.snippet: Iliac horns are bilateral, conical, bony processes that project posteriorly and laterally from the central part of the iliac bones of the pelvis.
evidence.explanation: Defines the pathognomonic iliac-horn feature.

evidence.snippet: Although iliac horns are pathognomonic of NPS, they occur in only approximately 70% of individuals with NPS
evidence.explanation: Quantifies iliac-horn frequency.

steps/11.description: Bilateral conical bony processes projecting posteriorly and laterally from the ilia; asymptomatic and radiographically detected. Considered pathognomonic, present in about 70% of affected individuals.

evidence.snippet: Kidney involvement, first manifest as proteinuria with or without hematuria, occurs in 30%-50% of affected individuals; end-stage kidney disease occurs in up to 15% of affected individuals.
evidence.explanation: Gives the proteinuria frequency for NPS nephropathy.

steps/12.description: Kidney involvement first manifests as proteinuria with or without hematuria in 30-50% of affected individuals; may be intermittent, remit, or progress.

evidence.snippet: Kidney involvement, first manifest as proteinuria with or without hematuria, occurs in 30%-50% of affected individuals
evidence.explanation: Documents hematuria as part of NPS renal involvement.

steps/13.description: Microscopic hematuria may accompany proteinuria in NPS nephropathy.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in LMX1B cause nail-patella syndrome, characterized by dysplasia of the patellae, nails, and elbows and FSGS with specific ultrastructural lesions of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM).
evidence.explanation: Establishes the FSGS pattern of NPS renal disease.

steps/14.description: NPS nephropathy shows FSGS-pattern glomerulosclerosis on light microscopy with the characteristic ultrastructural GBM lesion; specific LMX1B homeodomain variants can cause isolated FSGS without extrarenal features.

evidence.snippet: end-stage kidney disease occurs in up to 15% of affected individuals
evidence.explanation: Quantifies progression to ESKD.

steps/15.description: A minority (up to ~15%) of affected individuals progress to end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis or transplantation.

evidence.snippet: Primary open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension occur at increased frequency and at a younger age than in the general population.
evidence.explanation: Documents open-angle glaucoma as an NPS feature.

steps/16.description: Primary open-angle glaucoma occurs at increased frequency and at a younger age than in the general population, warranting lifelong ophthalmologic surveillance.

evidence.snippet: Primary open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension occur at increased frequency and at a younger age than in the general population.
evidence.explanation: Documents ocular hypertension in NPS.

steps/17.description: Elevated intraocular pressure without established glaucomatous damage occurs at increased frequency in NPS.

evidence.snippet: education regarding reduced pain and temperature sensation to avoid burns and injuries
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management confirms reduced pain and temperature sensation as an NPS feature.

steps/18.description: Reduced pain and temperature sensation, attributed to failed development of dorsal spinal cord nociceptive-relay interneurons; a source of unrecognized burns and injury requiring patient education.

evidence.snippet: Elevated levels of DSM-IV-TR ADHD Inattentive symptoms were reported on the CAARS by 22% of the NPS sample.
evidence.explanation: Reports the ADHD symptom frequency in the surveyed NPS cohort.

steps/19.description: Elevated self-reported ADHD (inattentive) symptoms in adults with NPS, hypothesized to relate to LMX1B's role in monoaminergic neuron development. From a single case-control symptom-survey study; preliminary.

evidence.snippet: The BDI-II Total score was elevated for 40% of the NPS sample.
evidence.explanation: Reports the depressive-symptom frequency in the surveyed NPS cohort.

steps/20.description: Elevated depressive symptoms co-occurring with ADHD symptoms in adults with NPS; from the same case-control survey and considered preliminary.

evidence.snippet: Lmx1b is essential for the specification of dorsal limb fates at both the zeugopodal and autopodal level with prominent phenotypes including an absence of nails and patellae.
evidence.explanation: Targeted Lmx1b disruption in mice ties loss of LMX1B function directly to failed dorsal limb specification.

evidence.snippet: These data indicate that LMX1B directly regulates the coordinated expression of alpha 3(IV) and alpha 4(IV) collagen required for normal GBM morphogenesis and that its dysregulation in GBM contributes to the renal pathology and nephrosis in NPS.
evidence.explanation: Links reduced LMX1B activity to dysregulation of its podocyte transcriptional targets.

evidence.snippet: LMX1B is emerging as a key transcription factor for normal mitochondrial function and its expression is much higher in TM3 cells than other limbal cells.
evidence.explanation: Identifies LMX1B as an active transcription factor whose loss perturbs the trabecular meshwork.

evidence.snippet: Analyses of lmx1b mutant mice have revealed the role of Lmx1b in the development of mesencephalic dopaminergic neurons and the serotonergic system
evidence.explanation: Mouse data establish LMX1B's role in monoaminergic neuron development, the substrate for the neurologic branch.

evidence.snippet: In Lmx1b(-/-) mice, expression of both alpha(3)IV and alpha(4)IV collagen is strongly diminished in GBM, whereas that of alpha1, alpha2 and alpha5(IV) collagen is unchanged.
evidence.explanation: Loss of the podocyte transcriptional program reduces the collagen chains needed for a normal GBM.

evidence.snippet: Kidney involvement, first manifest as proteinuria with or without hematuria, occurs in 30%-50% of affected individuals
evidence.explanation: The GBM filtration-barrier defect manifests as proteinuria with or without hematuria.

evidence.snippet: A small minority (5-10%) of individuals with NPS develop nephrotic-range proteinuria as early as childhood or young adulthood and progress to end-stage kidney failure over variable periods of time.
evidence.explanation: A subset with progressive nephrotic-range proteinuria advances to end-stage kidney failure.

evidence.snippet: Mitochondria in TM cells of V265D/+ mice are swollen with a reduced cristae area, further supporting a role for mitochondrial dysfunction in the initiation of IOP elevation in these mice.
evidence.explanation: Links LMX1B-mutant trabecular meshwork mitochondrial dysfunction to the initiation of IOP elevation.

evidence.snippet: Primary open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension occur at increased frequency and at a younger age than in the general population.
evidence.explanation: Elevated intraocular pressure manifests as ocular hypertension and open-angle glaucoma.

evidence.snippet: We also report on two NPS patient families with normal LMX1B coding sequence, but with loss-of-function variations in the LARM1/2 region
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates loss-of-function LMX1B (including non-coding enhancer) variants as the cause of NPS in patient families.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with an LMX1B mutation located in the homeodomain showed significantly more frequent and higher values of proteinuria compared to subjects carrying mutations in the LIM domains.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the mutation-location genotype-phenotype correlation for nephropathy risk.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that Icst is a dominant-negative allele of Lmx1b. These findings indicate a reassessment of whether nail-patella syndrome is always haploinsufficient.
evidence.explanation: Documents that a homeodomain missense allele can act by a dominant-negative mechanism rather than pure haploinsufficiency.

evidence.snippet: we screened 73 additional unrelated families with FSGS and found mutations involving the same amino acid (R246) in 2 families
evidence.explanation: Supports the isolated LMX1B-associated (R246) nephropathy allelic phenotype without extrarenal features.

evidence.snippet: LMX1B | HGNC:6654 | nail-patella syndrome | MONDO:0008061 | AD | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the LMX1B-nail-patella syndrome gene-disease relationship as Definitive (autosomal dominant).

genes/0.notes: NPS is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in LMX1B (missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, whole/partial gene deletions, rare translocations/inversions, and non-coding LARM enhancer variants). Haploinsufficiency is the predominant mechanism, although some homeodomain missense alleles that abolish DNA binding may act dominant-negatively. Mutation location carries genotype-phenotype information for nephropathy: homeodomain variants confer a higher proteinuria risk than LIM-domain variants, whereas no clear correlation exists for extrarenal features. Specific homeodomain missense variants at residue R246 (R246Q/R246P) cause an allelic, isolated LMX1B-associated FSGS/nephropathy without the classic nail/skeletal/ocular features, so LMX1B belongs on hereditary-FSGS gene panels even absent NPS skeletal findings.

evidence.snippet: angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors to control blood pressure and possibly to slow progression of proteinuria
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends ACE inhibitors for NPS nephropathy.

evidence.snippet: Chronic use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs because of the detrimental effect on kidney function.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists chronic NSAIDs as an agent to avoid in NPS.

evidence.snippet: The risk of developing preeclampsia may be increased in pregnant women with NPS
evidence.explanation: Basis for intensified pregnancy monitoring and transition off ACE inhibitors.

treatments/0.description: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors (and/or angiotensin receptor blockers) are first-line to control blood pressure and slow progression of proteinuria in NPS nephropathy. Chronic NSAID use should be avoided because of its detrimental effect on kidney function; ACE inhibitors are switched to pregnancy-safe alternatives before or upon recognition of pregnancy, which is also a period of increased preeclampsia risk warranting close monitoring.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: RAAS blockade reduces intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria.

evidence.snippet: angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors to control blood pressure and possibly to slow progression of proteinuria; kidney transplantation as needed
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists kidney transplantation as needed for ESKD in NPS.

treatments/1.description: Kidney transplantation for end-stage kidney disease.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Renal replacement for NPS-associated kidney failure.

evidence.snippet: MRI of joints to identify abnormal anatomy is important prior to surgery so that appropriate surgical treatment can be planned in advance
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes the orthopedic surgical approach and pre-operative MRI.

treatments/2.description: Orthopedic surgery for patellar instability, elbow contracture, or scoliosis, with pre-operative MRI of joints to characterize the abnormal anatomy before surgical planning.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Surgical correction of patellar instability and other skeletal deformities.

evidence.snippet: Orthopedic problems may be helped by analgesics, physical therapy, splinting, bracing, or surgery
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists conservative orthopedic management.

treatments/3.description: Analgesics, physical therapy, splinting, and bracing for orthopedic problems and joint instability.

evidence.snippet: standard treatment for decreased bone mineral density, hypertension, constipation, inflammatory bowel disease, glaucoma, epilepsy, and dental anomalies
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews includes standard glaucoma treatment in NPS management.

treatments/4.description: Standard glaucoma treatment (topical IOP-lowering pharmacotherapy, with laser or surgery for refractory cases) following early and lifelong ophthalmologic surveillance.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: IOP-lowering therapy to prevent glaucomatous optic nerve damage.

open_questions/0.rationale: Human NPS is dominantly inherited and largely attributed to haploinsufficiency, yet heterozygous Lmx1b-null mice have no phenotype while a heterozygous dominant-negative allele (V265D) does. This divergence means the standard mouse null does not model the human heterozygous state, and it is unresolved which human variants act by simple dosage loss versus dominant-negative interference - a distinction with implications for genotype-based prognosis and therapy.

evidence.snippet: Whole exome sequencing identified novel compound heterozygous mutations in VARS that segregated with the proband: a missense (c.3192G>A; p.Met1064Ile) and a splice site mutation (c.1577-2A>G).
evidence.explanation: Documents the two-allele lesion, one missense and one splice-site, that constitutes the primary molecular defect.

evidence.snippet: we uncovered that p.T1068M is clustered with three other pathogenic mutations in a 15 amino acid long stretch of the VARS1 anticodon-binding domain
evidence.explanation: Establishes the positional clustering of a subset of pathogenic alleles within the anticodon-binding domain.

evidence.snippet: Two variants were predicted to induce premature protein truncation leading to loss of VARS1 function.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that the allelic series includes truncating as well as missense alleles.

steps/1.description: The primary lesion is damage to both copies of VARS1 at 6p21.33, reported against transcript NM_006295.2. The published allelic series is dominated by missense changes distributed across the aminoacylation (tRNA-synt_1) and anticodon-binding domains, with a minority of true null alleles - a canonical splice-acceptor change that triggers nonsense-mediated decay, and premature termination codons. Two positional observations are worth keeping apart. Hiz and colleagues showed that a quarter of reported variants cluster within a 15-residue helix-turn-helix stretch of the anticodon-binding domain, which suggests a shared structural failure mode for that subset; but Friedman and colleagues found reduced aminoacylation activity irrespective of where in the protein the variant fell. Position therefore explains how particular alleles fail, while the functional convergence is what defines the disorder.

evidence.snippet: cDNA analysis on patient derived fibroblasts revealed that the splice site acceptor variant allele led to nonsense mediated decay, thus resulting in a null allele.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that one allele is functionally absent through transcript decay.

evidence.snippet: Further quantitation of the expression of VARS showed remarkably reduced levels of mRNA and protein in skin derived fibroblasts.
evidence.explanation: Measures the reduction in enzyme abundance directly in patient-derived cells.

steps/2.description: In the family reported by Stephen and colleagues, the splice-acceptor allele was shown by cDNA analysis of patient fibroblasts to be degraded by nonsense-mediated decay - a true null - and quantitation showed markedly reduced VARS1 mRNA and protein in those cells. This is a loss of enzyme, not a loss of enzyme quality, and it is one of the two routes by which patient cells arrive at insufficient charging capacity.

evidence.snippet: Patient primary cells show intact VARS protein but reduced enzymatic activity, suggesting partial loss of function.
evidence.explanation: Separates the specific-activity defect from any change in enzyme abundance, in patient-derived cells.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, irrespective of where the mutation occurred, we found reduced aminoacylation activity, suggesting that transferase activity reflects both the ability to bind tRNA as well as transfer the charged valine to the tRNA.
evidence.explanation: The key functional-convergence observation: alleles in different domains all converge on reduced charging, which is what licenses treating charging capacity as the rate-limiting quantity.

evidence.snippet: Here, we propose that these clustered mutations can destabilize the interactions between the anticodon-binding and the tRNA synthetase domains and thus hindering the optimal enzymatic activity of VARS1.
evidence.explanation: Supplies a structural mechanism for the loss of specific activity in the anticodon-domain allele cluster; explicitly a proposal from modelling, not a measurement.

steps/3.description: The second and more commonly documented route. In the Friedman cohort, western blotting showed intact VARS1 protein in patient fibroblasts while the aminoacylation assay showed specifically reduced valylation activity, with leucyl- and arginyl-tRNA synthetase activities preserved in the same lysates - the internal control that makes this a ValRS-specific defect rather than a general sickness of the cells. Structural modelling supplies a mechanism for the anticodon-domain cluster: destabilised contacts between the anticodon-binding and catalytic domains impair the interdomain coordination needed for efficient tRNA charging without abolishing catalysis outright.

evidence.snippet: Aminoacylation experiments on patient derived cells showed markedly reduced enzyme activity of ValRS suggesting the mutations to be loss of function.
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of reduced valylation activity in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: VARS encodes the only known valine cytoplasmic-localized aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the absence of a cytoplasmic paralogue, which is why the deficit cannot be buffered.

evidence.snippet: In silico, in vitro, and yeast complementation assays demonstrate that the underlying pathomechanism of these mutations is most likely a loss of protein function.
evidence.explanation: Independent orthogonal assays in a second cohort reach the same loss-of-function conclusion.

steps/4.description: The convergence point of both upstream arms and the rate-limiting quantity of the disorder. Cytoplasmic ValRS is the only enzyme that charges valine onto tRNA-Val, so there is no cytoplasmic paralogue to buffer the deficit - VARS2, the mitochondrial enzyme, serves a separate tRNA pool in a separate compartment and does not compensate. Measured aminoacylation activity is reduced in patient fibroblasts across independent cohorts.

evidence.snippet: The VARS gene encodes cytoplasmic valyl-tRNA synthetase (ValRS), an enzyme that is essential during eukaryotic translation.
evidence.explanation: Supports the link from the enzyme to translation in principle. Marked PARTIAL because it states the enzyme's role in translation generally and does not measure translational output in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in ARSs have emerged as a cause of recessive, often complex neurological disease traits.
evidence.explanation: Places the disorder in the recessive ARS class whose shared premise this node encodes. PARTIAL because it is a class-level statement, not a VARS1 translation measurement.

steps/5.description: The threshold step, and the premise the whole ARS-deficiency family rests on: residual charging capacity is adequate for most cells most of the time, and becomes limiting only where and when protein-synthesis demand is highest. In this disorder that means the brain during its period of maximal growth - proliferating neural progenitors and newly post-mitotic neurons - which is why an enzyme expressed in every cell in the body produces a phenotype that is almost entirely neurological, and why carrier parents with one functional allele are unaffected.

evidence.snippet: Another clue is acquired microcephaly, in the range of minus 5 SDs, observed in all but one subjects after 6 months of age.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the head-size deficit is acquired postnatally rather than present from conception in most patients.

evidence.snippet: Zebrafish modeling accurately recapitulated some of the key neurological disease traits.
evidence.explanation: Model-organism support that loss of vars function is sufficient to impair brain development. Deliberately not used as evidence for the human cellular mechanism - see the HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH discussion.

steps/6.description: The organ-level reading of the translational ceiling. Head growth in most reported children is normal or near-normal at birth and then falls away, typically slowing by one year of age, so the microcephaly is characteristically acquired and progressive rather than congenital - although congenital microcephaly at the severe end has been reported. The cellular correlate has been observed in the zebrafish vars knockout rather than in human tissue.

evidence.snippet: The hemispheric white matter was intensely gliotic with minimal myelination but preserved axonal density, with a few sudanophilic histiocytes, consistent with a myelination disorder.
evidence.explanation: The load-bearing observation: myelin deficient, axons preserved, and the authors' own reading that this is a myelination disorder.

evidence.snippet: The MRI findings together with brain neuropathology from GB31-II-6 demonstrate that pathogenic variants in VARS also show particular predilection for the cerebral white matter.
evidence.explanation: States the white-matter predilection explicitly, tying the imaging and the autopsy together.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, hypomyelination or delayed myelination was reported in four patients.
evidence.explanation: Independent cohort giving the radiological frequency of the myelination defect.

steps/7.description: The single autopsy reported in the VARS1 literature is mechanistically load-bearing and is curated as its own node rather than folded into cortical volume loss. In the child from family GB31, hemispheric white matter was intensely gliotic with minimal myelination but PRESERVED AXONAL DENSITY, with no cavitation or necrosis. Preserved axons with deficient myelin is the signature of a myelination disorder, not of axonal degeneration - which matters because it points the deficit at the oligodendrocyte, a cell with an exceptionally high protein-synthesis burden during myelination and therefore exactly the cell type the translational-threshold model predicts should fail first. Radiologically the same arm shows as hypomyelination or delayed myelination, reported in four of ten patients by Siekierska and colleagues, and as reduced white-matter volume with a thin corpus callosum.

evidence.snippet: Longitudinal assessment demonstrates progressive cortical atrophy and white matter volume loss.
evidence.explanation: The founding longitudinal-imaging observation on which the "cortical atrophy" element of the disease name rests.

evidence.snippet: Side-by-side comparison demonstrated progressive loss of cerebral cortical volume, with collapse of subcortical white matter volume, evident on both axial and midline sagittal images.
evidence.explanation: Same-patient serial imaging, which is what distinguishes progression from a static deficit.

evidence.snippet: Progressive cortical atrophy, considered a hallmark of NDMSCA, was notably absent in several of our cases.
evidence.explanation: Recorded as PARTIAL rather than REFUTE: it does not deny that atrophy occurs in the patients who have it, it denies that atrophy is a required feature of the entity. Kept on the node so the node is not read as obligatory.

steps/8.description: The feature that names the disorder, and the one whose status is genuinely contested. Longitudinal imaging in the Friedman cohort - the same child scanned in infancy and again years later - demonstrated progressive loss of cerebral cortical volume with collapse of subcortical white matter, which is the strongest evidence that this is a degenerative process superimposed on a developmental one rather than a static malformation. Thinning of the corpus callosum, reduced white-matter volume, delayed myelination and cerebellar atrophy accompany it in a subset. But it is not obligatory: the 2026 series states that progressive cortical atrophy, though considered a hallmark, was absent in several of their cases, and the two siblings reported by Okur and colleagues had biallelic VARS1 variants with no cortical atrophy at all.

evidence.snippet: Subjects present with a range of global developmental delay, epileptic encephalopathy and primary or progressive microcephaly.
evidence.explanation: Establishes epileptic encephalopathy as a core presenting feature of the disorder.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, a VARS1 knockout zebrafish model mirrors key human disease characteristics, exhibiting microcephaly and epileptiform activity
evidence.explanation: Model-organism support that epileptiform activity follows from loss of vars function.

steps/9.description: Seizures begin early - days to months of life in most reported children - and are characteristically drug-refractory, with myoclonic, focal and generalised types, infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia in a subset, and multifocal epileptiform discharges on EEG. The proximate substrate is presumed to be the malformed and depleted cortical network of the preceding node rather than a direct effect of ValRS on neuronal excitability; no channel-level or synaptic mechanism has been proposed or tested for VARS1. The zebrafish knockout independently exhibits epileptiform activity, which is the only experimental support that the excitability phenotype follows from loss of the enzyme rather than from something incidental to the human genotypes.

evidence.snippet: Most patients assessed with age-appropriate testing had profound delayed psychomotor development or severe intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: States the severity of the developmental endpoint in the largest reported cohort.

evidence.snippet: In addition, we observed a milder and non-progressive clinical presentation of NDMSCA in two siblings (Subjects 8 and 9).
evidence.explanation: Documents the mild end of the spectrum, which prevents this node being read as uniformly profound.

steps/10.description: The clinical endpoint: profound global developmental delay and intellectual disability, absent or severely limited speech, axial hypotonia with limb hypertonia and brisk reflexes, extrapyramidal movements, feeding difficulty often requiring tube feeding, and, in the more severely affected, death in early childhood from respiratory complications. The severity spectrum is wide and is not yet explained by genotype: at one end are infants who never acquire milestones and die before three years, at the other the two siblings of the 2026 series with preserved speech, independent ambulation and a non-progressive course.

edges/4.description: The abundance arm. A splice-acceptor allele degraded by nonsense-mediated decay, or a premature termination codon, removes enzyme from the cell before any question of per-molecule catalytic competence arises.

edges/5.description: The catalytic arm. Missense alleles reduce the valylation rate of the enzyme that is present, independently of how much of it there is.

edges/6.description: Less enzyme present means less valine charged per unit time regardless of the intrinsic competence of each remaining molecule.

edges/7.description: A lower catalytic rate per enzyme molecule reduces the steady-state pool of charged tRNA-Val by the same final common route as reduced enzyme abundance.

edges/8.description: A smaller pool of charged tRNA-Val sets a ceiling on the rate at which the cytoplasmic ribosome can elongate valine-containing nascent chains.

edges/9.description: A translational ceiling during the period of maximal brain growth limits progenitor expansion and neuronal survival, which is the developmental arm of the phenotype.

edges/10.description: The parallel white-matter arm, drawn from the translational ceiling directly rather than through neuronal loss. The autopsy pattern is what forces this topology: myelin is deficient while axons are PRESERVED, so hypomyelination cannot be the end-stage of neuronal death. It is a sibling consequence, in the cell whose protein-synthesis burden during myelination is highest and which the threshold model therefore predicts should fail first.

edges/11.description: Where the process continues past the developmental window, the same translational insufficiency produces ongoing tissue loss rather than a static deficit.

edges/12.description: A malformed and depleted cortical network is the substrate on which the epileptic encephalopathy arises.

edges/13.description: Reduced brain growth is the structural correlate of the profound developmental delay and intellectual disability.

edges/14.description: Deficient myelin is a direct contributor to the reduced white-matter volume and thin corpus callosum seen on imaging, alongside any cortical neuronal loss.

edges/15.description: Continuing tissue loss converts a static developmental deficit into a progressive clinical course in the subset in whom it occurs.

edges/16.description: Refractory early-onset seizures compound the developmental impairment, which is what the term epileptic encephalopathy asserts.

evidence.snippet: Among the candidate genes identified, we found PRUNE, VARS, and DHX37 in multiple families and homozygous loss-of-function variants in AGBL2, SLC18A2, SMARCA1, UBQLN1, and CPLX1.
evidence.explanation: The original identification of VARS1 as a candidate disease gene in multiple families with neurogenetic disease. Recurrence across families is the genetic argument that first implicated the gene.

evidence.snippet: Here we report an allelic series consisting of seven novel and two previously reported biallelic variants in valyl-tRNA synthetase (VARS) in ten patients with a developmental encephalopathy with microcephaly, often associated with early-onset epilepsy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the allelic series and the biallelic gene-disease relationship in an independent multi-family cohort.

evidence.snippet: Together with prior reports, our results provide strong additional evidence supporting VARS1 as a recurrent cause of autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorders and expand the known clinical and allelic spectrum.
evidence.explanation: The most recent independent confirmation of the gene-disease relationship, with an expanded allelic spectrum.

genes/0.notes:
Nomenclature and identity. HGNC:12651 is symbol VARS1, "valyl-tRNA synthetase 1", Entrez 7407, Ensembl ENSG00000204394, UniProt P26640, EC 6.1.1.9, gene MIM 192150 (OAK, `runoak -i sqlite:obo:hgnc info hgnc:12651 -O obo`, 2026-08-18). The cytogenetic location 6p21.33 is not in the HGNC record OAK returns and comes separately from NCBI Gene 7407 (E-utilities esummary, 2026-08-18). The former approved symbol was VARS, which is how the gene appears in every paper before 2019 including all three founding clinical reports, and the protein is universally called ValRS. Do not confuse with VARS2 (the mitochondrial enzyme), a different gene in a different compartment causing a different disease.
Allelic series, as published. Karaca and colleagues first reported c.2653C>T (p.Leu885Phe) and c.3173G>A (p.Arg1058Gln) in two consanguineous families with epileptic encephalopathy, as part of a large exome study rather than a dedicated clinical report. Stephen and colleagues reported compound heterozygous c.3192G>A (p.Met1064Ile) with the splice-acceptor c.1577-2A>G in an Indian family. Friedman and colleagues reported five further biallelic missense genotypes in seven individuals from five families; Siekierska and colleagues reported an allelic series of seven novel plus two previously reported variants in ten patients. Okur and colleagues reported c.65C>A (p.Ala22Asp) with c.3214T>C (p.Phe1072Leu). Hiz and colleagues added p.Thr1068Met. The 2026 series added ten further novel variants, including the synonymous c.1893G>C (p.Leu631=) and the nonsense c.2370G>A (p.Trp790*).
Recurrent alleles matter for reading the literature: p.Phe1072Leu, p.Arg404Trp, p.Arg1058Gln and p.Thr1068Met each appear in more than one report, which is why the cohorts cannot simply be summed into a case count. Note also that the same residue can carry different substitutions with different severity - Arg404 is reported as both Trp and Gln - so allele-level rather than residue-level reasoning is required.

evidence.snippet: seizures were refractory to triple therapy with Valproate, Levetiracetam, and Clonazepam
evidence.explanation: Documents both the drugs used and the frequent failure of multi-drug regimens.

evidence.snippet: At 10 months the seizures were controlled on Vigabatrin monotherapy.
evidence.explanation: The counter-case - seizure control was achieved on monotherapy in the child presenting with infantile spasms, so "refractory" is not universal.

treatments/0.description: The mainstay of active management, and symptomatic only. Agents used across the reported cohorts include valproate, levetiracetam, clonazepam, phenobarbital, lorazepam, tiagabine and vigabatrin. Outcomes are mixed and are worth stating precisely rather than as a blanket "refractory": several children remained refractory despite two- or three-drug regimens, while others were well controlled - one on valproate alone and one, presenting with infantile spasms, on vigabatrin monotherapy. There is no VARS1-specific antiseizure protocol and no evidence that any agent is preferentially effective in this genotype; drug selection follows ordinary paediatric epileptic-encephalopathy practice, with vigabatrin's role in infantile spasms being the usual syndrome-based choice rather than anything VARS1-specific.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Antiseizure medication acts on the excitability of the surviving cortical network. It does not touch the upstream aminoacylation defect, which is why it is symptomatic rather than disease-modifying and why control of seizures does not arrest the developmental or atrophic course.

evidence.snippet: Supplementation with cognate amino acids was described in 21 patients, with beneficial effects (e.g., improvements in growth, development, liver and lung disease) in the majority.
evidence.explanation: PARTIAL: establishes benefit across the ARS1-deficiency class, from which VARS1 is not separately reported. It is class-level evidence being applied to a member.

evidence.snippet: Treatment did not alleviate the most severe phenotypes.
evidence.explanation: The limiting caveat from the same review, kept alongside the benefit claim so the treatment is not read as more promising than the source supports - NDMSCA sits at the severe end of the class.

evidence.snippet: Current treatment approaches to rescue defective or dysfunctional tRNA synthetase mutants include supplementation with cognate amino acids and delivery of cognate tRNAs to alleviate bottlenecks in translation.
evidence.explanation: States the mechanistic rationale for substrate supplementation. `evidence_source` is OTHER because this is a narrative review of approaches, not a study reporting its own data.

evidence.snippet: Overall, the treatment was safe and well tolerated by all patients, but efficacy endpoints were not met as no significant improvements were observed in global, cognitive, or motor scores.
evidence.explanation: The only prospective trial of the strategy. PARTIAL, and deliberately so: it tested MITOCHONDRIAL ARS deficiencies (AARS2, DARS2), a different subclass from cytoplasmic VARS1, in adults rather than infants. It bears on the strategy, not on this disease directly, and it tempers rather than supports the therapeutic claim.

treatments/1.description: The only mechanistically targeted therapy proposed for this disease class, and it is proposed rather than demonstrated for VARS1. The rationale is direct from the enzymology: if the residual enzyme is hypomorphic rather than absent, raising substrate concentration might drive more flux through it, so supplying the cognate amino acid - valine here - could partially restore charging. Cognate amino acid supplementation has been described in 21 patients across the recessive ARS1 deficiencies with benefit in the majority, but NOT, in any cached source, in a VARS1 patient. Two caveats belong with any use of this entry: the same review states that treatment did not alleviate the most severe phenotypes, and the one prospective trial - in mitochondrial AARS2/DARS2 leukoencephalopathy, a different ARS subclass - found supplementation safe but failed its efficacy endpoints.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Substrate supplementation is aimed at the charging reaction itself - raising intracellular valine to push a hypomorphic enzyme toward higher flux. This is the only proposed intervention in the entry that targets the primary defect rather than a downstream consequence, and it is untested in VARS1 disease.

evidence.snippet: Two patients had feeding problems requiring feeding tubes (one had percutan gastrostomy tube).
evidence.explanation: Documents the supportive intervention actually delivered in reported patients.

treatments/2.description: Nutritional support including gastrostomy feeding where feeding difficulty warrants it, physical and occupational therapy for the motor impairment, and management of respiratory complications - which are the reported proximate cause of death in the most severely affected children. This is the substance of care in practice and is recorded as such rather than left implicit.

evidence.snippet: Whole exome sequencing identified novel compound heterozygous mutations in VARS that segregated with the proband: a missense (c.3192G>A; p.Met1064Ile) and a splice site mutation (c.1577-2A>G).
evidence.explanation: Documents the biallelic segregation on which recurrence-risk counselling and cascade testing depend.

treatments/3.description: Autosomal recessive inheritance gives a 25% recurrence risk to subsequent pregnancies of a carrier couple, and several reported families are consanguineous, so cascade carrier testing has real yield. Once a biallelic genotype is established, prenatal testing and preimplantation genetic testing become available options. No source cached for this entry reports the use of preimplantation testing in a VARS1 family, so it is described as available in principle rather than as established practice.

evidence.snippet: suggesting that cortical atrophy is not a distinguishing feature of NDMSCA.
evidence.explanation: The explicit statement by the largest cohort's authors that the feature naming the disorder is not distinguishing, which is what makes this an open question rather than a settled one.

evidence.snippet: Although our patients have no history of seizures or cortical atrophy, we suggest that the biallelic variants in VARS p.Ala22Asp and p.Phe1072Leu in this family are likely pathogenic and associated with NDMSCA, expanding the clinical phenotype of the condition.
evidence.explanation: The independent report of biallelic VARS1 disease without cortical atrophy, in siblings old enough that late emergence is unlikely.

open_questions/0.rationale: The disorder is named for cortical atrophy, and the founding longitudinal imaging demonstrated it convincingly in the individuals who had it. But the two largest subsequent reports both push against it as a defining feature: Okur and colleagues described biallelic VARS1 disease with no seizures and no cortical atrophy at all in two siblings aged 10 and 15 - old enough that late emergence is unlikely - and the 2026 series states that progressive cortical atrophy, though considered a hallmark, was notably absent in several of their cases, reporting it in five of thirteen. Two readings are compatible with these data and they have different consequences. If atrophy is severity-dependent, it is a marker of where a genotype sits on the residual-activity spectrum and its absence is prognostically good news. If it is age-dependent, the mildly affected individuals are simply not old enough or not imaged late enough, and their families are being given false reassurance. Nothing in the literature distinguishes these, because no cohort has been imaged serially to a common endpoint - the Friedman progression data come from a handful of children, and the 2026 cohort has a median age at last examination of three years.

evidence.snippet: Complementary approaches use inhibitors to target the integrated stress response, which can be dysregulated in tRNA synthetase diseases.
evidence.explanation: Note the hedge in the source - "can be dysregulated" - which is exactly the point of this gap. The ISR is a candidate mediator across the class and a therapeutic rationale, not a demonstrated step in VARS1 disease. `evidence_source` is OTHER because this is a narrative review.

evidence.snippet: Skin punches were collected at a single timepoint from each patient studied here, then expanded and used for enzymatic analysis.
evidence.explanation: Documents that the functional measurements were made in skin-derived fibroblasts, which is the substance of this gap.

open_questions/1.rationale: No. Every functional measurement in the VARS1 literature - aminoacylation activity, VARS1 protein abundance, mRNA level - has been made in skin fibroblasts, a cell type with no reported phenotype in this disorder. The step from "reduced valylation in fibroblasts" to "insufficient translation capacity in developing neurons" is the load-bearing inference of the whole entry and it is unmeasured: no polysome or ribosome profiling, no nascent-chain labelling, and no measurement of charged-tRNA pools has been published in any VARS1-deficient neural system. The threshold model that explains why a housekeeping enzyme produces a brain-restricted phenotype therefore rests on the phenotype it is invoked to explain. This is also why the integrated stress response, which is the obvious candidate mediator downstream of uncharged tRNA accumulation and is the rationale for ISR-inhibitor therapy across the ARS class, is deliberately NOT curated as a pathophysiology node here - it has not been demonstrated in VARS1 disease.

evidence.snippet: Zebrafish modeling accurately recapitulated some of the key neurological disease traits.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both what the model achieves and its stated limit - "some of the key traits" - which is the starting point for asking what a hypomorphic knock-in would add.

evidence.snippet: Patient primary cells show intact VARS protein but reduced enzymatic activity, suggesting partial loss of function.
evidence.explanation: Documents that the human genotypes are partial loss of function, which is the mismatch with a complete knockout.

open_questions/2.rationale: The zebrafish model recapitulates microcephaly and epileptiform activity, and it is the strongest available evidence that these follow causally from loss of the enzyme. But it is a knockout, and the human allelic series contains no null-over-null genotype - every reported individual retains residual charging capacity, which is exactly what the threshold model predicts must be true for the pregnancy to be viable. The model therefore tests sufficiency of complete loss, not the biology of partial loss, and it cannot address the questions the clinic actually asks: why severity varies so widely between genotypes, why two siblings with the same condition can have a non-progressive course, or whether raising substrate helps a hypomorphic enzyme. A knockout has no residual enzyme for substrate to act on, so it cannot even in principle be used to test valine supplementation.

evidence.snippet: Treatment with cognate amino acids is promising, but it remains challenging to distinguish treatment effects from natural history.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own statement of the evidential problem that makes this an open question rather than a recommendation.

evidence.snippet: Overall, the treatment was safe and well tolerated by all patients, but efficacy endpoints were not met as no significant improvements were observed in global, cognitive, or motor scores.
evidence.explanation: The only prospective trial result available for the strategy, in an adjacent ARS subclass; it is what tempers the expectation.

open_questions/3.rationale: The rationale is mechanistically clean and the intervention is nutritional rather than pharmacological, so the risk profile is favourable - the one prospective trial of the strategy found it safe and well tolerated. But three things argue for caution before this is presented to families as a promising option. Supplementation has been described in only 21 patients across the whole ARS1 class, in uncontrolled settings where treatment effect cannot be separated from natural history. The same review states that treatment did not alleviate the most severe phenotypes, and NDMSCA sits at the severe end. And the only prospective trial - in mitochondrial AARS2 and DARS2 leukoencephalopathy, a different ARS subclass in adults - failed its efficacy endpoints, with patients remaining stable rather than improving. The honest position is that valine supplementation is the best available therapeutic idea for this disorder and is entirely untested in it.

evidence.snippet: We describe loss of function mutations in serpin peptidase inhibitor, clade F, member 1 (SERPINF1) in two affected members of this family and in an additional unrelated patient with OI type VI. SERPINF1 encodes pigment epithelium-derived factor.
evidence.explanation: Identifies biallelic SERPINF1 loss-of-function mutations encoding PEDF as the cause of OI type VI.

evidence.snippet: Collagen analyses with cultured dermal fibroblasts displayed no evidence for impaired collagen folding, posttranslational modification, or secretion.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that type I collagen is normal in SERPINF1-related OI, establishing a non-collagen disease mechanism distinct from OI types I-IV.

evidence.snippet: Two deletions (p.F277del and the deletion of SERPINF1 exon 5) were associated with retention of PEDF in the endoplasmic reticulum and a stress response in osteoblastic cells.
evidence.explanation: Shows that in-frame SERPINF1 variants cause ER retention of PEDF and an osteoblast ER stress response, an alternative route to PEDF deficiency.

evidence.snippet: We identified a 25-year-old woman with severe OI whose dermal fibroblasts and cultured osteoblasts displayed minimal secretion of PEDF, but whose serum PEDF level was in the normal range.
evidence.explanation: An IFITM5 (BRIL) mutation producing an OI type VI-like phenotype via impaired osteoblast PEDF secretion confirms reduced PEDF as the proximate cause of the OI type VI mineralization defect.

steps/1.description: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in SERPINF1 abolish secretion of pigment epithelium-derived factor (PEDF), a secreted serpin-family glycoprotein normally produced by osteoblasts and osteocytes. Most pathogenic alleles are truncating (nonsense/frameshift) and eliminate the protein; rarer in-frame deletions/insertions yield a misfolded PEDF that is retained in the endoplasmic reticulum, triggering a stress response in osteoblastic cells. Type I collagen is normal, distinguishing this from the collagen-related OI types.

evidence.snippet: OCL differentiation, RANKL-mediated survival and bone resorption activity were inhibited by PEDF in a dose-dependent manner. PEDF upregulated osteoprotegerin (OPG), which naturally blocks OCL maturation, in primary osteoblasts and OCL precursor cells.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that PEDF restrains osteoclast differentiation and resorption via OPG upregulation and RANKL inhibition; loss of PEDF therefore increases osteoclastic resorption.

evidence.snippet: The subgroup of patients with OI type VI are affected by an increased bone resorption, leading to the same symptoms as observed in patients with an impaired bone formation.
evidence.explanation: Clinically frames OI type VI as a disorder of increased bone resorption, the basis for anti-resorptive (denosumab) therapy.

steps/2.description: PEDF normally upregulates osteoprotegerin (OPG) in osteoblasts and directly inhibits RANKL-mediated osteoclast differentiation, survival, and resorptive activity. In its absence the OPG:RANKL balance shifts toward RANKL, driving osteoclast overactivation and increased bone resorption. This resorptive arm is the rationale for the efficacy of the anti-RANKL antibody denosumab in OI type VI, and it conforms to the conserved increased-osteoclastic-resorption pattern.

evidence.snippet: LTD cells synthesized Sclerostin, matrix extracellular phosphoglycoprotein (MEPE) and dentin matrix protein (DMP-1) and their synthesis was reduced by treatment with PEDF.
evidence.explanation: Shows PEDF suppresses osteocyte sclerostin (and MEPE, DMP-1); loss of PEDF therefore derepresses sclerostin and impairs Wnt-dependent bone formation.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that type VI OI is a moderate to severe form of brittle bone disease with accumulation of osteoid due to a mineralization defect, in the absence of a disturbance of mineral metabolism.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the defining lesion of OI type VI as osteoid accumulation from a matrix mineralization defect with normal systemic mineral metabolism.

evidence.snippet: quantitative bone histomorphometry in femurs of mature Pedf null mutants revealed reduced trabecular bone volume and the accumulation of unmineralized bone matrix.
evidence.explanation: The Pedf-null mouse recapitulates the human defect, showing accumulation of unmineralized bone matrix and reduced trabecular bone.

evidence.snippet: In this study, PEDF delivery increased trabecular bone volume/total volume by 52% in 6-mo-old PEDF-KO mice but not in wild-type mice.
evidence.explanation: Restoring PEDF rescues bone mass in the OI type VI mouse model, confirming PEDF deficiency as the driver of the bone phenotype and supporting PEDF replacement as a therapeutic strategy.

steps/3.description: PEDF suppresses osteocyte expression of sclerostin (SOST) and other osteocyte genes through ERK/GSK-3beta/beta-catenin signaling, supporting Wnt-dependent osteoblast function and orderly matrix mineralization. Without PEDF, sclerostin is derepressed and Wnt signaling is disturbed, osteoblasts fail to mineralize matrix normally, and unmineralized osteoid accumulates with a prolonged mineralization lag time. The disorganized lamellae produce the characteristic polarized-light "fish-scale" pattern.

evidence.snippet: Fractures were first documented between 4 and 18 months of age. Patients with OI type VI sustained more frequent fractures than patients with OI type IV.
evidence.explanation: Documents the post-natal onset and high fracture burden that define the clinical fragility of OI type VI.

evidence.snippet: Fractures of long bones and severe vertebral compression fractures with resulting deformities were observed as early as the first year of life in these individuals.
evidence.explanation: Documents long-bone fractures and severe vertebral compression fractures with deformity in SERPINF1-mutant OI type VI patients.

steps/4.description: The convergence of increased osteoclastic resorption and defective osteoblast matrix mineralization produces mechanically weak bone. Clinically this manifests as recurrent fractures beginning after the onset of weight-bearing, universal vertebral compression fractures, progressive long-bone deformity and bowing, kyphoscoliosis, and short stature.

edges/1.description: Loss of PEDF removes its upregulation of OPG and restraint of RANKL, increasing osteoclastic bone resorption.

edges/2.description: Loss of PEDF derepresses osteocyte sclerostin and disturbs Wnt-dependent osteoblast function and matrix mineralization.

edges/3.description: Excessive osteoclastic resorption reduces bone mass and contributes to fragility and fractures.

edges/4.description: Defective mineralization and excess unmineralized osteoid yield mechanically weak bone prone to fracture and deformity.

evidence.snippet: Hence, loss of pigment epithelium-derived factor function constitutes a novel mechanism for OI and shows its involvement in bone mineralization.
evidence.explanation: Establishes SERPINF1/PEDF loss of function as the causative mechanism of OI type VI.

evidence.snippet: A single homozygous truncating mutation, affecting SERPINF1 on chromosome 17p13.3, that was embedded into a homozygous stretch of 2.99 Mb remained.
evidence.explanation: Independent exome-sequencing identification of homozygous truncating SERPINF1 mutations at 17p13.3 in recessive OI.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in SERPINF1 (17p13.3), encoding pigment epithelium-derived factor (PEDF), cause OI type VI. Most are truncating (nonsense/frameshift) null alleles; rarer in-frame deletions/insertions cause ER retention of misfolded PEDF. SERPINF1-related OI is recessive with complete penetrance for biallelic null alleles.

evidence.snippet: We now present the results after 2 years of treatment and demonstrate a long term benefit as well as an increase of bone mineral density, a normalization of vertebral shape, an increase of mobility, and a reduced fracture rate.
evidence.explanation: Two-year clinical data show denosumab improves BMD, vertebral shape, mobility, and fracture rate in OI type VI.

evidence.snippet: After two years on denosumab, he presented with symptomatic hypercalcemia due to the denosumab-induced, hyper-resorptive rebound phenomenon.
evidence.explanation: Documents the denosumab rebound phenomenon (symptomatic hypercalcemia) in OI type VI and motivates the alternating long-acting bisphosphonate strategy to mitigate it.

treatments/0.description: Denosumab, a monoclonal antibody against RANKL, directly targets the increased osteoclastic bone resorption that drives OI type VI, and is the mechanism-directed treatment of choice. In children with OI type VI, two years of denosumab increased bone mineral density, normalized vertebral shape, improved mobility, and reduced fracture rate. The short-acting, reversible anti-resorptive effect carries a rebound risk: abrupt discontinuation or end-of-interval offset can cause hyper-resorptive rebound with symptomatic hypercalcemia, which can be mitigated by alternating denosumab with a long-acting bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid).

evidence.snippet: Patients with OI type VI are known to have a poor response to such a bisphosphonate treatment.
evidence.explanation: Documents the characteristically poor bisphosphonate response in OI type VI, motivating anti-RANKL therapy instead.

evidence.snippet: patients who received intravenous bisphosphonate treatment had an increase in lumbar spine areal bone mineral density, a higher final height z-score, and some reshaping of vertebral bodies
evidence.explanation: Long-term data show bisphosphonates produce only partial benefit (some BMD, height, and vertebral-shape improvement) in OI type VI, consistent with limited efficacy relative to anti-resorptive denosumab.

treatments/1.description: Intravenous bisphosphonates are standard for most OI types, but OI type VI responds poorly because the lesion is increased resorption acting on unmineralized osteoid rather than impaired bone formation; denosumab is preferred.

evidence.snippet: Fractures of long bones and severe vertebral compression fractures with resulting deformities were observed as early as the first year of life in these individuals.
evidence.explanation: The long-bone fractures and resulting deformities documented in OI type VI are the indication for intramedullary rodding and corrective orthopedic surgery.

treatments/2.description: Intramedullary (telescoping) rod fixation and corrective osteotomy stabilize and realign deformed, fracture-prone long bones; spinal stabilization may be needed for progressive kyphoscoliosis.

evidence.snippet: We now present the results after 2 years of treatment and demonstrate a long term benefit as well as an increase of bone mineral density, a normalization of vertebral shape, an increase of mobility, and a reduced fracture rate.
evidence.explanation: Improved mobility with treatment underscores the role of rehabilitation in preserving function in OI type VI.

treatments/3.description: Physiotherapy, safe strengthening and mobility training (including hydrotherapy to minimize fracture risk), and adaptive aids preserve function and mobility.

evidence.snippet: 22q13 genomic anomalies include terminal deletions of 22q13 (89 %), terminal deletions and interstitial duplications (9 %), and interstitial deletions (2 %).
evidence.explanation: The large PMS cohort shows that most cases are terminal 22q13 deletions.

evidence.snippet: The scientific literature suggests that up to 40% of individuals with PMS have kidney disorders, yet little research has been conducted on the renal system to assess candidate genes attributed to these disorders.
evidence.explanation: Review evidence supports renal anomalies as a deletion-region feature requiring candidate-gene assessment.

steps/0.description: Most Phelan-McDermid syndrome cases are terminal 22q13.3 deletions that include SHANK3 and variably remove adjacent genes. This contiguous-deletion branch explains why some non-neurological features, especially renal anomalies, are enriched in deletion cases but not clearly attributable to SHANK3 point mutations alone.

evidence.snippet: Almost all of these deletions include the gene SHANK3 which encodes a scaffold protein in the postsynaptic densities of excitatory synapses, connecting membrane-bound receptors to the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence.explanation: Phelan and McDermid's comprehensive review establishes SHANK3's role as a postsynaptic scaffold protein and its centrality to PMS neurological features.

evidence.snippet: Our analysis therefore supports haploinsufficiency of the gene SHANK3, which codes for a structural protein of the postsynaptic density, as a major causative factor in the neurological symptoms of 22q13 deletion syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Wilson et al. found that all 45 testable patients were deleted for SHANK3, supporting its role as the critical gene.

evidence.snippet: ProSAP2 is a good candidate for this syndrome, because it is preferentially expressed in the cerebral cortex and the cerebellum and encodes a scaffold protein involved in the postsynaptic density of excitatory synapses.
evidence.explanation: First paper linking SHANK3 (ProSAP2) disruption to 22q13.3 deletion syndrome, via a balanced translocation that disrupted the gene.

steps/1.description: SHANK3 is a master scaffolding protein at the postsynaptic density of glutamatergic synapses. It connects membrane-bound receptors including NMDA and AMPA receptors to the actin cytoskeleton. Loss of one copy of SHANK3 is the primary molecular lesion underlying core neurological features of Phelan-McDermid syndrome.

steps/2.description: SHANK3 deficiency reduces postsynaptic scaffold organization at glutamatergic synapses, producing fewer structurally mature excitatory synapses and impaired glutamate receptor localization.

evidence.snippet: We show that PMDS neurons have reduced SHANK3 expression and major defects in excitatory, but not inhibitory, synaptic transmission.
evidence.explanation: Shcheglovitov et al. used iPSC-derived neurons from PMS patients to demonstrate selective excitatory synaptic deficits, providing direct human cellular evidence for E/I imbalance.

evidence.snippet: Cellular, electrophysiological and biochemical analyses uncovered defects at striatal synapses and cortico-striatal circuits in Shank3 mutant mice.
evidence.explanation: Peca et al. showed cortico-striatal circuit defects in Shank3 knockout mice, supporting disrupted neural circuit function.

steps/3.description: Loss of SHANK3 disrupts the balance between excitatory glutamatergic and inhibitory GABAergic signaling. iPSC-derived neurons from PMS patients show major defects in excitatory but not inhibitory synaptic transmission, with reduced AMPA- and NMDA-mediated currents and fewer excitatory synapses, while inhibitory transmission remains intact.

evidence.snippet: Clinical presentations included features of bipolar disorder, catatonia, psychosis, and loss of skills
evidence.explanation: Kolevzon et al. systematically reviewed 56 PMS cases with neuropsychiatric decompensation, establishing the pattern of late-onset psychiatric features.

steps/4.description: A subset of individuals with PMS experience significant neuropsychiatric deterioration beginning in adolescence or adulthood, with features of bipolar disorder, catatonia, psychosis, and progressive loss of previously acquired skills. Mean age of onset is approximately 20 years. The underlying mechanisms are not fully understood but may involve age-dependent vulnerability of SHANK3-deficient neural circuits.

evidence.snippet: this syndrome is characterized by neurological deficits which include global developmental delay, moderate to severe intellectual impairment, absent or severely delayed speech, and neonatal hypotonia
evidence.explanation: Phelan and McDermid's review identifies global developmental delay as a core neurological feature of PMS.

steps/5.description: Most individuals with PMS show significant global developmental delay apparent in the first year of life, affecting motor, cognitive, and language milestones.

evidence.snippet: only five (19%) used some words spontaneously to communicate
evidence.explanation: Soorya et al. prospectively evaluated 32 PMS patients and found that only 19% used any spontaneous words, confirming severe speech impairment as a hallmark.

evidence.snippet: all patients showed some degree of mental retardation and severe delay or absence of expressive speech, regardless of deletion size
evidence.explanation: Wilson et al. found universal speech delay/absence across all deletion sizes in 56 patients.

steps/6.description: Absent or severely delayed expressive language is a hallmark feature. In prospective evaluation, only 19% of patients used some words spontaneously to communicate.

evidence.snippet: Most patients (77%) exhibited severe to profound intellectual disability
evidence.explanation: Soorya et al. prospectively assessed cognitive function in 32 PMS patients and found the majority had severe to profound intellectual disability.

steps/7.description: Moderate to profound intellectual disability is present in the majority of individuals with PMS. In prospective studies, 77% exhibited severe to profound intellectual disability.

evidence.snippet: this syndrome is characterized by neurological deficits which include global developmental delay, moderate to severe intellectual impairment, absent or severely delayed speech, and neonatal hypotonia
evidence.explanation: Neonatal hypotonia is listed as one of the four core neurological features in the definitive PMS review.

steps/8.description: Hypotonia is frequently the first clinical sign, often noted at birth or in early infancy, and contributes to feeding difficulties and delayed motor milestones.

evidence.snippet: The sample was characterized by high rates of autism spectrum disorder: 27 (84%) met criteria for autism spectrum disorder and 24 (75%) for autistic disorder.
evidence.explanation: Soorya et al. used ADOS and ADI-R gold-standard instruments to establish a high ASD prevalence in PMS.

evidence.snippet: more than 50% of patients show autism or autistic-like behavior, and therefore it can be classified as a syndromic form of autism spectrum disorders (ASD)
evidence.explanation: Phelan and McDermid noted >50% ASD prevalence across >600 documented cases.

steps/9.description: A high proportion of individuals with PMS meet diagnostic criteria for autism spectrum disorder. In prospective evaluation with gold-standard instruments, 84% met criteria for ASD and 75% for autistic disorder.

evidence.snippet: the proportion reporting an autism spectrum disorder, seizures, and cellulitis, or presenting with lymphedema or abnormal reflexes increased with age
evidence.explanation: Sarasua et al. documented increasing seizure prevalence with age in 201 PMS patients.

evidence.snippet: Seizures were reported three times more often among patients with a de novo deletion of the maternal rather than paternal chromosome 22.
evidence.explanation: Parent-of-origin effect on seizure susceptibility in PMS, with maternal deletions conferring higher risk.

steps/1.description: PPCD-associated genes encode transcription factors that regulate cell-state transitions and converge on ZEB1. ZEB1 (PPCD3) loss-of-function causes haploinsufficiency that derepresses epithelial genes. OVOL2 (PPCD1) and GRHL2 (PPCD4) are EMT-suppressing factors that directly repress ZEB1 and are normally absent from the corneal endothelium; PPCD mutations cause their ectopic expression. Transcriptomic and immunohistochemical studies of PPCD endothelium show decreased ZEB1, increased OVOL2/GRHL2, and aberrant activation of the Wnt signaling pathway (nuclear accumulation of phospho-beta-catenin), consistent with a shared GRHL2-OVOL2-ZEB1 axis disturbance.

steps/2.description: The central, convergent mechanism of PPCD. Normal corneal endothelial cells are post-mitotic, neural-crest-derived cells with a hexagonal monolayer morphology. In PPCD, the endothelium undergoes metaplasia toward an epithelial-like phenotype, acquiring epithelial morphology, epithelial gene expression (E-cadherin, cytokeratin 7), microvilli, and an aberrant proliferative/migratory behavior. These cells can overgrow the trabecular meshwork and iris. The cell-state switch reflects dysregulation of the ZEB1 EMT axis: ZEB1 normally maintains the mesenchymal/endothelial state by repressing epithelial genes, while OVOL2 and GRHL2 are EMT-suppressing transcription factors that repress ZEB1 and drive mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET). Loss of ZEB1 (PPCD3) or ectopic activation of OVOL2 (PPCD1) or GRHL2 (PPCD4) all push the endothelium toward the epithelial state, explaining the indistinguishable phenotypes.

steps/3.description: The transdifferentiated, epithelial-like endothelium produces an abnormal, thickened, multilaminar basement membrane (Descemet membrane) with posterior collagenous layers. In ZEB1-related PPCD, loss of ZEB1 transcriptional repression leads to ectopic expression of basement-membrane collagen COL4A3 (collagen type IV alpha 3) by corneal endothelial cells, a target shared with the Alport syndrome COL4A3 gene. This aberrant matrix underlies the characteristic vesicular, band-like, and geographic opacities at the level of Descemet membrane seen clinically.

evidence.explanation: Natural-history data support progressive acuity decline in RPGR cone/cone-rod disease.

evidence.explanation: This RPGR cohort paper explicitly names rod-cone dystrophy among RPGR outcomes.

evidence.explanation: This RPGR family study supports macular atrophy as an RPGR-related retinal degeneration phenotype.

evidence.explanation: The RPGR ORF15 cone-rod dystrophy families showed photophobia as part of the phenotype.

evidence.explanation: The RPGR splice-variant series reports color vision disturbance in most affected patients.

evidence.snippet: Retinitis pigmentosa GTPase regulator (RPGR) gene sequence variants account for the vast majority of X linked retinitis pigmentosa (RP), which is one of the most severe forms of RP.
evidence.explanation: This review supports RPGR as the principal causal gene in the X-linked RP branch of the family.

evidence.snippet: Variants in the X-linked retinitis pigmentosa GTPase regulator gene (RPGR) and, specifically, in its retinal opening reading frame-15 isoform (RPGRORF15) may cause rod-cone (RCD), cone, and cone-rod dystrophies (CDs and CRDs).
evidence.explanation: This natural-history study supports RPGR, especially RPGRORF15, as the shared causal gene across multiple subtype branches.

evidence.snippet: RPGR | HGNC:10295 | RPGR-related retinopathy | MONDO:0100437 | XL | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the RPGR-RPGR-related retinopathy gene-disease relationship as definitive with X-linked inheritance.

genes/0.notes: Pathogenic RPGR variants, especially in RPGRORF15, unify the rod-cone, cone-rod, and cone-dominant branches within a single ciliary disease family.

evidence.snippet: Recent advances have been made in animal models using subretinal RPGR-mediated gene therapy, which has shown an increase in structural and functional survival of photoreceptors
evidence.explanation: Preclinical animal-model data show subretinal RPGR gene augmentation improves photoreceptor structural and functional survival.

evidence.snippet: phase I/II/III clinical trials are currently ongoing (NCT03252847, NCT03116113 and NCT03316560)
evidence.explanation: This review reports that human RPGR gene-therapy trials across phases are ongoing, confirming clinical translation of retinal gene augmentation.

treatments/0.description: Subretinal delivery of an adeno-associated viral vector carrying a functional RPGRORF15 coding sequence aims to restore connecting-cilium trafficking and slow photoreceptor degeneration. Retinal gene augmentation has advanced from animal models into human phase I/II/III clinical trials and is expected to benefit most when applied before inner-retinal remodeling.

evidence.snippet: The questioning of patients and family made it possible to retrieve an history of castor seeds or castor oil ingestion
evidence.explanation: Establishes castor seed ingestion as the exposure history recovered across the collected human cases.

evidence.snippet: Intoxication was mostly accidental (37 cases).
evidence.explanation: Supports the claim that this exposure is usually accidental.

evidence.snippet: The pathogenesis of ricin toxicity following inhalation has been investigated in many animal models, including the non-human primate (predominantly the rhesus macaque), pig, rabbit and rodent.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that this route's evidence base is animal models, which is why every phenotype downstream of it is graded MODEL_ORGANISM.

evidence.snippet: in recent years, several terrorist attempts to utilize weaponized ricin delivered by sharp or explosive devices were planned
evidence.explanation: Establishes the delivery modes this exposure describes.

evidence.snippet: it is considered to be a high-risk chemical for living beings under the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons1 and is also classified as a Category B biological agent by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention2
evidence.explanation: Source for the regulatory status asserted in the disease description. Quoted verbatim including the trailing superscript reference markers the source text carries.

evidence.snippet: post-mortem examinations in a single well-known case involving the assassination of Georgi Markov, suggested that cardiac arrest due to necrosis of the cardiac conducting tissue may be the direct cause of death
evidence.explanation: The one well-documented human instance of this route, and what its autopsy suggested. Quoted as the hypothesis the source states it to be.

evidence.snippet: Exposure to ricin can occur by oral ingestion, inhalation or parenteral intoxication, while the features and severity of ricin toxicity vary markedly with the route of exposure.
